encodingDesc.p: Single supplied OCR witness. Source wording retained, including unresolved OCR and editorial readings that differ from Ihm; this is not a proofread transcription. Running heads, marginal line/citation digits and signatures are removed from the Latin display. Hyphenation within pages is joined mechanically. Duplicate scans 33, 34 and damaged 70 are excluded in favor of 35, 36 and 72. Archive and inventory record all exclusions. Chapter and section navigation follows Ihm (perseus-lat2); source commentary section headings remain in the text. No missing Latin is supplied from Ihm. Critical apparatus is preserved separately by source page in the Latin back matter, without guessed lemma attachment.

OCR word-break hyphens were removed in a subsequent editorial cleanup; genuine compound hyphens were retained. Cross-page words and three interfering marginal-number/signature cases were repaired. Exact changes are recorded in hyphen-cleanup.json; original OCR and pre-cleanup XML remain archived.

Commentary paragraphs have been recovered from OCR line openings that repeat Latin words/phrases. Supported lemmas are marked mentioned linked by ana to a note type="commentary" with bold highlighting and section-level corresp to Butler–Cary Latin. Elliptical, inflected and abbreviated lemmas are preserved as written. The markup identifies discussed wording, not an exact word-offset alignment. Candidate matches in running prose were rejected on contextual review; lemma-review.json records decisions.

Recognized literal author/work references are encoded as bibl with citedRange; abbreviated wording and OCR numbering are preserved without invented expansions or external identifiers. Immediate semicolon-separated numeric continuations point back to the explicit reference. Quoted English glosses following lemmas are marked gloss.

The Sidgwick Aeschylus commentary is the structural model: mentioned/@ana links to note[@type="commentary"]/@xml:id; gloss marks translations; cit[@type="textual"] groups verified bibl/quote pairs. No external CTS identifiers are invented for unresolved abbreviations. This pass marks 19 reviewed source-quotation pairs; other quotations require further review.

div.p: § 1. annum sextum decimum. According to Suetonius, Caesar 8,1 was born in 100 B. C. (see 86. 1). The date is therefore 85-84 B. C. See p. xiv on the year of Caesar's birth.

p.note: . C. Iulius Caesar, brother of Sextus Caesar (cos. 91 B. C.; see C. I. L. (ed. 2) i, pp. 27, 152). He is probably to be identified with the C. Iulius Caesar of C. I. L. (ed. 2) i, p. 199, who was Xvir stlitibus iudicandis, quaestor, praetor, and governor of Asia with the title of pro consule. He died at Pisae (Plin. 7. 181).

. In 84 B. C. according to Suetonius. This accords with Velleius Paterculus (2. 43. 1), who describes him as paene puer, and with Plutarch (Caes. I. Ι οὔπω πάνυ μειράκιον ὤν). But it conflicts with Velleius' further statement a Mario Cinnaque creatus, which would make the date 86 B. C. See p. xv. This priesthood to which he was thus early appointed was of a very primitive character. The flamen Dialis was priest of Jupiter and was subject to a vast number of strange taboos, some of which would have been most inconvenient to Caesar, if taken seriously; e. g. he might not ride on horseback, or set eyes on an army, or pass the night outside his own house (Gell. 10. 15. 3, 4; Liv. 5. 52. 13). It was essential that he should be married, and he might not divorce his wife (Gell. 10. 15. 23), while if his wife died he automatically ceased to be flamen (Gell. 10. 15. 23). Hence the divorce of Cossutia and his marriage to Cornelia must both have preceded his appointment. This priesthood was taken from him by Sulla (1. 2) and not restored (Vell. Pat. 2. 43. 1).

. Nothing further is known of her. dimissa = 'divorced'. It would be natural to take it as meaning no more than that the engagement was broken off. But Plutarch (Caes. 53) speaks of Pompeia as Caesar's third wife, which shows that he regarded Cossutia as the first wife. dimittere is commonly used in this sense. Cp. Suet. Aug. 62. I Claudiam dimisit intactam. Cp. also Deutsch, Class. Philol., 1917, pp. 93-6.

: The toga praetexta was worn by boys till they assumed the toga virilis, a ceremony which normally took place between the ages of 14 and 17 (rarely later or earlier; see Marquardt, Privatleben, i, pp. 28 sqq.). Marriage, though theoretically legal at the age of puberty, did not take place till puberty was publicly acknowledged by the assumption of the toga virilis. See Marquardt, 1. c.

, 'betrothed'; she could not have married a praetextatus, though apparently she married him as soon as it was legal. (A rare word, first found in Vell. Pat. 2. 65. 2, and not again before Suetonius: common, however, in later Latin.)
. For her career cp. 21; 26. 1. Cp. also Plut. Caes. 5. 3.

. See Vell. Pat. 2. 41. 2 (where he contrasts Caesar's refusal with Piso's compliance); Plut. Caes. I. I. As regards the date, seeing that Sulla was dictator from 82-79 B. C. and that the events of ch. 1. 2-3 must have taken at least one or two years and were all anterior to Sulla's death in 78 B. C., Caesar's refusal probably belongs to 82-81 В. С.

div.p: § 2. gentiliciis hereditatibus. While for all practical purposes here this means no more than his 'family estates', the gens as a whole had an interest in the property of each individual member, me for 'according to the rules of regular intestate succession, in default of the suus heres, property lapses to the proximus agnatus and then to the gentiles. . as a whole, for there is no proximus gentilis' (Greenidge, Roman Public Life, p. 15).

p.note: . Plutarch (Caes. 1. 2) speaks of 'ill-health' only. For Caesar's health see 45. 1; but anybody might get malaria.

. Cp. Plut. Caes. 1. 2 (Caesar hid a long time in the Sabine country, fell into the hands of Sullan soldiers, and only escaped by bribing their commander, Cornelius); cp. Suet. 74. I Cornelius Phagites. For similar adventures of Marius and Crassus cp. Plut. Mar. 36-46 and Crass. 4-5.

. For similar intervention on the part of the Vestals cp. Cic. Font. 46; Suet. Tib. 2. 4; Vit. 16; Tac. A. 11. 32; H. 3. 81. Their presence conferred the right of sanctuary; see Marquardt, Staatsverw. iii, pp. 323 sqq.

. C. Aurelius Cotta, brother of Caesar's mother Aurelia ; exiled in 91 B. C. by the Variana quaestio (Cic. de Or. 3. 3. 11), returned with Sulla (Cic. Brut. 311) and became consul in 75 B. C. (C. I. L. (ed. 2) i, p. 154); a good orator (Cic. Brut. 202-10).

div.p: § 3. Caesari multos Marios inesse. For this mot see Plut. Caes. I (where it is placed with less probability before Caesar's flight). Cp. 45. 3 for another utterance of Sulla probably delivered on the same occasion. Sulla was less bloodthirsty than his agents (Vell. Pat. 2. 41. 2 magis ministris Sullae quam ipso conquirentibus eum ad neсет).

p.note: . Military service was a necessary qualification for office (Plut. Pomp. 22. 4); but it is uncertain whether in the first century B. C. a fixed period of service was prescribed (Mommsen, Staatsr. (ed. 3) i, pp. 510-12). Plutarch makes Caesar's service in the East take place immediately after his escape from Sulla, i. e. not later than 79 B. C. The same date is given by the reference to the siege of Mitylene (below). Mithridates had been conquered in 81 B. C. (App. Mithr. 6). Mitylene refused to submit to Rome; cp. Liv. Epit. 89. The date of the siege must have been 80-79 В. С.

. Marcus Minucius Thermus. Cp. Aurel. Vict. 78 contubernalis Thermo in Asiam profectus. Scarcely perhaps the same Thermus who was left in Asia by Flaccus as propraetor and deprived of his command by Fimbria in 86 B. C., as that Thermus was a Marian and is unlikely now to have been conducting operations during the dictatorship of Sulla. Still, men have been known to change sides, and Fimbria may have converted him into a Sullan! praetoris = strictly pro praetore; cp. Cat. 10. 10; Tac. Α. 1.74; 4.43; and below 7. 1.

. The word implies that he was living in Thermus' quarters, and is the regular term used to describe the relations between a commander and his aide-de-camp. Cp. Cic. Planc. 27-8; Cael. 73; also below 42. I.

. Presumably to get ships from Nicomedes to assist in the siege of Mytilene. Α Γάϊος Ιούλιος is mentioned as a Roman envoy to Gythium at some time shortly before 71 B. C. (Dittenberger, Sylloge, 3rd ed., no. 748, 1. 23). According to Drumann-Groebe (Gesch. Roms. iii, pp. 128-9) this was Julius Caesar. In this case his mission to Laconia was no doubt for the same purpose as the mission to Nicomedes.
. Nicomedes III Philopator (91-74 B. C.), allied with Rome against Mithridates (App. Mithr. 11-20. 60).
. Such is the spelling on coins and the majority of inscriptions. But the form Mitylene is found in literature and some inscriptions.

. A crown of oak-leaves, usually given ob cives servatos (Gell. 5. 6. 11). Appian (2.106) states that some of Caesar's statues showed the oak-wreath ὡς σωτῆρι τῆς πατρίδος; this finds some confirmation in the corona querna of Augustus, Tiberius, etc., but no other author mentions it in the case of Caesar. For its bestowal on Caesar at Mitylene cp. Luc. I. 358.

. Cos. 79. For the details of the campaign of Servilius against the pirates cp. H. A. Ormerod (J. R. S. xii, pp. 35 sqq., and Piracy in the Ancient World, pp. 213 sqq.), who holds that Servilius was on this service from 78 to 74 B. C. and got to work in 77 B. C. Caesar's stay with Servilius must belong to 78 B. C., since he returned to Rome Sullae morte comperta (d. 78 в. с.). M. Lepidum... diffisus. M. Aemilius Lepidus, cos. 78 B. C., with Q. Lutatius Catulus, attempted to repeal the laws of Sulla and was overthrown by Pompey and Catulus in the battle of the Campus Martius; cp. Plut. Pomp. 16; App. 1. 107; Livy, Epit. 90. For his character cp. Licinianus, 36 fin. erat natura turbulentus et inquietus; also Or. Philippi in Sall. H. 1. 77; R. Holmes, R. R. i. 363-9.
, 'less promising than he expected'.

div.p: § 1. Cornelium Dolabellam. There were two of this name: (i) cos. 81 B. C. and afterwards procos. of Macedonia (Cic. Pis. 44); (ii) praetor 81 B. C.; propraetor of Cilicia. It is to (i) that this passage refers (cp. Ascon., p. 26, Clark). For Caesar's speech cp. 55. 1; Plut. Caes. 4. 1; Val. Max. 8. 9.3; Vell. Pat. 2. 43. 3 (nobilissima accusatio); Gell. 4. 16. 8; Cic. Brut. 317. Dolabella was defended by Cotta and Hortensius. The trial took place in 77 В. С. Note that Suetonius makes no mention of Caesar's prosecution of C. Antonius in 76 B. C. (Ascon., p. 84, Cl.; Plut. l. c.).

p.note: . For extortion under the lex Cornelia of Sulla (cp. Cic. Rab. Post. 8).

. The date appears to have been late in 75 B. C. (hibernis mensibus). For Caesar accused C. Antonius at Rome in 76 B. c. (Drumann-Groebe, iii, p. 130, n. 4). This is borne out by Velleius (2. 41-2), who, while he says no more of the adventure with the pirates than that it took place after his escape from Sulla, states that after Caesar had captured the pirates he went to Iunius, governor of Asia and Bithynia. Now Bithynia was left to Rome by Nicomedes in his will early in 74 B. C. (see Marquardt, Staatsverw. (ed. 2), i. 349, n. 8). Plutarch (Caes. 2. 2) states that after his escape from Sulla Caesar went to Bithynia and was captured on leaving. After his capture of the pirates he went to Iuncus, governor of Asia, to get authority for punishing the pirates. He then went to Rhodes en route for Rome, and on his return home accused Dolabella. This would place his adventure with the pirates in

div.p: 78 B. C. But Iuncus was almost certainly governor of Asia and Bithynia in 74 B. C., and identical with the lunius of Velleius (Nipperdey would read luncus in that passage). See note on supplicio (4. 2).

p.note: . The same Molon who taught Cicero (Cic. Brut. 312, 316; Plut. Cic. 4. 2); he held a middle position between the Asiatic and Attic schools (Susemihl, Gesch. der Alex. Lit. ii. 489-93). For Caesar's gifts as an orator see ch. 55.
. Off Caria to the SW. of Miletus. Polyaenus *(8. 23. 1) makes this take place off Cape Malea; but Plutarch (Caes. 2. 2) confirms Suetonius and says that Caesar went to Miletus for his ransom.

. See H. A. Ormerod, Piracy in the Ancient World (especially ch. 6). Cp. also Cic. Leg. Man. 32-5; Dio 36. 20-3; Plut. Pomp. 24. It is not surprising to find that Caesar supported the lex Gabinia (Plut. Pomp. 25. 3), which resulted in the suppression of the pirates by Pompey; for many years they had virtually held the command of the seas.
. Presumably a slave or freedman.
, 'valets'.

div.p: § 2. quinquaginta talentis. So, too, Val. Max. 6. 9. 15. Plutarch, however, represents this as being Caesar's offer in answer to the pirates' demand for 20 talents, which is not incredible; cp. Ormerod (op. cit., p. 32, n. 6) for the story of a Spanish grandee who objected to being rated at no more than 100 piastres! The ransom was obtained at Miletus (Plut. Caes. 2. 2) by public subscription (Vell. Pat. 2. 42). (Plutarch (Crass. 7. 6) says that Crassus' good nature was inexhaustible, however provoking Pompey and Caesar might be, 'although Caesar, on his capture by pirates in Asia, exclaimed "Crassus, how delighted you will be to hear of my capture". A cryptic remark which, perhaps, means no more than that Caesar was heavily in Crassus' debt, and the likelihood of those debts ever being paid was now remote. The remark is obviously ironical.)

p.note: , 'on the spot'.

. From Miletus (Plut. Caes. 2. 2) on his own authority (Vell. Pat. 2. 42. 2). Whether such requisitions were legal is scarcely relevant to the present passage, but cp. the new inscription from Delphi in Suppl. Epigr. Gr. i. 161, which places a general responsibility on all the dwellers on the coast for the prevention of piratic depredations (the passages cited by Ormerod (op. cit., p. 55) do not seem to bear on this point). Polyaenus (8. 23. 1) tells a more romantic story (reminiscent of the capture of the brigands in Apul. Met. 7. 5 sqq.) of casks containing swords and drugged wine, brought by a trusty slave from Miletus.
. See note on Rhodum above. Velleius (2.42. 2) states that Caesar went to Iunius, governor of Bithynia and Asia;

div.p: he wished to sell the pirates and sent a dispatch to that effect, but Caesar anticipated him and crucified them. Plutarch (Caes. 2. 2) says that Caesar recovered his ransom, locked the pirates up in Pergamum, approached Iuncus, governor of Asia; Iuncus reserved the case, whereupon Caesar returned to Pergamum and crucified them (see note on 74. 1). For Iuncus cp. the fragment of Caesar's speech pro Bithynis, preserved by Gellius (5. 13. 6): vel pro hospitio regis Nicomedis vel pro horum necessitate quorum res agitur refugere hoc munus, M. Iunce, non potui. nam neque hominum morte memoria deleri debet, quin a proximis retineatur, neque clientes sine summa infamia deseri possunt, quibus etiam a propinquis nostris opem ferre instituimus. Nicomedes is evidently dead, and Iuncus is presumably governor of Bithynia (74 В. С.). M. Iuncus was not improbably M. lunius Juncus; cp. the M. Iunius Juncus of C. I. L. vi. 3837. In that case there is no need to emend Junius to luncus in Velleius. (It is to be noted that M. Iunius Silanus, governor of Asia 76-75 B. C. (see Münzer, Pauly-Wiss. i, col. 1095), cannot have been in charge of Bithynia. He Bithynia appears to have been succeeded by M. Iuncus 75-74 (during the opening months in charge of Bithynia as well). Note also that the older texts of Plutarch wrongly state that Caesar went to Iunius not Iuncus.)

p.note: . Cp. Plut. Caes. 2. 2.
. At the beginning of the third Mithridatic war. Little is known of Mithridates' movements, except along the shores of the Propontis, and the scene of Caesar's exploit cannot be traced.
. Used loosely in the sense of provincials, without special reference to the civitates liberae ac foederatae.

. The auxilia of this period would be a rude militia (Cheesman, Auxilia of the Roman Empire, pp. 10-11). If Caesar's father was, as seems probable, once governor of Asia, the success of his son in raising troops on his own initiative is more easily explained.

. Twenty-four tribuni militum were appointed annually in the comitia tributa (Sall. Iug. 63. 4). The tribunate was not at this date an essential preliminary to the holding of high honours, but was often held by young nobles or equites. See Marquardt, Staatsverw. (ed. 2) ii, pp. 364 sqq. For Caesar's election see Plut. Caes. 5. I (elected over the head of a certain C. Pompilius). The date is probably 73 B. C. There is no record of Caesar being in Asia after Lucullus took over the command in the summer of 74 B. C.
. The power of the tr. pl.

div.p: had been crippled by the reforms of Sulla. Agitations for its restoration had been led by C. Aurelius Cotta (Caesar's maternal uncle) in 75 B. C. (Ascon., p. 78, Cl.); by L. Quinctius in 74 B. C. (Plut. Luc. 5. 7; Sall. H. 3. 48, §§ 12-13); and by Licinius Macer in 73 B. C. (Sall. H. 3. 48. 21). Caesar's activity on behalf of the tribunicial power on this occasion would seem to have been primarily in connexion with the agitation of 73 B. C., but is likely enough to have extended to the time of its restoration in the consulship of Pompey (70 в.с.).

p.note: . L. Cornelius Cinna, suspected subsequently, though without sufficient ground, of being an accomplice in Caesar's assassination; praetor in 44 B. C. (see ch. 85).

. Lepidus died of disease (Plut. Pomp. 16.4; App. 1. 107; Flor. 2. 11. 7); Liv. Epit. 90 merely says periit. He did not long survive his defeat in the battle on the Campus Martius. See note on M. Lepidum in ch. 3.
. Sertorius held out for the Marian cause in Spain 77-73 B. C. The final surrender of his followers did not probably take place till 72 B. C. (R. Holmes, R. R. i, p. 384).

. Cp. Sall. H. 3. 47; Dio 44. 47. 4. This law de reditu Lepidanorum is probably distinct from the lex Plotia de vi (see Botsford, Rom. Assemblies, p. 424; R. Holmes, R. R. i, pp. 385-6; Pais, Ricerche, iii, pp. 377-80). As regards the date Greenidge and Clay (pp. 206-7), Botsford (p. 413, n. 4), and R. Holmes suggest 73 or 72 B. C. On the whole 72 B. C. is more likely. The most suitable moment for the law would be after the collapse of the Sertorian army, which contained many of the associates of Lepidus. (The reference to iudiciorum perturbationes, restitutio damnatorum, etc., in Cic. Leg. Agr. 2. 10 seems to be a hit at this law.)
. An informal speech before the popular assembly (Botsford, op. cit., pp. 139-51). For the speech see Gell. 13. 3. 5, where a few words are quoted.

div.p: § 1. quaestor. This office makes him a senator. The date is uncertain. See 7. I aetate and 8 consules . . . retinuissent, notes.

p.note: . The widow of Marius (Plut. Mar. 6. 3). The imagines of Marius were displayed on this occasion (Plut. Caes. 5. 1).

. On laudationes (funeral orations) in general see Schanz, Gesch. R. Litt. i, § 19. Plutarch (Caes. 5. 1-2) states that laudationes for old women were common, but that a laudatio over a young wife was a novelty. For an exquisite laudatio of a wife cp. the famous laudatio Turiae (C. I. L. vi. 1527).

. Through Marcia the wife of Caesar's grandfather C. Iulius Caesar. Cp. the head of Ancus Marcius on the coins of the triumvir C. Marcius Censorinus (87 B. C.); Grueber, Coins R. Rep. in B. M. i, p. 301. Cp. M. Aurelius' descent from Numa (Scr. Hist. Aug. M. Ant. Phil. 1. 6).

. Grandmother of Iulus, founder of the gens Iulia. The head of Venus is shown on Caesar's coins. See Grueber, op. cit. i, pp. 543-52; ii, p. 469, and pls. 54-5; with Anchises, ii, p. 469, and pl. 110, no. 20. Cp. also Dittenberger, Sylloge (ed. 3), 760 τὸν ἀπὸ ᾿Αρεως καὶ ᾿Αφροδίτης θεὸν ἐπιφανῆ (Ephesus 48 B. C.). For the temple of Venus Genetrix cp. 61. I n. For other divine pedigrees cp. Plut. Ant. 4. I Hercules); Suet. Galb. 2 Jupiter and Pasiphae); L. Mamilius (head of Ulysses on coins-Grueber, i, pp. 97, 343); also G. F. Hill, Hist. Rom. Coins, pl. 11, nos. 58-9.

div.p: § 2. Pompeiam duxit. Suetonius implies that this took place before he went to Spain. Plutarch dates the marriage after his return (Caes. 5. 3). Either date is possible; it may be noted that Suetonius is not strictly chronological. Q. Pompei. Q. Pompeius Rufus, cos. 88 (Liv. Epit. 77; Plut. Sull. 8. 6; App. 1. 56); son-in-law of Sulla (Vell. Pat. 2. 18); relationship to Pompey the Great unknown. P. Clodio. See 74. 1. For the story of the intrigue and Clodius' sacrilege at the rites of the Bona Dea in the house of Caesar see Cic. Att. 1. 12-16; Fam. 1.9; Plut. Caes. 9-10; Dio 37. 45-6. A detailed account of the scandal in Drumann-Groebe, ii, pp. 176 sqq.

§ 1. obvenit. Sc. sorte. Though occasionally quaestors were assigned to special duties by superior magistrates (e. g. Liv. 30. 33; Cic. Att. 6. 6. 4), sortitio was the normal method of allotting quaestors to the various provinciae quaestoriae ; cp. Cic. Verr. 2. 1. 34; Phil. 2. 50. praetoris = pro praetore (cp. 2. 1). C. Antistius Vetus (Vell. Pat. 2. 43. 4; Plut. Caes. 5. 3). The date is not known, but see below on Alexandri imagine.

p.note: . Cp. note on conventibus in ch. 56. 3. For the delegation of an assize-district to a subordinate cp. Cic. Att. 5. 21. 6 (Q. Volusius vice Cicero in Cyprus); Div. in Caec. 56 (Lilybaeum). For his behaviour as quaestor cp. Vell. Pat. 2. 43. 4 praetura quaesturaque mirabili virtute atque industria obita in Hispania.

. For Gades (Cadiz) as an assize town see Plin. 3. 7 iuridici conventus ei quattuor, Gaditanus Cordubensis Astigitanus Hispalensis (Baetica in the 1st cent. A. D.). Gades later received the franchise from Caesar (Liv. Epit. 110; Dio 41. 24. 1).
. Probably originally a temple of Melkarth, the Punic Hercules. Cp. the Herakleion at Tyre (Herod. 2. 44. 1).

. Plutarch (Caes. II. 3) and Dio (37. 52. 2) both record this incident as occurring in Caesar's praetorship. But the story has more point if Caesar were approximately the same age as Alexander after his conquests in the East, than if he were several years older as he would be in 61-60 B. C. Plutarch says that he read about Alexander in a book. But there is no reason to doubt the story about the image. Gades had a Greek element in its population (see Cary, J. H. S., 1924, pp. 171-2). Cp. also Julian, Symp. 320-6 (Caesar and Alexander contend περὶ πρωτείων before Jupiter).

. Alexander was born in 356 B. C., returned to Babylon in 325 B. C., and died in 323 B. C. The quaestorship could not be held before the age of 30 (Mommsen, Staatsr. (ed. 3) i, pp. 570-1). The lower limit for Caesar's quaestorship is 68 B. C. (3 years before holding the aedileship), the upper is 72 or 70 B. C. according to the view held concerning Caesar's birth (102 or 100 B. C.). See p. xiv. See also note on 8 consules...retinuissent.
. Cp. Marius' demand for release in Sall. Iug. 64. Conversely, Cicero made his quaestor stay on in Cilicia after his departure (50 B. C.); see Att. 6. 6. 3.

div.p: § 2. somnio. So, too, Dio 37.52.2. Plutarch, however (Caes. 32. 4), makes the dream take place at Ravenna in Jan., 49 B. C. Cp. Hippias' dream before Marathon (Herod. 6. 107. 1).

p.note: . For the status of the Transpadanes, dating from the close of the Social War, cp. Hardy, Problems in Rom. Hist., pp. 43-54. For Caesar's interest in them cp. Suet. 9. 3; Sall. Cat. 49. 2 (Caesar attacks C. Piso for his government of Gallia Cisalpina); Dio 41. 36. 3 (Caesar gives them the franchise by the lex Roscia).

. This statement is rejected by Hardy (loc. cit.). It is not improbable that it comes from the same sources as the stories in the ensuing chapter. Transpadane Gaul was at any rate a district that could provide fine fighting-men at a pinch, as the frequency of Caesar's levies of troops at a later date suggest (B. G. I. 24; 7. 1. 1; B. C. 3.87.4; Cic. Att. 7. 7. 6).
. Probably a reference to Marcius Rex (cos. 68 B. C.), who went to Cilicia in the same year (Dio 36. 15. 1). In that case Caesar must have left Spain in the spring of 68 B. C.

div.p: § 1. aedilitatem. 65 B. C. Plut. Caes. 5.4; Dio 37.8.1; Caes. В. С. 3. 16. 3. For the plot mentioned below, which was to have E 2
been carried out on Jan. I, see p. xviii. For Caesar's record as aedile see ch. 10. He had held the post of curator viae Appiae prior to the aedileship (Plut. l. c.).

p.note: . Cos. with Pompey in 70 В. С. For Caesar's financial and political relations with Crassus see 4.2 quinquaginta talentis; II. I Aegyptus; 13. I aeris alieni; 18. I sponsorum; 19. 2 Crassum reconciliavit. The shows mentioned in to were probably beyond Caesar's unaided credit, and a connexion with Crassus att his date is probable enough. P. Sulla. P. Cornelius Sulla, nephew of the dictator Sulla. He was at a later date accused of complicity in the Catilinarian conspiracy of 63 B. C. and defended by Cicero in 62 B. C. (Cic. Pro Sulla). Cicero disproves his connexion with that conspiracy, but fails to clear him of complicity in the earlier conspiracy of 65 B. C. For the plot of Sulla and Autronius see p. xix; also Sall. Cat. 17-18. Sulla was legatus of Caesar in the campaign of 48 B. C. (Caes. B. C. 3. 51, 89, 99).

. His name was Publius, not Lucius; see Dittenberger, Sylloge (ed. 3), no. 748, 11. 23-4; so, too, Sall. Cat. 18. 2, etc. He was involved in the plot of 63 B. C. (Sall. Cat. 17.3; 47. 1; 48. 7), was accused before a quaestio (presumably de vi) in 62 B. C. and condemned (Cic. Sull. 6. 18-20).

. Elected consuls in 66 в. с. (for 65 B. C.), they were condemned, and L. Cotta and L. Torquatus were elected consuls in their place (Cic. Sull. I and passim; Sall. Cat. 18. 2; Liv. Epit. 101; Dio 36.44.3; 37.25.3).
. Under the lex Calpurnia of 67 B. C., which prescribed as penalties for illegal canvassing (i) a fine, (ii) permanent exclusion from office and the senate. See Greenidge, Legal Procedure, p. 425.
. On Jan. I.

. Sallust (Cat. 18) states that the consuls were to have been attacked on Jan. 1, the senate in the attack on Feb. 5 (the original scheme having been postponed). But Cicero (Sull. 68), Livy (Epit. 101) and Dio (36. 44. 3) only mention the design against the consuls. It is true that Cicero (Tog. Cand. Ascon., p. 92, Cl.) speaks of caedem optimatum and again (Muren. 81) of the 'massacre of the senate'. These passages, however, may be mere embroideries, and the story as given by Sallust may be a compromise.
. The dictatorship had become unpopular and had not been employed since the third century, save rei publicae constituendae causa (cp. constituta ad arbitrium re publica below).

div.p: § 2. Tanusius. An obscure annalist of the close of the Republic; mentioned by Seneca (Ep. 93. 11), and perhaps to be identified with the Gabinius of Strabo (17.3.8, p. 829) and probably with the Ganysius or Tanysius of Plutarch (Caes. 22. 3).

p.note: . C. Scribonius Curio, cos. 76 B. C., a distinguished orator and the author of a dialogue in which he denounced Caesar for his conduct in Gaul, although the imaginary date of the dialogue was in Caesar's consulate of 59 B. C.; see Cic. Brut. 210-19. For specimens of his abuse of Caesar see 49. I and 52. 3.
. A wealthy senator (Cic. Att. 1. 12. 1; 3.15.3; 4.15.5). Cicero wrote two books of letters to him (Nonius 509, 1. 20), but all of these are lost. For Cicero on Caesar see p. xiv, n. 1.
, 'did not appear on the day'. Cp. Cic. Fam. 10. 25. 2 multi .. annum petitionis suae non obierunt. •

div.p: § 3. Actorius Naso. Gossip is cited from him in 52. 1; he is otherwise unknown.

p.note: . A prominent figure in the plot of 65 B. C. in which he was to play the part of bravo (Cic. Tog. Cand. Ascon., pp. 92-3, Cl.; Muren. 81; Sall. Cat. 18-19); see p. xviii. As regards his mission to Spain, Sallust (Cat. 19. 1) says that he was sent to Spain with the support of Crassus; but there is otherwise no evidence for the statements of Actorius. (Cp. also C. I. L. (ed. 1) i, no. 598).

. A Ligurian tribe identical with the Ambrones of Plut. Mar. 19. 7 and Dio 44. 42. 4. See Deutsch, Class. Phil. (1921), pp. 256-9. It is possible that Ambronas (C. Barth) or Ambrones (Beroaldus) may be the correct reading.
. Cp. 8 n.
. He was killed in a mutiny of Spanish cavalry in Spain (Sall. Cat. 19). Dio (36.44. 5) says, however, that he was killed by natives in Spain.

div.p: § 1. comitium...forum. For games in the comitium cp. Liv. 27. 36.8; in the forum Suet. Caes. 39. 1; Aug. 43. 1; Tib. 7. 1; Liv. 25. 30. 15. basilicas. Public halls on the north side of the Forum on either side of the comitium; the Basilica Porcia, built 184 B. C., and the Basilica Fulvia et Aemilia, built 179 B. C. (see Platner, Topog. Rome, pp. 194-9 and 230).

p.note: . At the Megalesia (April) and Ludi Romani (Sept.); see Dio 37. 8. 1. For venationes in general see Friedlaender (Eng. Tr.) ii. 62-74; for ludi cp. ibid. 2. 19-40. For the sumptuousness of Caesar's displays cp. Plut. Caes. 5.4; App. 2. I. I. Plutarch (Caes. 4. 2) and Appian opian (1. (1. c.) point out that Caesar had always been liberal with his money; cp. also Sall. Cat. 54. 2.

div.p: M. Bibulus. His colleague in the aedileship, praetorship (Caes. B. C. 3. 16. 3), and in the consulship (cp. 19. 1; 20. 2, etc., below). For the mot of Bibulus here cited cp. Dio 37. 8. 2.

p.note: . The temple stood on the south side of the Forum and was built in 484 B. C. The present remains belong to Tiberius' reconstruction in A. D. 6 (Suet. Tib. 20). See Platner, Topog. Rome, pp. 180-3.

div.p: §2. gladiatorium munus. Cp. Friedlaender (Eng. Tr., ii, pp. 41-62). For this gladiatorial show cp. Plut. Caes. 5.4 (320 pairs); Plin. 33. 53 (silver equipment); Dio 37. 8. I (in memory of Caesar's father). There were restrictions imposed upon such shows soon afterwards, the lex Tullia of 63 B. C. prescribing that no shows might be given within two years of candidature for office (Cic. Sest. 133; Vat. 37); in 22 B. C. a law was passed limiting the display to 120 pairs of gladiators (Dio 54.2.4). Here, however, Suetonius indicates executive action, such as an edict of the consul or praetor urbanus, based on a senatus consultum, which restricted Caesar's plans.
§ 1. Aegyptus. Crassus as censor made an abortive attempt in 65 B. C. to get Egypt annexed (Plut. Cr. 13. 2; Cic. Leg. Agr. 2. 44). Caesar was presumably acting as his agent in the matter.

p.note: . Suetonius is mistaken; the senate did not give Ptolemy this title till 59 B. C. (Caes. B. C. 3. 107. 2). This was the regular term for a dependent king. See E. Matthaei, Cl. Q., i, pp. 182-204; P. C. Sands, Client Princes of the Roman People, Part I.
. Another error. This did not take place till 58 or 57 B. C. (Cic. Fam. 1. 1-7; Q. F. 2. 3. 2; Dio 39. 12-16).
. Especially Catulus, Crassus' colleague in the censorship (Plut. loc. cit.), and Cicero (de Reg. Alex. 3. 1, ed. Baiter and Keyser, xi, pp. 32-3).

. For Caesar's connexion with Marius see 6. I (note on Juliam amitam). For this incident cp. Vell. Pat. 2. 43. 4 (adversante nobilitate); Plut. Caes. 6. 1-2 (his opponents accuse him of attempting to establish a tyrannis). For the tropaea cp. Propert. 3. 11. 46 statuas inter et arma Mari.

. This quaestio was established by Sulla (Dig. 48. 8.1; Cic. Rosc. Am. 11). Caesar as ex-aedile would be president of the quaestio (64 B. C.; Ascon., pp. 90-1, Cl.). Suetonius does not mention that Caesar got Catiline acquitted, when prosecuted in this court by the optimates by way of stultifying Caesar (Ascon., 1. c.; Dio 37. 10. 3).
. Cp. Lex Iulia Municipalis 122 (in a list of persons disqualified from sitting on municipal senates) queive

div.p: ob caput Romani referundum pecuniam praemium aliudve quod cepit ceperit.

p.note: . It is not clear whether this implies special legislation or refers to Sulla's generic law de Proscriptione, of which clauses are cited in Cic. Verr. 2. 1. 123; Rosc. Am. 126. Strachan-Davidson (Problems of R. Crim. Law, ii, p. 34) suggests that Caesar considered the exemption of Sulla's agents cancelled by Sulla's statute de vi (or rather de sicariis). It is hard to suppose that Caesar seriously took this view; but it might well have been used as a debating point.

. For this affair see especially Dio 37. 26. 8 and Cicero's speech pro Rabirio (63 в. с.). Caesar made use of the tribune Labienus to accuse Rabirius under the ancient and virtually obsolete form of trial by duumviri perduellionis, the institution of which is described by Livy (1. 26). Many difficult problems are involved in the story of the trial. But this much seems clear, that (i) the duumviral court was constituted by a rogatio, (ii) the court pronounced Rabirius guilty, (iii) the case was re-heard. The main cruces as regards the procedure are: (i) Wasthe duumviral court anything more than a court of first instance, a sort of Grand Jury? (ii) Was the final trial an appeal or a trial de novo? (iii) In the latter case, how was the sentence of the duumviri quashed? Dio (37.27. 3) states that the assembly was dissolved by the action of the praetor Metellus in lowering the red flag on the Janiculum, which he did because the Comitia were clearly going to condemn the accused. Suetonius, however, at the end of this chapter clearly implies that Rabirius was acquitted. See Hardy, Problems of R. Hist., ch. 1; R. Holmes, R. R. i, pp. 452-5; Meyer, Caesars Monarchie (2nd ed.), pp. 549-63; Strachan-Davidson, op. cit. i, pp. 188-204; Heitland's edition of Cicero, Pro Rabirio, Introd. (the ancient authorities cited in full). The evidence is not sufficient to warrant any definite conclusion.
. Actually thirty-seven years. Rabirius denied having killed Saturninus (Cic. Rab. 18).

. Dio (37.27. 2) says that Iulius and Lucius were chosen by the praetor, presumably the praetor urbanus. But the praetor urbanus, Metellus Celer, was a staunch optimate and would hardly have chosen Julius Caesar if he could have avoided it. On the other hand, if recourse was had to the lot, there was probably collusion. (Hardy (loc. cit.) suggests that the choice was pure luck and against Caesar's will.)
. Hardy suggests that the duumviral court was a mere Grand Jury or 'chose to consider itself as such'. This scarcely squares with tradition.
. Dio (l. c.) states that Rabirius, as a result of this

div.p: appeal, was tried before the comitia centuriata, where he was defended by Hortensius and Cicero. Meyer accepts this view; Hardy and R. Holmes hold that there was a trial de integro.

p.note: . The allusion may be merely to his designs on Egypt (11), or may refer generally to his hopes for the future.

. On the death of Metellus Pius (Dio 37.37. 1). Caesar was an ordinary pontifex since 73 B. C. (Vell. Pat. 2. 43. 3). Sulla's reformed constitution prescribed co-optation as the method of appointment, but the tribune Labienus on Caesar's behalf prescribed election by seventeen tribes (a re-enactment of the law of Domitius Ahenobarbus, 104 B. C. Cp. Dio (loc. cit.); Cic. Leg. Agr. 2. 16-18; Vell. Pat. 2. 12. 3; Suet. Ner. 2.) The office was restricted to patricians, and the tenure was for life (App. 5. 131). Caesar presumably sought the office rather for the prestige and financial advantages which it conveyed than for any political value that control of all religious observances may possess. The date is uncertain. Plutarch (Caes. 7. 1) is vague, but mentions it, like Suetonius, between the restoration of the Tropaea Mari and the Catilinarian conspiracy. Sallust definitely places it before the Catilinarian conspiracy (Cat. 49. 2), while Dio puts it after the plot (37.37.1, 2). The earlier date is the more probable. The title of Pontifex maximus is frequent in inscriptions relating to Caesar and (as in the case of his successors) occurs frequently on his coins (Grueber, Coins R. Rep. in B.M., i, p. 545).

. Plutarch (Caes. 5. 4) puts his debt at '1,300 talents' before he had entered on any office. At a later date (61 B. C.) Crassus stands security for 830 talents (Plut. Caes. 11. 1 ; Cr. 7.7). Cp. also Suet. 18. 1; App. 2.1; Catull. 29. 14-17. The Pontifex maximus had the usufruct of endowments (Marquardt, Staatsverw. iii, pp. 216-17), and the office might well be of value to a bankrupt !
. Comitia were generally early (Plut. C. Gracch. 13. 2; Varro, L. L. 6. 92, etc.; see Mommsen, Staatsr. (ed. 3) i. 378).
. Aurelia; see 74. 2.
. Plutarch, more precisely, quotes his words as 'You will see me an exile' (Caes. 7. 1).
. Servilius Isauricus (cp. 3. 1) and Catulus the princeps senatus (Plut. Caes. 7. 1; Vell. Pat. 2. 43. 3; Cic. Pis. 6). According to Plutarch, Catulus tried to bribe Caesar.

div.p: § 1. Praetor creatus. Probably in Aug. 63 B. C. The elections were delayed, but probably not for very long (Hardy, Cat. Consp., pp. 43-4).

p.note: . Following upon the exposure of Catiline's accomplices at a session of the senate on Dec. 3 (Cic. Cat. 3) the senate met on Dec. 5 to advise Cicero on further procedure. On this debate see especially Cic. Cat. 4; Att. 12. 21; Sall. Cat. 50-3. For modern discussions see Strachan-Davidson, Prob. of R. Crim. Law, i, pp. 240-5; Hardy, Cat. Consp., ch. 9; R. Holmes, R. R. i. 273-82.

. For the substance of Caesar's speech see Sall. Cat. 51. Was the custody to be detentive or penal? Plutarch (Caes. 7.2; Cic. 21. 1) and Appian (2.6) state that the conspirators were to be detained merely pending a regular trial. But Cicero (Cat. 4. 7) speaks of sempiterna vincula, while Sallust (Cat. 51. 43) and Dio (37. 36. 1-2) say that their goods were to be confiscated and their case not to be reopened. The evidence of these three authors is overwhelming. The proposal was abnormal under the Republic; see Mommsen, Strafr., pp. 299, 947, 960, where he denies the use of penal imprisonment, except under the Empire, and then only as an aggravation.
. See especially the veiled threat in Sallust (Cat. 51. 36) ubi hoc exemplo per senatus decretum consul gladium eduxerit, quis illi finem statuet aut quis moderabitur?

. Cos. 62 B. C. As consul elect he was the first to speak and opted for immediate execution. After Caesar's speech Cicero tried to counteract the effect by his Fourth Catilinarian and thus reopened the rogatio sententiarum. Silanus, speaking first again, ate his words and spoke against execution.

div.p: §2. Cicerone. fratre. Quintus Cicero was praetor elect, and therefore presumably spoke before Caesar on the first rogatio sententiarum; he now, like Silanus and others, changed his view.

p.note: . Cato, great-grandson of Cato the Censor, showed himself a constant opponent of Caesar (cp. 19.1; 20.4; 30.3;56.5). He was now tribune elect. His speech was clear and forcible (cp. Cic. Att. 12. 21; Plut. Cic. 21. 2; Vell. Pat. 2. 35. 3). Sallust (Cat. 52) gives his version of the speech. But he omits the incriminations of Caesar which are recorded by Plutarch (Cat. 23. 1), Velleius (2. 35. 3), and Appian (2. 6), as well as his criticism of Silanus (Plut. l. c.).

. Plutarch (Caes. 8. 2) mentions Curio (probably the younger) and Cicero. Suetonius is wrong when he states that this took place in the senate. Plutarch and Sallust (Cat. 49) are clearly right when they make it happen as he was leaving the senate. sedentem deseruerint is also suspicious, being curiously reminiscent of the similar desertion of Catiline (Cic. Cat. 1.7; 2. 12). But Suetonius is probably right as against Sallust,

div.p: who places the incident on Dec. 4, though Caesar did nothing provocative on that day.

p.note: . But Plutarch (Caes. 8. 3) states that Caesar defended himself at a later meeting of the senate and was protected by Cicero, a statement which he (Cic. 21. 2) more nearly defines by describing the sitting of the senate as one in which the confiscation of estates was discussed. Plutarch's account seems more in keeping with Caesar's character.

. Cos. 78 B. C., and now princeps senatus (see note on ch. 13 competitores). He had checkmated the designs of Crassus and Caesar upon Egypt in 65 B. C. (Plut. Crass. 13. 2), had stood against Caesar for the pontificatus maximus in 63 B. C. (Plut. Caes. 7. 1), and had tried to involve Caesar in the measures to be taken against Catiline's accomplices (Sall. Cat. 49. 1). Caesar was now striking back against a personal opponent and one of the leaders of the optimates.

. The temple of Jupiter had been badly damaged in the fire of 83 B. C. (Plut. Sull. 27. 11; App. 1. 83) and the restoration entrusted to Catulus (cp. monumentum Catuli in Cic. Verr. 4. 31. 69), who dedicated the new temple in 69 B. C. (C. I. L. (ed. 1) i. 592; Tac. H. 3. 72; Suet. Aug. 94. 8, etc.), his name being inscribed thereon.

. This does not necessarily imply a popular iudicium. It is true that Caesar accused Catulus of embezzlement (Dio 37.44. 1) and demanded an account of his expenditure, but it is possible that he proposed no more than a bill transferring the work to Pompey (cp. ad alium below) on the ground of Catulus' malpractices. The actual punishment of Catulus would have been left to the quaestio de rebus repetundis.
, 'attendance on the new consuls'; who went, escorted by the senators, on their first day of office to pay their respects to Iupiter Capitolinus, whose temple was under reconstruction.

, 'dropped his proceedings'. Apparently he did no more than denounce Catulus to the people on Jan. 1, and pave the way for the rogatio which he promulgated. An interval of 24 days was necessary between the promulgatio and actual rogatio ; Mommsen, Staatsr. iii, pp. 375-6 (Botsford, R. Assemblies, pp. 259- 60, makes the interval 17-24 days). The assembly for the rogatio never took place, and such indictment of Catulus, as may have been contemplated, was likewise dropped. actio suggests legal proceedings, but may be used in a more general sense.

div.p: § 1. Metello. Quintus Caecilius Metellus Nepos, Tr. Pl. in 62 B. C. in the interests of Pompey (Plut. Cat. 20; Hardy, Cat. Consp., ch. 10; R. Holmes, R. R. i, pp. 466-7). He was consul in 57 В. С.

p.note: . Only one such law is recorded, namely, that in which Metellus proposed the recall of Pompey to restore order and crush Catiline (Dio 37. 43. 1) or to overthrow Cicero's δυναστεία (Plut. Cic. 23. 2; see also Cat. 26. 2). He had on the last day of 63 B. C. refused to let Cicero address the people on the ground of his execution of the conspirators. Cicero had denounced him in the senate on Jan. 1, 62 B. C., and Metellus had returned to the attack on Jan. 3 (Cic. Fam: 5.2.6-9). But there is no evidence that he proposed to bring forward a lex on the subject (cp. Dio 37.42. 3).
. More especially by Cato and Minucius Thermus (Plut. Cat. 26-9). The proceedings were attended with violent rioting.

. Suetonius is alone among our authorities in saying that Caesar was suspended by a decree of the senate. Dio (37.43. 3) says that the senate passed the decretum ultimum, and that as a result Metellus took refuge with Pompey, after which Caesar lay low for fear a decree should be passed against him as had been passed against Metellus. It is not clear whether Dio means this latter decree to be identical with the decretum ultimum (which was perfectly general in terms) or with an earlier decree which he describes (37.42. 3) as being passed after Metellus' attack on Cicero, to the effect that any person attacking those responsible for the execution of the conspirators should be regarded as a public enemy. Plutarch likewise is silent as to the infliction of any penalty on Caesar, and says that after the flight of Metellus, when it was proposed to deprive Metellus of his office, Cato intervened and persuaded the senate to take no action (Cat. 29. 2). It is, however, possible that Caesar's activities as praetor were suspended by the declaration of a iustitium, as was done in the case of Sulpicius (88 B. C.; see Plut. Sull. 8. 6), or that a special senatus consultum was directed against Caesar and Metellus between the two decrees mentioned by Dio (see above). In this case we may compare the decree suspending Cinna in 87 B. C. (Vell. Pat. 2. 20; App. 1. 64). See also note on in integrum restituit below.
. Presumably he was in charge of one of the quaestiones perpetuae, as he is nowhere spoken of as praetor urbanus or peregrinus. Cp. for ius dicere 43 n.
. Perhaps in virtue of the ultimum decretum, see above.

div.p: § 2. in integrum restituit. Suetonius again is our only

authority. It may refer to the removal of a iustitium (see above), if a iustitium had really been proclaimed, or of the special decree suspending both Metellus and Caesar. Or it may again have occurred on the occasion when Cato intervened to prevent Metellus being deprived of his office (Plut. Cat. 29. 2; see above). In any case the suspension was only for a few days, as is clear from biduo post (above).
§ 1. socios Catilinae. For previous attempts to incriminate Caesar and suspicions about his complicity see p. xxi, and cp. Sall. Cat. 49. 1 and Plut. Caes. 7-8; Cic. 20. 3; Cat. 23. 1. Novium

p.note: . The MSS. give quaestorem. But there is no evidence that quaestors had any jurisdiction in the quaestiones perpetuae (Mommsen, Staatsr. (ed. 3) ii, pp. 543-4; Strafr., p. 156). Novius must have been a quaesitor, or president of a quaestio (in this case probably the quaestio de vi). In that case Novius must have been at least of aedilician standing and cannot be identical with L. Novius, tr. pl. in 58 B. C. (Ascon., p. 47, Cl.).
. An agent of Cicero's in 63 B. C. (Att. 2. 24. 2); of equestrian standing, but a rogue (cp. Dio 37. 41. 2). See note on induxit praemiis (20. 5).

. An accomplice who turned against his fellow-conspirators (Sall. Cat. 23; 26; 28. 2). Sallust, like Suetonius (cp. primus... detexerat), makes him the first to give information of the plot. He was a senator (Sall. 17. 3) and was in a position to raise the subject by an egressio relationis.
. At a special meeting of the senate on Dec. 4 (Cic. Cat. 4. 5; 10).

, an autograph undertaking'. Autographs played a large part in the detection of the accomplices on Dec. 3, 63 в. С. (Cic. Cat. 3. 10, 12). The document produced by Vettius was clearly regarded as a forgery. Cp. the forged letters by which Sertorius was decoyed (Plut. Sert. 26. 3).

div.p: § 2. Ciceronis. Cicero had helped to save Caesar on Dec. 5 (see note on pauci ... protexerint in 14. 2). But cp. also Cicero's letter to Axius quoted in 9. 2; also p.

p.note: . Probably about the same time as Crassus (for which cp. Plut. Cic. 15; Dio 37. 31. 1), i. e. shortly before Oct. 21, when the senatus decretum ultimum was passed (Cic. Cat. 1. 4, 7). See Hardy, Cat. Consp., p. 58.

. Not as security, but as a penalty. Cp. Lex Quinctia de aquaeduct. 1. 18 tum is praetor... multa pignoribus cogito coercito. The pignora were sometimes destroyed in conspectu populi Romani. Cp. direpta supellectile and Cic. de Or. 3. 1. 4; also Phil. 1. 5. 12. See Greenidge, op. cit., pp. 336-7.

. In virtue of his authority as praetor. Imprisonment might be (i) preventive custody in order to secure the presence of a prisoner at a trial; (ii) coercitio, i. e. imprisonment for contumacy on a magistrate. Instances of the use of coercitio save by tribunes are rare, but Caesar in his consulship ordered, if he did not carry out, the same penalty in the case of Cato (see note on 19. 4). In the case of Novius, the exercise of coercitio is clear from the language used by Suetonius; and it is almost equally certain in the case of Vettius. He might no doubt have been indicted for calumnia, but the promptness of Caesar's action suggests penal rather than preventive procedure. See Greenidge, Legal Procedure, p. 333; Mommsen, Strafr., p. 48; also next note. For further examples cp. the coercitio of Tarquinius (63 B. C.) by order of the consul Cicero (Sall. Cat. 48. 6); of Vettius himself by the tribune Vatinius (59 B. C.; see below on 20. 5); of Metellus Celer by the tribune Flavius (60 B. C.; see Dio 37. 50). minorem potestatem: i.e. he challenged the right of Novius as quaesitor (see above) to summon him, a praetor, before his court. Cp. Mommsen, Staatsr. (ed. 3) i, 153.

div.p: §1. sortitus Hispaniam. His province also as quaestor (see 7. 1).

p.note: , 'sureties'. Crassus stood surety for 830 talents (Plut. Caes. II. 1; Crass. 7. 7). Appian (2.8) says that his debts amounted to 25 million sesterces. Cp. also note on 13. I aeris alieni.

, a necessary correction for the MSS.' ordinarentur. The ornatio provinciae = the vote of funds and appointment of staff. Cp. Cic. Pis. 5; Att. 3. 24. 1; Sall. Jug. 27. 5). Meyer (Caesars Monarchie, p. 56) suggests that Caesar did not even wait for the lex curiata conferring the imperium. For a possible parallel cp. App. Claudius, cos. 54 B. C. (Cic. Fam. 1. 9. 25).
. Probably an actio civilis. Later on he became liable to criminal charges (cp. 23. 1; 30. 3), but in 61 B. C. he had for the time being made his peace with the optimates (cp. 16. 2 and 17).
: i. e. in the interval between the expiry of his praetorship at Rome and the conferment of the imperium on him as pro praetore.

. His campaigns are described thus: Plutarch (Caes. 12):-Caesar raises to new cohorts in addition to the existing 10, defeats the Lusitani and Callaeci (Portugal and Galicia), reaches the 'outer sea', and is acclaimed imperator (cp. Liv. Epit. 103 Lusitanos subegit). Dio (37.52-3) :-He is wilfully aggressive, chases the people of the Herminian mountains (between the lower Tagus and Douro) to the Ocean, sails from Gades to

div.p: Brigantium, and subdues the natives (cp. also Dio 44. 41. I for the version given by Antony in his funeral oration). Appian (2.8):- He subdues all Spain and sends much money to the treasury. (Plutarch (l. c.) refers to his settlement of debts incurred by the inhabitants; creditors to be paid in instalments; cp. also Cic. Balb. 43.)

p.note: . So too Dio 37. 54. 1. Cicero did the same in 50 B. C. (Att. 6. 6. 3). Sulla's law definitely ordered governors to leave in 30 days after their successor's arrival (Cic. Fam. 3. 6. 3), but does not seem expressly to have forbidden a premature departure.
. Suetonius, Plutarch (Cat. 31. 2), Appian (2. 8), and Dio (37.54. 1-2; somewhat confused) are all in virtual agreement.

div.p: §2. edictis comitiis. Usually held in July (Mommsen, Staatsr. (ed. 3) i, p. 584, n. 5).

p.note: . It is not clear at what date personal attendance became obligatory. On the strength of Cic. Leg. Agr. 2. 24 Mommsen holds that perhaps it was not till 62 B. C. (Staatsr. (ed. 3) i, p. 503, n. 1). Appian, however, says that Caesar knew that candidature in absentia was illegal, but that others had done it (2.8). Suetonius, Plutarch, and Dio either state or imply the same. The question of personal attendance becomes a burning issue in 52-49 B. C. (see 28. 2).
. He would lose the imperium, and with it the possibility of holding a triumph on crossing the pomerium ; cp. Cic. Fam. 1. 9. 25.
. The granting of this privilege was an ancient right of the senate, recently regulated by the lex Cornelia of 67 B. C. (Ascon., pp. 57-9, Cl.).

. Plutarch, however (Caes. 13. 2), says that Caesar had a strong backing, but (Cat. 31. 2) Cato opposed him furiously and talked the proposal out (κατανάλωσε τὴν ἡμέραν- his favourite form of obstruction); cp. Dio 37. 54. 2; App. 2. 8. (For Cato's talents for such methods cp. 20. 4; Cic. Att. 1. 18. 7; Plut. Cat. 43. 3; Caes. B. C. 1. 32. 3; see also Groebe in Klio, v. 229-35, where all the instances are collected.)

div.p: § 1. Lucio Lucceio. He had accused Catiline in the optimate interest in 64 B. C. (Ascon., pp. 90-1, Cl.). He was also an historian (cp. Cic. Fam. 5. 12. 2). For Cicero's comments on the candidature cp. Att. 1. 14. 7 (Feb., 61 B. C.) Lucceius valde petiturit; 1. 17. 11 (Dec., 61 B. C.) Caesar is planning a deal with Lucceius; 2. 1. 9 (June, 60 B. C.) Caesar and Lucceius are in league; 2. 1. 6 (June, 60 в. с.) Caesar's prospects are good.

p.note: : i.e. Lucceius'.

. A similar compact is found between Catiline and C. Antonius in 64 B. C. (Ascon., pp. 82-3, Cl.) and between Pompey and Crassus in 71 B. C. (Plut. Pomp. 22. 1-2; Crass. 12. 1-2), and again in 56 B. C. (24. I below).

. On Cato's rectitude at elections see especially Plut. Cat. 44 and 49. But he could bribe when it was in the interests of the State (e republica); cp. his corn-dole in 63-62 в. с. (Plut. Cat. 26. 1; Caes. 8. 4).

div.p: §2. silvae callesque. The senate designed to relegate Caesar to a 'commissionership of forests and cattle drifts' in Italy. The view taken by some modern scholars that the phrase means one of the less important provinces overseas, e. g. Corsica (see J. C. Rolfe, Am. Journ. Philol. (1915), pp. 323-31), is clearly untenable. Suetonius' phrasing indicates that the silvae callesque was the actual title of the province, not a mere description of it. The consular provinces would have to be decreed before the actual election in accordance with the lex Sempronia of C. Gracchus (123 or 122 B.C.). But the senate had probably little doubt as to the result of the election.

p.note: . Plutarch (Pomp. 47. 1; Crass. 14. 1) says that Caesar formed the triumvirate with a view to becoming consul, and (Caes. 13-14) that he formed it before the elections (so too Dio -37.54. 3, and by implication Livy-Epit. 103), which amounts to much the same thing. Velleius (2. 44. 1) postdates the triumvirate to 59 B. C. Cicero (Att. 2. 3. 3) shows that it remained a secret till Dec., бо в. с., and Dio also (37.58. 1) says that it was kept a secret. Appian (2. 8), while agreeing that its formation preceded the elections, seems to make the initiative proceed from Pompey, not a very probable hypothesis. Probably the pact was made before the elections, but after the provinces were decreed. See R. Holmes, R. R. i. 474-6.

. He had previously received Caesar's support in connexion with the lex Gabinia (67 B. C.; cp. Plut. Pomp. 25. 3), the lex Manilia (Dio 36. 43. 2), and later in 62 B. C., when he supported the proposals of Metellus Nepos (see on 16 above). Pompey was now much irritated against the senate, who had refused to confirm his acta and to give land to his veterans (Plut. Lucull. 42. 6; Cat. 31. 1).

. For Caesar's previous relations with Crassus see 9 and notes on 11 (Aegyptus) and 18. I (sponsorum). Cp. also pp. xviii-xxi. Crassus and Pompey had been consuls in 70 B. C. For their quarrels see Plut. Pomp. 22-3; Crass. 12; App. 1. 12. There had been further disagreement in 61 B. C. (see Plut. Luc. 42. 5-6 and App.2.9). It is not improbable that Crassus had a grudge against the senate; he had a hand in the Asian tax-contracts (Cic. Att. 1. 17. 9) which the senate had just refused to revise (Att. 2. 1.8; June, 60 в. с.).

. There were no standing orders for publishing senatus consulta or leges (except treaties), and the minutes of the senate were kept, if at all, by the presiding magistrates. Augustus suppressed publication, but not redaction of the senatus acta (Suet. Aug. 36), though the acta diurna populi went on as before (Tac. A. 3. 3. 2; 16.22. 6; 13. 31. 1; Plin. Ep. 9. 15. 3). For the transmission of acta abroad in private news-letters cp. Cic. Fam. 2. 8.1; 12. 22. I; 12. 23. 2; 12. 28.3; Att. 4. 15. 3; Q. F. 3. 2. 3. See Mommsen, Staatsr. (ed. 3) iii, pp. 418-19; 1017-21; Boissier, Tacitus (Eng. Tr.), pp. 198-229; W. Riepl, Das Nachrichtenwesen bei den Gr. und Römern, pp. 380-94.

. According to tradition there was originally only one set of lictors, which each of the consuls used in turn (Cic. Rep. 2. 55; Liv. 2. 1. 8). At some later date each consul was given his own set of lictors, who preceded him. Caesar slightly altered this usage, making an orderly precede him and the lictors follow him during each month in which Bibulus was in charge of public business (fasces haberet). See Mommsen, Staatsr. (ed. 3), i, PP. 39, 40.

. Distinct from the later lex Campana of sect. 3 (below). In this earlier law the allotments were to be provided over the whole of Italy with the exception of Campania. The bill met with such difficulties in the senate that Caesar abandoned dealing with that body and passed his bill through the people. See Dio 38. 1-7 (by far the clearest and most satisfactory account of his proceedings that has come down to us). But he also threw over his exception as regards the Campanian lands, and produced a second bill providing for the distribution of the ager Campanus and the campus Stellas (see sect. 3, notes). This is borne out by Cicero; in Att. 2. 7. 4 (April) he refers to the original law. In Att. 2. 16. I (early May) he speaks of the Campanian proposal as something fresh (omnis (omnis exspectatio largitionis agrariae in agrum Campanum videtur esse derivata). He further speaks of the second proposal as Campana lex in Att. 2. 18.2, which indicates that it was distinct from the first proposal. For briefer allusions to the agrarian legislation see Plut. Cat. 32. 1; Caes. 14. 1; Liv. Epit. 103; App. 2. 10 (where no express distinction is made between the two proposals). For a full discussion see Cary, Journ. Philol., no. 70 (1920), pp. 174-90.

. Cp. Cic. Att. 2. 9. 1; 2. 19. 2; Prov. Cons. 45. Bibulus clearly exercised his right of spectio, i. e. announced se servaturum de caelo (cp. Cic. Sest. 78; Dio 1. c. and 38. 13. 3-5). This is what Dio means by his 'proclamation of a sacred period

div.p: (see next note). The patrician magistrate had this right of watching for omens. The plebeian magistrates, the augurs and private citizens, could only report unfavourable omens when they occurred. See Greenidge, Rom. Publ. Life, pp. 172-3.

p.note: . Bibulus, on the first reference of the law to the people, had expressed his disapproval and asserted that the people should not have the law during his year of office, however much they might desire it. Finally, when he had no excuse for delaying the proceedings further, he proclaimed 'a sacred period, during which the people could not legally meet in the assembly Caesar none the less fixed a day for the passage of the law. Bibulus forced his way through the crowd into the Forum. On his attempting to speak against Caesar he was pushed down from the temple of Castor into the mob and roughly handled. He made no further appearance in public, but contented himself with notifying Caesar whenever he made any proposal that he had established a 'sacred period' (ἱερομηνίαν). So Dio (38. 6. 1-5). Cp. also Cic. Vat. 21-2; Plut. Cat. 32; Caes. 14.4-7; Pomp. 48; App. 2. 11.
. Apparently the meeting in Bibulus' house recorded by Appian (2.11). This meeting would be unofficial; the official meetings had to be held in a templum.
. No individual senator who would venture to make any proposal against the all-powerful consul Caesar.

. Cp. Cic. Dom. 39; Har. resp. 48; Fam. 1. 9. 7; Dio 38.6.1-5; Plut. Caes. 14.4; Pomp. 48. 4. His seclusion lasted for eight months (from May-end of year); App. 2. 11; Vell. Pat. 2. 44. 6. The edicta were notifications to the effect that all Caesar's legislation was null and void. They were more than mere formal notices (cp. 49. 2 where one is cited; Cic. Att. 2. 19.5 (copies sent to Atticus); 2. 20. 4 edicta eius et contiones describunt et legunt; ib. 6 comitia Bibulus cum Archilochio (scathing) edicto in ante diem XV Kal. Nov. distulit).

div.p: § 2. nomine. Iulius; cognomine, Caesar.
§3. campum Stellatem. Land to the north of Volturnus, between Cales and Casilinum (Liv. 22. 13. 5).

p.note: , 'consecrated by our ancestors' (Dat. agent). He apparently repeated this sacrilege later; cp, Dio. 43. 47. 4 (45 B. C.), where he is accused of putting up to auction all public lands, not only the profane, but also the consecrated. The date of the conquest of this territory is not known. But for such consecration cp. Cic. Dom. 128 ut imperator agros de hostibus captos consecraret.

. Revenue-producing ager publicus, now converted into quiritary property. The territory was made ager publicus in 211 (Liv. 26. 16.8). Plutarch (Cat. 33. 1) describes it as almost all Campania. Cicero on the other hand goes to the opposite extreme (Att. 2. 16. I qui ager, ut dena iugera sint, non 3333 F

div.p: amplius homines quinque milia potest sustinere). But, according to Suetonius, 20,000 were settled there.

p.note: : i. e. there was no ballot, but apparently they were selected by the XXviri who had charge of the distribution. Appian (2. 10) and Dio (38. 7. 3) agree with Suetonius that only citizens with at least three children were eligible. Velleius (2. 44. 4) and Plutarch (Cat. 33. 1) say that the land was distributed to the poorer citizens. None of these authors mention Pompey's veterans who were settled under both laws (Dio 38. 5. 1 (First Law) and Cic. Phil. 2. 101 (Second Law)), and to whom the provision as to the size of their family probably did not apply. See Cary, J. Phil., no. 70 (1920), p. 183, n. 2.

. Cp. Caesar's policy in 46 B. C. (Dio 43. 25. 2 πολυπαιδίας ἆθλα ἐπέθηκεν); also later the policy of Augustus as expressed in the lex Iulia et Papia Poppaea (Tac. Ann. 3. 25-8, ed. Furneaux, pp. 440-2).

. This affair had dragged on since 61 B. C.; cp. Cic. Att. 1. 17.9; 1.18.7; 2. 1. 8; Q. F. 1. 1. 33; App. 2. 13. It is clear that only the tax-contracts of Asia were in question (Att. 1. 17. 9; Q. F. I. 1. 33). Cicero says that the equites had no case. This suggests that Caesar may have been bribed; but there is no evidence for this (R. Holmes, R. R. i, p. 323, n. 1). Probably he gave relief to the contractors to oblige Crassus (Cic. Att. 1. 17. 9).
, 'a third of the sum they were due to pay'. Cp. Dio 38. 7. 4.

. Vague statements to this effect, referring to the East, are to be found in Cic. Att. 2. 9. I qui regna, qui praedia tetrarchis, qui immanes pecunias paucis dederunt; Vat. 29. 36. The only recorded act of this kind is the conferment of the title rex et amicus on Ariovistus (Caes. B. G. 1. 35. 2; Plut. Caes. 19. 1; Dio 38. 34. 3), and that had the consent of the senate. It might, however, conceivably refer to the confirmation of Pompey's acta by the people (Plut. Pomp. 48. 3), involving the restoration of their kingdoms to various kings, the establishment of twelve tetrarchs in Galatia, etc. (see Pocock, Ed. of Cic. in Vat., pp. 169–70).

div.p: § 4. interpellantem. Plutarch (Caes. 14. 5) seems to imply that this incident occurred when Cato was protesting against the terms of Caesar's command in Gaul, but (Cat. 33. 1) states definitely that Cato's protest was directed against the Campanian land-law. Dio (38. 3. 2) makes him protest, apparently, against the first land-law. Appian (2. 6), however, associates the incident with the Campanian land-law. Dio says that it took place in the senate, Appian in the Forum, while Plutarch seems implicitly to agree with Appian, though he makes no definite statement. Suetonius definitely says

p.note: . The arrest of a senator in the Forum is more likely than in the Curia. But there is no means of determining the exact occasion. For Cato as an obstructor cp, note on 18. 2.
. Cp. note on in carcerem in 17.2. Cato was soon released (Dio, Plut. ll. cc.).

. Cos. 74 B. C. The real conqueror of Mithridates; he felt that Pompey had reaped the laurels that were rightfully his, and obstructed the confirmation of Pompey's acta, etc., in the senate (61-60 в. с.); cp. Plut. Pomp. 46. 3; Luc. 42.6; App. 2. 9; Dio 37. 49. 4). Dio says (38. 7. 5) that Lucullus did not oppose Caesar. Suetonius here gives the reason why. The occasion of liberius resistendi was presumably the confirmation of Pompey's acta. Plutarch (Luc. 42. 6), however, says that Lucullus was driven from the Forum on this occasion.

, 'fear of false charges being brought against him'. Perhaps charges of res repetundae or the like (cp. the complaints made against Lucullus by money-lenders in Asia in Plut. Luc. 20. 4). Lucullus was actually accused soon afterwards by Vettius of being privy to the alleged plot to murder Pompey (see below on induxit Vettium).

. In his defence of C. Antonius, his former colleague in the consulship (Cic. Vat. 27; Dio 38. 10. 1). Cicero had warned Pompey not to enter the triumvirate (Fam. 6. 6.4; Phil. 2. 23), had refused to join it himself (Att. 2. 3. 3), had refused a seat on Caesar's land-commission, a legatio, and a legatio libera (Prov. Cons. 41; Att. 2. 18. 3). He did not openly oppose Caesar in the senate (Att. 2. 23. 3), but carried on his forensic work and seems to have spoken too freely on behalf of C. Antonius.

. Caesar had let him off lightly over the scandal of the Bona Dea (6. 2) ; ; cp. App. 2. 14, where it is pointed out that Caesar turned a private grievance to useful purpose and did one enemy a good turn to secure his revenge upon the other.

. Clodius' main motive for hostility to Cicero was the fact that the latter had disproved his alibi, when put on his trial for sacrilege in connexion with the incident of the Bona Dea (Cic. Att. 2.1.5; Dom. 80; Quint. 4. 2. 88). For Cicero's attitude towards Clodius see his speeches and letters passim, more especially De Domo 36-42.

. This attempt was made in 60 в. с. Clodius failed to secure election to the tribunate because his transfer to the plebs had not been effected, as it should have been, by a lex curiata (Dio 37. 51. I).
. April, 59 B.C. (Cic. Att. 2. 9. 1). See also Plut. Caes. 14.7; Cat. 33.3; App. 2. 14; Dio 38. 12. 1-2; Vell. Pat. 2. 45.

div.p: Cicero and Lucullus were involved; the others agree with Suetonius in regarding the plot as trumped up for political purposes. It is not quite clear how far the affair was the work of Caesar himself and how far that of an agent (e. g.) such as Vatinius. See R. Holmes, R. R. i, pp. 479-82; Pocock, In Vat., pp. 167, 183 sqq.

p.note: . Vettius was again imprisoned (as in 17. 2), and there killed (Cic. Vat. 26; Plut. Luc. 42. 9; Dio 38.9.4; App. 2. 12). Appian and Dio merely say that he was killed; Cicero and Plutarch say that he was strangled. For the tendency to believe in poison, cp. 74. 1; Cic. pro Caelio; Tac. Ann. 2. 69. 5 and Suet. Tib. 52. 3 (Germanicus); Tac. Ann. 4. 8 and Suet. Tib. 62. I (Drusus, son of Tiberius); Tac. Ann. 12. 66. 4 and Suet. Claud. 44. 2 (Claudius); Tac. Ann. 13. 15. 4 and Suet. Ner. 33. 2 (Britannicus).

div.p: § 1. Calpurniam. Daughter of Calpurnius Piso (cos. 58 в. с.), and Caesar's fourth and last wife, though he nearly divorced her in 52 B. C. (see 27. I sibique filiam eius (sc. Pompei) in matrimonium petit Fausto Sullae destinatam). Cp. Plut. Caes. 14.4; Pomp. 47. 4; Cat. 33. 3; Dio 38.9; App. 2. 14 (βοῶντος Κάτωνος διαμαστροπεύεσθαι τὴν ἡγεμονίαν).

p.note: . Caesar's only daughter (cp. I. 1). Pompey's wives were five in number: (i) Antistia (88-2 B. c.); (ii) Aemilia; (iii) Mucia, who bore him three children and was divorced in 61 B. c. : cp. 50 1 (suspected intrigue with Caesar); (iv) Iulia, a happy marriage, but she died in 54 B. C.; see Plut. Pomp. 47.4; 48.5;53; Crass. 16. 1; Caes. 14. 3; Cic. Att. 2. 17. 1; Vell. Pat. 2. 44. 3. (v) Cornelia, daughter of Metellus Scipio.

. Brother of Servilia (see 50. 2) and uncle of Brutus, whom he adopted. Pompey to appease him for being thus robbed of Iulia, offered him his own daughter in exchange, though she was betrothed to Faustus Sulla, whom she eventually married (Plut. Caes. 14.3; Pomp. 47.4; App. 2. 14; Dio 38. 9).

. There was normally a fixed order, beginning with consuls designate (at such times of the year as there were any), then proceeding to the consulares, praetorii, aedilicii, or tribunicii, and finally to the quaestorii. It rested with the presiding magistrate in what order he should ask members of the separate classes to speak. See Greenidge, Rom. Publ. Life, p. 268, and for a more detailed discussion, Willems, Le Sénat, ii, pp. 179-94. For Caesar's action see Gell. 4. 10. 5 C. Caesar in consulatu quem cum M. Bibulo gessit quattuor solos extra ordinem (i. e. out of senority) rogasse sententiam dicitur; ex his quattuor principem rogabat M. Crassum; sed postquam filiam Cn. Pompeio desponderat, primum coeperat Pompeium rogare (he cites Tiro and Ateius Capito as his authorities).

div.p: § 1. Socero generoque. Piso and Pompey.

p.note: . The MSS. give Gallias

. The simplest correction is Galliam (Bentley, who would also, need. lessly, read quae for cuius). The singular may be used generically, including both Cisalpine and Narbonese Gaul, or may refer merely to the province which he first received. Both provinces were border lands with a weak frontier, and the populations adjoining could always supply pretexts for attack. Further, Cisalpine Gaul in the first century B. C. had become the chief recruiting ground of the Roman armies; an enterprising commander could rely on a supply of soldiers and plenty of opportunities for using them to further his ambitions.

. Our other authorities are not explicit as to whether Illyricum was an addition or at this time formed part of Cisalpine Gaul. But they do not contradict Suetonius' statement that it was an addition (probably attached by a special clause in the Lex Vat. See next note).

. Dio (38.8.5) and Orosius (6. 7. 1) agree with Suetonius in distinguishing between the lex Vatinia and the later senatus consultum conferring Transalpine Gaul. Plutarch (Pomp. 48.3; Caes. 14.5; Cat. 33. 3) and Appian (2. 13) confuse the two measures. All these sources, with Velleius (2.44.5), agree that the term for which these provinces were assigned was five years. It expired on March 1, 54 B. C. (Cic. Prov. Cons. 37), from which it follows that it commenced on March 1, 59 B. C. See note on in quinquennium (24. 1); Marsh, Foundations of R. Emp., pp. 271-8. For an interesting sketch of Vatinius' career see Pocock, In Vat., p. 29.
. See previous note. The proposal was made by Pompey and Crassus (Plut. Crass. 14. 2; Cic. Att. 2. 3).

. Gallia Comata, the land of the 'long-haired Gauls', is interpreted by R. Holmes (Conquest of Gaul (ed. 2), p. 41) as meaning that his commission gave him the right to include... the whole of independent Gaul north of the Province (Narbonensis) within his sphere of action'. But there is no evidence to support this, nor was such authorization necessary, since circumstances made it necessary for him to protect the frontiers of the Province from northern invaders, and his invasion of independent Gaul followed as a matter of course. Gallia Comata should certainly mean 'un-Romanized Gaul' only, but Suetonius may have used the words loosely. See note on in provinciae formam (25. 1).

div.p: § 2. insultaturum. The story seems almost incredible. Truculence was not a characteristic of Caesar. But the account is explicit, and the incident is alleged to have taken place frequenti senatu, which tells against its being pure fiction.

p.note: , etc. An obscene jest, alluding to the Nicomedes scandal. If the story is true, this is the earliest authority now extant for the scandal (see 2.1; 49; 52.3). Caesar is represented as replying with a jest, whereas later (see on 49 and Dio 43. 20. 1) he takes the matter more seriously, and denies the story on oath. It is impossible to form any judgement as to the truth of the scandal; such scandals were common form' at Rome by this time, and no importance attaches to them; great men have been the victims of scurrilous gossips in all ages, and at Rome it was possible to give such scandals a publicity such as has fortunately not been possible in all ages.
. Assyria is meant, but Syria is elsewhere used as including Assyria (e. g. in the geographer Mela, 1. 11. 62).

. Semiramis was historically the Assyrian queen-regent Sammu-ramat (811-808 B. c.); but she seems also to have gathered round her in Greek and Roman legend attributes and legends of the Babylonian goddess Istar (see Camb. Anc. Hist., iii, pp. 27 and 183-4). For stories of her licentiousness see Diod. 2. 13. For the name used abusively cp. Cic. Prov. Cons. 9, where Gabinius is spoken of as a Semiramis.
. Amazon legends are widespread in ancient historians. They have been conjectured to represent a matriarchal or a beardless people. But all explanations are pure conjectures.

div.p: § 1. Gaio Memmio. Quaestor of Pompey in Spain (Cic. Balb. 5); pro-praetor tor of Bithynia (Catull. 10 and 28) in 57-8 B.C.; consul 54 B. C. (see c. 73; Cic. Att. 4. 17. 2), and probably identical with the patron of Lucretius; befriended by Caesar at a later date (see 73; Cic. Q. F. 3. 8. 3). He is quoted in 49. 2. L. Domitio. See 24. I; consul with Memmius in 54 B. C.; for this episode cp. Suet. Ner. 2. 2. He was always one of Caesar's chief opponents.

p.note: . The senate were asked to decide eis legibus senatum non teneri, on the ground of violence and disregard of auspices; Schol. Bob. ad Cic. Sest., p. 297, Or. and ad Cic. Vat. xx, p. 317, Or. For previous cases see Cic. de Leg. 2. 14; Ascon., pp. 68-9, Cl. (Saturninus and Drusus). For later discussion of Caesar's laws see especially Prov. Cons. 45 sqq.

: i. e. dared the senate to make inquiry into the matter. Cp. Catiline's action on Nov. 8, 63 B. C., when he challenged Cicero to make a relatio instead of merely fulminating against him (Cat. 1. 20). For Caesar's speech cp. Schol. Bob. ad

. He did not leave Rome till about the middle of March, when on receipt of news from Gaul, he travelled from Rome to Geneva in eight days (Plut. Caes. 17. 3) to deal with the Helvetians, who were intending to cross the Rhone on Mar. 28 (Caes. B. G. 1. 6. 4). He had been encamped outside the gates of Rome till Clodius had passed his law against Cicero (Cic. Red. Sen. 32; Sest. 41).
. The quaestor consulis in 59 B. C. His name and the alleged offence are unknown.

. The name is given to any preliminary proceedings necessary before the main case comes on; e.g. a divinatio to decide which of two or more would-be prosecutors should be selected; or an inquiry into the legal status of the parties or into some legal point which must be determined before the indictment can be framed. See Greenidge, Legal Procedure, pp. 149 and (more especially) 459. There is no evidence as to the precise nature of their case.

. Nothing else is known of this Antistius or of the charge brought against Caesar. If it were a capital charge, it would have been brought before the comitia centuriata, if a pecuniary charge, before the concilium plebis tributum. See Greenidge, Legal Procedure, pp. 329 sqq. and 342. Mommsen (Staatsr. (ed. 3) ii, p. 326), arguing from Cic. in Verr. 1. 38 (iudiciis ad senatorium ordinem translatis sublataque populi Romani in unum quemque vestrum potestate), maintains that with the establishment of the quaestiones perpetuae the right of accusation by the tribunes had been abolished. But the present case tells against this view. On the whole subject see Hardy, Problems of Rom. Hist., ch. 1.

. Caesar appealed to the college of tribunes and they intervened. For the intervention of other tribunes against a colleague cp. Cic. Vat. 21 and Dio 39. 39. 7, where tribunes try to imprison (i) Bibulus in 59 B. C., (ii) Crassus in 54 B. C., and are stopped by their colleagues. Also Liv. 24. 43. 4 (213 В. С.).

. A lex Memmia (113 В. С.) protected absentes reipublicae causa (Val. Max. 3.7.9). Mommsen (Strafr., p. 353) cites Dig. 3. 3.54; 48. 2. 12). Caesar was already technically absens reipublicae causa, if the indictment took place when he was cum imperio ad portas.

div.p: §2. obligare ... magistratus. Cp. 27. I omnibus vero circa eum, etc. For specific instances see 29. I and 73 (Memmius).

p.note: , 'a bond'.

div.p: § 1. L. Domitius. See note on 23. I and below on detrudendi Domiti. He had hoped to be elected consul for 55 B. C., but was prevented by force of arms (Dio 39. 31; Plut. Pomp. 52; Cat. 41 (instigated to attack Caesar by Cato); Crass. 15; Caes. 21. 3; App. 2. 17 (who attributes the use of such force to Pompey)). He did actually become consul in 54 B. C., but had been cowed, and kept quiet. The statement of Suetonius (Ner. 2) consul imperatorem ab exercitibus Gallicis retrahere temptavit is incorrect. The threats mentioned here were uttered in 56 B. C. Suetonius makes no mention of Cicero's attempts to break up the triumvirate, which were likewise frustrated by the conference at Luca.

p.note: : i. e. by arranging for a successor to take over command on Mar. 1, 54 B. C.; compare the proposals against which Cicero spoke in the De Prov. Cons. (17) delivered in June, 56 B. C.

. The modern Lucca. The conference took place towards the end of April, 56 B. C. The attitude of the opposition was becoming serious. Cato and Cicero were working against Caesar, as also was Domitius. See more especially Cic. Fam. 1. 9 and Q. F. 2. 5; Plut. Pomp. 51.2; Caes. 21.2; Crass. 14.4; App. 2. 17. See also our ed. of Cic. Prov. Cons. Appendix (26-40). It is worth noting that Luca was in Cisalpine Gaul; (i) Caesar did not leave his province; (ii) it was convenient to Pompey who was about to sail for Sardinia from Pisae or Labro (Livorno); see Q. F. 2.5.3.

. See note on L. Domitius above. In the onslaught upon Domitius, there mentioned, one man was killed, while Cato and other of Domitius' friends were wounded. There had been riots previously during Domitius' canvassing, and there were further riots afterwards, involving a certain amount of bloodshed (see Liv. Epit. 105; Plut. Pomp. 52; Crass. 15; Cato 41-2; App. 2. 17; Dio 39. 27-36 (detailed)). According to the latter (31. 2) P. Crassus the younger brought some of Caesar's troops to Rome to secure the election of his father and Pompey. See also note on filiam amisit in 26. I for the effect of these riots on the health of Julia.
, 'a second consulship'. Pompey and Crassus had been consuls in 70 B. C., and the statutory ten years' interval had elapsed.

. The reading of cod. Reg. II (13th cent.) in the British Museum; a certain correction of the older MSS. perfecitque utrumque ut (or et ut), etc. Pocock (In Vat., p. 165) cites Caes. B. G. 8. 53 and Vell. Pat. 2. 46. 2 to show that Pompey and Crassus were the formal movers of the prorogatio, and

div.p: Plut. Pomp. 52. 4 and Liv. Epit. 105 to show that this was carried into effect by the tribune Trebonius.

p.note: . So also Cic. Att. 7. 7.637.9.4; Phil. 2. 24; Vell. Pat. 2. 46.2; Plut. Caes. 21.3; Pomp. 52.4; Crass. 15.7;. App. 2. 17-18. Dio (39.33.3; 44.43.2) curtails Caesar's second term to three years, which is almost certainly the result of a misapprehension as to the date at which his proconsulship began. Caesar's first quinquennium ran from March 1, 59 B. C., to March 1, 54 B. C. (Cic. Prov. Con. 37). The second quinquennium in all probability ran on from the latter date to March 1, 49 B. C. Several attempts have been made of recent years to prove that Caesar's second term ended some time in 50 B. C. Such theories are mostly based on allusions to the expiry of Caesar's command in Cicero's correspondence. But the passages in question are all of them inconclusive. For a full discussion of the evidence see Holmes, R. R. ii, pp. 299-307, and especially Hardy, Problems of R. Hist., pp. 150-206. For the best statement of the case in favour of an earlier date of expiry cp. F. B. Marsh, The Foundations of the Roman Empire, pp. 279-90.

div.p: § 2. legiones. Nominally 6,000 men each (R. Holmes, Conquest of Gaul (ed. 2), pp. 559-63).

p.note: . Caesar had received three legions by the lex Vatinia with Cisalpine Gaul, and one from the senate with Transalpine Gaul. By 57 B. C. he had raised his forces to eight legions (Dio 38. 8.5; Caes. B. G. 1. 10 and 2. 8). In 56 B. C. his recruitments up to date were legalized and pay provided (Cic. Fam. 1. 7. 10; Prov. Cons. 28; Balb. 61). He raised two legions more in the winter of 54-3 B. C. (B. G. 6. 1. 4). See R. Holmes, Conquest of Gaul (ed. 2), pp. 557, 731-2.
