. The Fifth Legion, and probably one of the raw legions raised in 51 B. C. (Caes. B. G. 8. 24. 2 and 26 (R. Holmes, Conquest of Gaul (ed. 2), pp. 802-4; Drumann-Groebe, iii, p. 708). It must have been composed of native Gauls, not resident Italians, as is clear from the name alauda (Celtic for the 'lark': lit. 'crested one'. Glück, Jahrb. f. Phil., cxiii, p. 166). Such enrolments of peregrini in the legions are not previously recorded, though they become common from the time of the second triumvirate down to the reorganization by Augustus. The alauda was represented on their helmets (Plin. 11. 121). See W. Kubitschek in Pauly-Wissowa, xii, 2, cols. 1564-71 (legio V Alaudae).

. This was not without precedent. Marius had enfranchised a thousand Camerini in spite of protests (Plut. Mar. 28. 3). Pompeius Strabo had done the like for Spaniards after the Social War (de consilii sententia ; cp. also Diodor. 37. 17 Ἰούλιος ὁ ὕπατος (cos. 90), offers franchise to a Cretan for betraying a position): see Dessau, Inscr. R. Select. 8888; J. H. Stevenson,

div.p: J. R.S. ix, pp. 95-101. Pompey had done the same after the Sertorian War (singillatim); this was legalized by special statute (Cic. Balb. 19; see also 24, where he speaks of other single enfranchisements). Under the Empire, diplomata were regularly given to ex-service peregrini.

§ 3. ultro lacessitis. This statement assumes that the Bellum Gallicum is misleading or worse. Some modern historians have accepted this view (e. g. Ferrero, Greatness and Decline of Rome, ii, pp. 336-51; S. Reinach, Rev. de Philologie (1915), pp. 29-49). But these critics have been damagingly answered by R. Holmes, Cl. Qu. (1909), pp. 203-15; R. R. ii, pp. 271-9. For a judicial summary cp. T. Frank, R. Imperialism, ch. 17.

p.note: . Suetonius is our only authority for this statement. It is probable that he refers to the grant of ten legati in 56 B. C. The normal number of legati to a consular command was three. But Caesar had nominated ten, and his action was not ratified till that date (see Cic. Fam. 1. 7. 10; Prov. Cons. 28; Balb. 61 imperatori decem legatos decrevit). It is clear from these passages that Caesar desired the decree, and it is possible that Suetonius has misunderstood his authorities. Nor can Dio (39. 25. 1) be right when he states that these legati were to form the usual commission of ten appointed to organize a conquered province. Had this been so Cicero would not have said (Prov. Cons., 1. c.) that senators raised the question as to whether there was any precedent for the appointment of ten legati.

. This occurred in 55 B. C. after the defeat and annihilation of the Usipetes and Tencteri. Caesar had granted them three days truce, and the battle arose, according to him, from a gross breach of the armistice by the enemy (B. G. 4. 1-16). But he had refused to listen to the German chiefs who came to explain the alleged breach of the truce, and had arrested them. This was represented by Caesar's enemies as a breach of the ius gentium, which recognized the inviolability of envoys, and Cato made the proposal mentioned by Suetonius (see Plut. Caes. 22. 3; Cat. 51. 1); who his supporters (nonnulli) were is not recorded. For precedents for such action cp. Liv. 9. 10 (surrender of the consuls of the Caudine Forks) and App. Iber. 83; Plut. Tib. Gr. 7 (surrender of Mancinus in the Numantine War, 137 В. С.). ...

. In 57 B. C.: 15 days (B. G. 2. 35.4; Cic. Prov. Cons. 25-6; Plut. Caes. 21. 1); all these passages (as also Cic. Balb. 61) emphasize that this was without parallel, 10 days being the previous maximum (in honour of Pompey; cp. Prov. Cons. 27). In 52 B. C.: 20 days (B. G. 7.90.9). In 46 B. C.: 40 days (Dio 43. 14. 3). In 45 B. C.: 50 days (Dio 43. 42. 2). A supplicatio was a public thanksgiving taking the form of prayers at all the temples, often accompanied by processions.

div.p: § 1. novem annis. 58-50 В. С. The first eight years were occupied with fighting, the last given to organization of his conquests.

p.note: . 3,200 Roman miles = approx. 2,940 English miles. Plutarch (Caes. 15. 3) says that Caesar took more than 600 towns, conquered 300 tribes, killed a million men, and captured two millions.
. The reference is probably to the Aedui and Remi, perhaps also to the Lingones. Cp. B. G. 8.49.3; Jullian, Hist. de la Gaule, iii, p. 570, n. 5.

. The new conquests were tacked on to Gallia Narbonensis to begin with; cp. App. 2. 111 (D. Brutus, governor of the whole of Transalpine Gaul, 48-46 B. c.). In 44 B. C. Gallia Comata was separated from Narbonensis. Narbonensis was assigned to Lepidus (Dio 43.51.8; 45. 10. 6; App. 2. 107), while Munatius Plancus was in command of Comata (Nic. Dam. 28; Cic. Phil. 3. 38; Fam. 10. 1-26). It was left to Augustus to give G. Comata a regular organization in three provinces (Belgica, Lugdunensis, Aquitania) and to grant provincial charters. CCCC = quadringenties centena millia (40 million sest.). The number is given in only one MS., but is confirmed by Eutropius (6. 17. 3), who follows Suetonius very closely in 6. 17-25. This statement is prima facie in contradiction to that in B. G. 8. 49. 3, where Hirtius says itaque honorifice civitates appellando, principes maximis praemiis adficiendo, nulla onera nova iniungendo, defessam tot adversis proeliis Galliam condicione parendi meliore facile in pace continuit. This impost can therefore scarcely date from 51-50 B. C., as Suetonius would imply. R. Holmes (Conquest of Gaul (ed. 2), p. 838) suggests that the tribute may have been fixed in advance 'just as in 54 B. C. Caesar fixed the tribute which Britain was to pay annually to the Roman people' (B. G. 5. 22. 4), though the country had not been formed into a province.

div.p: § 2. ponte fabricato. B. G. 4. 17.

p.note: . Cp. B. G. 4. 20. 2 quae omnia (sc. insulam, genus hominum, loca, portus, aditus) fere Gallis erant incognita. neque enim temere praeter mercatores illo adiit quisquam neque iis ipsis quicquam praeter oram maritimam atque eas regiones quae sunt contra Gallias notum est. For the first expedition cp. 4. 20-38; for the second see 5. 8-23.
. B. G. 5. 22. 4 obsides imperat et quid in annos singulos vectigalis populo Romano Britannia penderet constituit. For hostages only cp. 4. 21.5; 27.5; 36.235.20. 4.
. B. G. 5. 10-11 (40 ships lost) 54 B. C.; he had lost 12 in a minor mishap in the preceding year (4. 29 and 31).
. B. G. 5. 26-37 (54 B. C.); see note on in Germania (58. 1).
. Aurunculeius Cotta (B. G. 2. II. 3).

div.p: §1. matrem. Aurelia. See 74. 1.

p.note: . In 54 B. C., as the result of the shock of seeing Pompey's toga stained with blood shed in the riots (see note on L. Domitius 24. 1), Julia gave birth prematurely to a daughter (Vell. Pat. (2.47. 1-2) says a son), mother and child died within a few days of one another; cp. Plut. Caes. 23. 4; Pomp. 53. 3-4; Vell. Pat. 1. c.; Dio 39. 64. 1; Val. Max. 4. 6.4; Luc. I. 111-21; also Sen. ad Marc. 14. 3 Caesar cum Britanniam peragraret nec Oceano continere felicitatem suam posset, audiit decessisse filiam publica fata secum ducentem... tamen intra tertium diem imperatoria obiit munia et tam cito dolorem vicit quam omnia solebat.
. Clodius was killed by Milo early in 52 B. C. See Cic. Mil. passim, and more especially Ascon., pp. 30–6, Cl.

. Dio (40. 50-1) gives a somewhat similar account of the movement to make Caesar consul with Pompey. The proposal was impracticable from Caesar's point of view. He had his work to finish in Gaul, his imperium did not expire till March 1, 49 B. C., and difficulties might have been raised by his opponents on the ground that the legal interval of ten years had not elapsed since his first consulship, though the latter argument would lose force from the fact that Pompey suffered from the same disqualification. He therefore took occasion to make another proposal on his own behalf ut absenti sibi, quandoque imperii tempus expleri coepisset, petitio secundi consulatus daretur. It was all-important to him to return to Rome as consul, not as a private person seeking election; otherwise he would run the risk of impeachment on some ground or other by Cato or some other intransigeant opponent. Cp. App. 2. 25; Plut. Pomp. 56. 2 (an alternative proposal was made that his term in Gaul should be further extended). There were negotiations at Ravenna in 52 B. C. between Caesar and Cicero (acting for Pompey). Cicero promised to support his desire (Att. 7. 1. 4). The result was the 'Law of the Ten Tribunes', passed with Pompey's support (Att. 8. 3. 3) and granting the privilege of standing in absentia at such time as he might desire it (Caes. B. C. 1. 32. 3; Cic. Att. 7. 3.4; Liv. Epit. 107; Dio and App. 1. c.). For the sequel see 28. 3 and 30. 2 sqq.
. See note on in quinquennium 24. Ι.
. In the De Prov. Cons. (34) Cicero expresses the hope that one or two summers more may see the conquest completed

div.p: , i. e. in 55 or 54 B C. But Caesar's most difficult campaign (against Vercingetorix) was yet before him. ...

§ 2. forum incohavit. The Forum Iulium on the north of the Forum Romanum. A rectangular court (115 m. by 30 m.) with the temple of Venus Genetrix in the middle. Parts of the enclosing wall are extant. The site was cleared in 54 B.C. (Cic. Att. 4. 16. 14 = 4. 17. 7); dedicated in 46 B. c. (Dio 43. 22. 2) on the 25th or 26th Sept. (C. I. L. (ed. 2) i, pp. 219 and 240); completed by Augustus (Mon. Anc., ch. 20). See Platner, Topogr., p. 276.

p.note: . ICO million sesterces. So, too, Pliny (36. 103). Cicero (Att. 4. 16. 14 = 4. 17. 7) says in this connexion, 'The friends of Caesar, that is to say, myself and Oppius, have thought nothing of spending 60 million (contempsimus sexcenties HS)'. But the sum mentioned by Cicero may not have covered all the expenses.

, 'a gladiatorial show and a public banquet'. Cp. the show which he had given in 65 B. C. (10. 2), which according to Dio was in memory of his father (37.8.1). The first record of such memorial games is found in 264 B. C. (games given by M. and D. Brutus in memory of Iunius Pera; Liv. Epit. 16; Val. Max. 2. 4. 7).
, 'for which a contract was given to the victuallers'.
. Not found before Suetonius, and in him only here.

div.p: § 3. infestis spectatoribus: i. e. when the spectators showed their hostility, and there was a risk of their demanding the death of the beaten gladiator by turning down their thumbs.

p.note: , 'in a gladiatorial school'. But in 31. I we find him intending to build a gladiatorial school at Ravenna, while he himself says that he kept gladiators at a school in Capua at the outbreak of the civil war (B. C. 1. 14. 4). For details of such schools cp. Mau-Kelsey, Pompeii, pp. 155-8.
. And yet lanistae (professional trainers) were made infames in the lex Iulia Municipalis (123).
. Probably among the collection of letters ad Familiares mentioned in 56. 6.
, 'orders'.

. A special grant of money to pay the legions was made in 56 B. с. (Cic. Prov. Cons. 28; Balb. 61; Fam. 1. 7. 10). But there is no evidence that this involved the doubling of their pay; it would have been hard to persuade the senate to pass such a measure; the grant actually made was probably to provide pay for the legions raised on Caesar's own authority. Suetonius gives no clear indication of date, and it is possible that Caesar made the increase out of the spoils of war on his own authority, and made the change permanent by continuing this rate of pay in the civil

div.p: war. duplicavit suggests a personal act, rather than the authority of the senate. For his generosity to his soldiers cp. 38. I and 67. 1. Marquardt (Staatsverw. (2nd ed.) ii, p. 95) argues that he increased the pay from 1,200 asses (old) to 3,600 asses (new), i. e. from 120 denarii to 225.

p.note: . The monthly ration was, according to Polybius (6. 39. 13), two-thirds of an Attic medimnos of corn without meat or other solid food (i. e. about a quart daily). See Drumann-Groebe, iii, pp. 731-5.

. Cp. B. G. 7. 89. 5 ex reliquis captivis (after the fall of Alesia) toto exercitu capita singula praedae nomine distribuit. For other examples of his generous gifts from the booty taken cp. B. G. 7. 11. 9; 8.4.1; Cic. Att. 8. 14. 1.
. Ursinus conjectured ex praeda. But the correction, though not improbable (see preceding note), is not imperative.

div.p: § 1. Octaviam. Grand-daughter of Caesar's sister Iulia, who married C. Atius Balbus. Their daughter Atia married C. Octavius, to whom she bore Octavia and Octavius (Augustus). Pompey refused the offer; she remained the wife of Marcellus (for whom see 29. 1), and had Antony for her second husband. 6

p.note: , as a match'. condicio is used both of the state of marriage and the person married.

. Faustus Cornelius Sulla, son of the dictator; served in the army of Pompey in Asia, and distinguished himself as a soldier (Joseph. Ant. Jud. 14.69; Bell. Jud. 1. 149, 154). He was quaestor in 54 B. C. (Ascon., p. 20, Cl.), fought for Pompey in Macedonia, and afterwards took part in the African campaign. He married Pompey's daughter. For his fate see 75. 3 n.

. Cp. 23.2; 29. 1. His debtors included Cicero (Cic. Fam. 1. 9. 12; Att. 5. 1. 2, etc.) and Rabirius Postumus (Cic. Rab. Post. 41). For Caesar's largesse in general see App. 2. 17. Crassus had adopted the same methods (Plut. Cr. 3. 1).
. Cicero was among the invited (Att. 2. 18.3); he did not go, but sent C. Trebatius (Fam. 7. 6-22).

. The word is primarily used of a dole of food or oil, of the measure of a congius (nearly six pints), and then comes to be used of gifts of money as well. It is even used of gifts among friends as here, occurring in this sense in Caelius ap. Cic. Fam. 8. 1. 4, and in Seneca, Quintilian, and elsewhere.
. So, too, Dio 40. 60. 4.
. Especially Curio (29. 1) and Dolabella (36. 1).

. Cp. Plut. Caes. 28. 1, where he insists that Caesar had long planned to destroy Pompey. It is worth noting that Caesar disappointed the hopes of his bankrupt friends; cp. 42. 2 (debts not cancelled as they had hoped, though some relief given).

div.p: § 1. reges...adliciebat. No instances seem to be recorded of gifts of captives, or of military assistance.

p.note: . The only clear instances seem to be Tralles, which put up a statue to him before Pharsalus (Val. Max. 1. 6. 12), and Mytilene, which Caesar gratified in 45 B. C. by a decree sanctioning new financial regulations proposed by that city (Cagnat, Inscrr. Gr. ad rem Rom. pertinentes, iv. 33 a-b, and notes ad loc.). Honorific inscriptions, in which Caesar is called 'god', 'benefactor', or 'saviour', have been found at Mytilene (Cagnat, iv. 51, 67a, 79 c, 80b); Pergamum (ibid. iv. 303-7); Chios (ibid. iv. 929, and C. I. G. 2215); Athens (I. G. iii. 428; cf. Ditt. Syll. (3rd ed.) 759); Megara (I. G. vii. 62); Thespiae (I. G. vii. 1835); Ceos (I. G. xii. 5. 557); and Ephesus (Ditt. 760); Dittenberger and Purgold, Inschrift. von Olympia, no. 365. But most of these texts are dated, by references to Caesar's second consulship or to his second and third dictatorships, to the years 48-45 B. C.

div.p: § 2. M. Marcellus. M. Claudius Marcellus, quaestor in 65 в. с. (Plut. Cat. 18. 3), consul in 51 B. C.; the dates of the intermediate magistracies are uncertain. A strong supporter of Pompey, he contributed in no small degree to the outbreak of the civil war, but took no part in the struggle after Pharsalus. He is the Marcellus of Cicero's pro Marcello. For his murder at Athens see Sulp. ap. Cic. Fam. 4. 12.

p.mentioned: de summa se re publica acturum
p.note: , 'would bring forward a matter of supreme importance to the state'.

, etc. The statement is not quite accurate. Caelius in a letter to Cicero (May 24, 51 B. C.), Fam. 8. 1. 2, states that Marcellus had as yet made no proposal de provinciis consularibus; he postponed action till Sept. 29 (Fam.8.2.2; 8.4.4; 8. 8. 5), when he merely got the senate to instruct the consuls of 50 B. C. to bring forward a proposal de prov. cons. as from Mar. I of that year. The text of the resolution is given in Fam. 8. 8. 5. Dio (40. 59) and Appian (2. 26) make virtually the same statement as Suetonius.
. The war was virtually at an end after Alesia, and entirely at an end by the autumn of 51 В. С.
. See 26. 1. on egit cum tribunis for earlier negotiations on this subject in 52 B. С.

, since Pompey, despite his subsequent legislation, had not annulled the decree of the people'. obrogasset is an early emendation for abrogasset. abrogo in classical Latin governs the accusative, and in the other two passages where Suetonius employs the verb he follows classical usage (Cal. 26. 3; Tib. 61. 3). The plebi scitum is the Law of the Ten Tribunes (see note on 26. 1). nec = not also. The language is elliptical. Pompey's law (see next note) would automatically have annulled the plebi scitum (cp. Liv. 9. 34.7 ubi duae contrariae leges sunt, semper antiquae obrogat nova), but was altered subsequently so that exception was made in special cases.

div.p: § 3. legem de iure magistratuum. Shortly after the Law of the Ten Tribunes, passed with the support of Pompey (Cic. Att. 8. 3. 3), granting Caesar the privilege of candidature in absentia, Pompey passed a law reordaining that all candidates must present themselves in person. He then irregularly altered the law, making an exception in favour of cases where special leave had been granted. It is hard to believe that Pompey acted per oblivionem. The only plausible explanation of this discreditable affair is that given by Meyer (Caesars Monarchie, p. 243) to the effect that the law was passed when Caesar was in trouble at Gergovia, and altered by Pompey after his success at Alesia. (This law is explicitly spoken of by Dio (40. 56. 1) as separate from the law, passed about the same time, which prescribed that five years must elapse between tenure of praetorship or consulship and the holding of a provincial command.)

p.note: . Cp. Cic. Phil. 1. 16.
. The Roman Record Office (cp. Cic. Phil. 5. 12; 12. 12; Liv. 39. 4).

. Cp. Tac. A. 3. 28. I suarum legum auctor idem ac subversor; Cic. Att. 8. 3. 3 lege quadam sua ('all his very own'); Dio 40. 56. 3 (where it is apparently treated as valid; Suetonius shows a like unconcern over this astonishing irregularity).
. In the classical and technical sense of a 'law passed with special reference to an individual'. ...

p.mentioned: colonis quos rogatione Vatinia Comum deduxisset
p.note: . Probably the same lex Vatinia which conferred the command of Cisalpine Gaul upon Caesar (22. 1). On the status of Comum see Hardy, Problems of R. Hist., ch. 5; R. Holmes, R. R. ii. 317-20. Probably it was a Roman colony composed mainly of ex-service men. It may be added that to show that he refused to recognize their status as citizens, Marcellus had one of them scourged (Cic. Att. 5. 11. 2; Plut. Caes. 29. 1; App. 2. 26).

div.p: § 1. principem civitatis. An informal term applied by Cicero to Pompey (Prov. Cons. 41; Red. Sen. 4; Sest. 84; Planc. 93; Att. 8. 9. 4; Fam. 1. 9. 11, etc.). For Cicero's conception of the functions of such a princeps see fragments of the fifth book of the de Republica and Strachan Davidson (Cicero, pp. 293-4). The title is also given more widely to Pompey, Crassus, and others in Vat. 10, and to Antony's grandfather in Phil. 1. 34, and to Caesar himself in Fam. 6. 6. 5.

p.note: . Cp. Dio 40. 59.1; Cic. Fam. 8. 8. 6-8 (where texts of three senatus auctoritates of Sept. 29, 51 B. C., are given; they show that they were vetoed by C. Pansa and three other intercessores.

. So, too, Dio 1. c. Sulpicius, an eminent lawyer, and a warm friend of Cicero, was not a man of action, but a lover of peace (cp. Cic. Fam. 4. 1. I defensorem pacis; 4. 3. I tua in hoc pestifero bello cavendo sententia; 8. 10. 3 nosti Marcellum quam tardus sit, Servius quam cunctator; see also Pro Murena 22 sqq., and Phil. 9). He was neutral in the civil war and became governor of Achaia in 46 B. C. (Fam. 4. 4. 2).

. The husband of Octavia. This fact did not prevent him from being hostile to Caesar on the outbreak of the civil war (Dio 40. 59-64; App. 2. 26-31). He was pardoned by Caesar and survived him (d. 40 B. c.). fratri patrueli = first cousin. M. Marcellus (cos. 51 B. C.) M. Marcellus (aed. 91 в.с.) C. Marcellus (cos. 49 в.с.) C. Marcellus (praet. 80 в.с.) C. Marcellus (cos. 50 в.с. m. Octavia)

. L. Aemilius Paulus, son of Lepidus (cos. 78 B. C.) and brother of the triumvir Lepidus. Quaestor 60/59 B. C. to C. Octavius in Macedonia (Cic. Att. 2. 24. 3, where it is stated that Vettius claimed him as accomplice in the alleged plot against Pompey). Cur. aedile in 55 B. C., he became heavily indebted by his rebuilding of the Basilica Aemilia et Fulvia; cp. Cic. Att. 4. 16. 14 = 4. 17. 7 (begun in 64 B. C.); Plut. Caes. 29. 2 and App. 2. 26 (continued with the aid of Caesar's money); Dio 49. 42. 2 (finished in 34 B. C.). At first an extreme optimate (Sall. Cat. 31. 4), he is described by Appian (1. c.) as having been a bitter enemy of Caesar. But he was inactive during his consulate, having received a huge 3333 G

div.p: bribe from Caesar (App. 1.c. (1,500 talents); Plut. Caes. 29. 2; Pomp. 58. 1 (1,500 talents)).

p.note: . C. Scribonius Curio, son of the consul of 76 B. C. (see 9. 3). Born 84 B. C.; quaestor 54 B. C. (It is often inferred from Cic. Fam. 2. 6. 1 and Phil. 2. 4 that Curio was quaestor in Asia in 54 B. C. These passages merely prove that he visited Asia in that year. But the quaestorship of Asia was held at that time by one L. Sestius Pansa (Fränkel, Inschriften v. Pergamon, nos. 406-7, Chapot, La province romaine d'Asie, p. 320).) He had become heavily indebted through the magnificence of the games given in memory of his father in 52 B. C. (cp. Plin. 36. 116-20; Plut. Cat. 46. 3). At first a staunch optimate (Cic. Att. 2. 8. 1; 2. 18. 1; 2. 24. 2), and as late as Aug. 1, 51 B. C., on bad terms with Caesar (Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8. 4. 2 eum non mediocriter Caesar... valde contempsit). But on becoming tr. pleb. for 50 B. C. he was won over by a huge bribe from Caesar (1,000,000 HS, Schol. Luc. 4.820; 10,000,000 HS, Vell. Pat. 2. 48. 4; 60,000,000, Val. Max. 9. 1.6; 2,700,000, Serv. ad Aen. 6. 621; more than 1,500 talents = c. 40,000,000 HS, App. 2. 26). For his desertion to Caesar see Cael. ap. Cic. Fam. 8.6.5; Plut. Caes. 29.2; Pomp. 58. 1; App. 2. 27-30; Dio 40. 60; Luc. 1. 269; 4.819 (momentumque fuit mutatus Curio rerum). His chief services to Caesar were as bribery agent (Plut. Ant. 5. 1) in support of Antony's candidature for the tribunate, in vetoing the motion of the consul, C. Marcellus (April or May), for the recall of Caesar (Cic. Fam. 8. 13.2; App. 2. 27-8), and in checkmating Marcellus by an adroit manœuvre on Dec. I (proposal that both Caesar and Pompey should resign). Marcellus, infuriated by this proposal, at once authorized Pompey to raise troops against Caesar, and Curio joined Caesar at Ravenna on Dec. 10. For his death in Africa see ch. 36. The details of Curio's tribuneship are obscure. See R. Holmes, R. R. ii, 308- 310.
. An epithet which is not borne out by other authorities. ...

div.p: § 2. obstinatius agi. After the debate in the senate on Dec. I (see note on Curionem above) the consul C. Marcellus visited Pompey, placed a sword in his hand, and commissioned him to raise troops against Caesar. Pompey accepted provisionally ('provided I can find no better way'), and by Jan. 1, 49 B. C., had troops close to Rome (Plut. Pomp. 59. 1; App. 2. 31; Dio 40. 64 and 66; Caes. B. C. 1. 2. 6). On Dec. 10 Pompey had told Cicero that war was certain (Cic. Att. 7. 4. 2).

p.note: . (i) C. Claudius Marcellus, brother of M. Claudius Marcellus (cos. 51 B. C.; see 28. 2), a strong partisan of Pompey; he disappears from view early in the civil war. (ii) L. Cornelius Lentulus Crus (praetor 58 B. C.), a violent optimate (Caes. B. C. 1. 4. 2) hot for war, who did his best to dragoon the senate

div.p: into war in January, 49 B. C. (Caes. B. C. 1. 1. 2), but fled from Rome on the approach of Caesar; he was eventually put to death in Egypt a few days after the murder of Pompey (Caes. B. C. 3. 104 ; Plut. Pomp. 80. 4).

p.note: . Probably the letter mentioned by Caesar in B. C. 1. I. It was brought from Ravenna in three days by Curio, who reached Rome on Jan. 1. Lentulus refused to allow its discussion in the senate, where it was, however, read aloud; it was also read to the people by Antony as tr. pleb.; cp. Dio 41. 1. 1; App. 2. 32; Plut. Pomp. 59. 2; Caes. 3. 1 (where he seems to imply that there were two letters to the same effect, one read by Curio and the other by Antony). In this letter Caesar renewed the offer of simultaneous disarmament (proposed by Curio and carried by the senate a month previously (see on Curionem above)), but said that if forced to defend himself he would do so. Cicero (Fam. 16. 11. 2-Jan. 12, 49 B. C.) describes the letter as follows: Caesar minaces ad senatum et acerbas litteras miserat, et erat adhuc impudens qui exercitum et provinciam invito senatu teneret; he goes on to say that Antony and Q. Cassius went off with Curio to join Caesar nulla vi expulsi.

. The privilege granted by the plebi scitum known as the Law of the Ten Tribunes; see 26. 1. Cp. also Caes. B. C. 1. 9. 2 doluisse se quod populi Romani beneficium sibi per contumeliam ab inimicis extorqueretur (from a letter sent from Ariminum to Pompey about Jan. 17, in which he probably echoes a phrase used in the letter to the senate to which Suetonius here refers).

. For the problems connected with this proposal see p. xxii. For later offers of Caesar see Meyer, Caesars Monarchie, pp. 292-309. For Caesar's conciliatory attitude in general cp. Vell. Pat. 2. 48 and 49. 3.

: i.e. until he had actually entered on his consulship. If it meant 'until his election as consul in the summer of 49 B. C.', he would have been privatus for the remainder of the year and liable to prosecution. Appian (2.32 ἕως ὕπατος ἀποδειχθείη) must be wrong, while Plutarch's language (Caes. 31. 1 μέχρι οὗ τὴν δευτέραν ὑπατείαν μέτεισι) is ambiguous like that of Suetonius.

div.p: § 1. neque senatu interveniente: i.e. since the senate would not intervene in favour of the suggested compromise.

p.note: . His arrival at Ravenna must have been not later than Dec. 13 or 14, when Curio joined him there. The date of his arrival in Cisalpine Gaul is uncertain. See R. Holmes, R. R. ii, pp. 323-6. G2

div.p: §2. Pompeius dictitabat. This is not recorded elsewhere. If Pompey made such a statement in all seriousness, it shows how thoroughly he underrated his opponent and misinterpreted his character.
§ 3. alii timuisse dicunt. This explanation is largely true, as the whole struggle round the question of Caesar's candidature shows.

p.note: . Cp. his previous suggestion that Caesar should be handed over to the Germans (24. 3 nonnulli dedendum; note. Throughout the years 52-49 B. C. he was one of Caesar's chief antagonists; see Plut. Cat. 47-52; Pomp. 61; Caes. B. C. I. 4. 1 ; 1. 32. 3; Vell. Pat. 2. 49. 3).

. Suetonius or those whom he quotes have expressed themselves confusedly. Milo protected himself by bands of armed men, but did not surround the court with armed men when he stood his trial. It was Pompey who did so to secure Milo's conviction (Ascon., p. 41, Cl.; Caes. B. C. 3. 1.4).

div.p: § 4. quod: i. e. the view expressed by alii above.

p.note: . 76 B. C.-A. D. 5 (Tac. Dial. 34. 7; Euseb. Chron. 2020); orator, poet, historian, soldier, and statesman. He was with Caesar at the crossing of the Rubicon (Plut. Caes. 32), fought under Curio in Africa (App. 2. 45); at Pharsalus (App. 2. 82); probably tr. pleb. in 47 B. C., when he suppressed Dolabella's escapade at Rome (Plut. Ant. 9); at Thapsus (Plut. Caes. 52) and in the second Spanish campaign (Cic. Att. 12. 38. 2); praetor in 45 B. C.; returns to Spain, which he holds with three legions after Caesar's death (App. 4. 84; Dio 45. 10; Vell. Pat. 2. 73. 2; Cic. Fam. 10. 32). Consul 40 B. C. He wrote a history of the civil war in 17 books (Suidas), which began with the year 60 B. C. (Hor. Od. 2. 1. 1) and extended at least as far as the death of Cicero (see the striking fragment on Cicero in Sen. Suas. 6. 24).
, etc. Plutarch cites the same remark on the authority of Pollio (Caes. 46. 1).

div.p: § 5. De Officiis. See 3. 82.

p.note: . A palpable gloss. The lines are from Phoen. 524.
: i.e. Cicero. See loc. cit.: quos dicam, ut potero, incondite fortasse, sed tamen ut res possit intellegi.

div.p: § 1. sublatam tribunorum intercessionem. On Jan. I Antony and Q. Cassius had vetoed the proposal of Metellus Scipio that Caesar should resign his command on Mar. 1, 49 B. C., or else be declared a public enemy (Caes. B. C. 1. 2; Dio 41. 2. 2), and the decree therefore remained on record merely as an auctoritas, a

'resolution' without legal force. On the 7th the senate met and passed the decretum ultimum (Cic. Fam. 16. 11. 2; Caes. B. C. 1. 5; Cic. Phil. 2.52-3). Antony and Cassius had been warned to leave the house if they wished to avoid violence, whereupon they departed with curses and vaticinations of woe from Antony; Pompey had stationed troops round the senate house (App. 2. 33). Plutarch (Caes. 31. 3) says that they were driven from the senate with abusive language; Dio (41. 3. 2) that they departed, little concerned; Cicero (Fam. 16. 11. 1) that no force was used against them (nulla vi expulsi). Caesar on receipt of the news made the most of the incident to kindle his troops to indignation (B. C. 1. 7 ; Suet. 33. 1).

p.note: . Cp. the equally detailed and essentially similar story in Plutarch (Caes. 32. 2), which is based on Pollio. He watches gladiators at practice; then home to dinner, where he stays but a short time, telling his guests to expect his speedy return. His more intimate friends steal away also, and rejoin him by different roads. He himself uses a hired carriage, and after making a detour, reaches the Rubicon. After hesitation on the brink, and telling his friends that their passage will be the beginning of great woe for many, he cries 'Let the die be cast'. Cp. also App. 2. 35; Plut. Pomp. 60. 1-2; Caes. B. C. 1. 8. 1 (simply Ariminum proficiscitur).

div.p: § 2. provinciae finis. The Aesis at Ancona used to be the boundary, but on the constitution of the Cisalpine Province the frontier was withdrawn northwards. See Marquardt, Staatsverw. (ed. 2) i, p. 218.

p.note: . The more intimate friends who were with him (Plut. App. 1. c.); Asinius Pollio was among them.

. Cp. Plut. App. (1. c.) for a slightly different version. ostentum. A curious and very striking story. If true, it must have been prearranged by Caesar. Appian (2. 36) provides a es a large selection of portents of a more stereotyped character; Lucan (1.526) and Pliny (2. 92) mention a comet, confirmed (according to Drumann-Groebe, iii, p. 375 n.) by Chinese annals. Dio (41. 14.3) records an eclipse at Dyrrhachium in March or April. Suetonius did not get this portent from Pollio, else Plutarch (1. c.) would assuredly have mentioned it in his account cited above. For other portents cp. Suet. 88 (also Vesp. 5). (Lucan (1. 186) has conceived a striking vision of patriae trepidantis imago bidding Caesar stay his hand.)
. Appian and Plutarch (1. c.) both make him say 'Let the die be cast'; Erasmus therefore, perhaps rightly, conjectured esto for est.
. The 13th legion (Caes. B. C. 1. 7. 8; App. 2. 34; Plut. 32. 1 (with 300 cavalry)).

. For the substance of his address to his troops on the treatment of the tribunes cp. B. C. 1. 7. Plutarch (Caes. 31. 2) and Appian (2. 33) merely say that he showed the tribunes (who had fled disguised as slaves) to the troops; both make him do this before the crossing of the Rubicon, while still at Ravenna. But Caesar's statement (B. C. 1. 8. 1) that he met the tribunes at Ariminum (though the news of their treatment had reached him at Ravenna) is conclusive, even without the support of Dio (41. 4. 1) and Lucan (1.231 sqq.). See R. Holmes, R. R. ii, pp. 334-6.

. 400,000 sesterces (cp. cum milibus quadringenis below). The statement is incredible; at most a limited number of centurions occasionally rose to be knights. Suetonius' explanation must be correct. It is worth noting that Suetonius very rarely gives his reasons for acceptance or rejection of a story as he does here.
. The gold ring worn by equites and senators. See Mommsen, Staatsr. iii, pp. 514-19.

div.p: § 1. ordo et summa rerum. Suetonius gives a brief summary of the commentaries of Caesar, Hirtius, etc.

p.note: . See Caesar, B. C. 1. 11-13, 15-16; R. Holmes, R. R. iii, ch. 14, and pp. 353 sqq. The Italian campaign falls between Jan. II and Mar. 18 (R. Holmes, pp. 377-9). L. Domitio. See 23. 1. 24. 1. L. Domitius on the strength of this appointment, after his release at Corfinium, took over the defence of Massilia (B. C. 2. 3. Ι).

. A tumultus (state of war in Italy) had been declared by the senate early in January, after passing the decretum ultimum on Jan. 7. See R. Holmes, R. R. iii, p. 354. The phrase, therefore, means something more than 'irregularly'. Rolfe, who translates it thus, interprets the phrase as meaning that the lex Sempronia, which provided that the consular provinces should be assigned before the election of the consuls who were to hold them, was violated. But quite apart from the special circumstances created by the decretum ultimum and the declaration of a tumultus, the lex Sempronia must have been superseded rather than supplemented by the law of Pompey (52 B. C.), enacting an interval of five years between the praetorship or consulate at Rome and the tenure of a provincial command.
. Cp. Caes. B. C. 1. 6. 5 provinciae decernuntur duae consulares, reliquae praetoriae; Scipioni obvenit Suria, L.

div.p: Domitio Gallia; Philippus et Cotta privato consilio praetereuntur, neque sortes eorum deiciuntur. Domitius had been consul in 54 B. C., and the five years' interval was duly observed. The date of the appointment was probably between the passing of the decretum ultimum on Jan. 7 and Jan. 12, at which date Cicero (Fam. 16. 11. 3) shows that the Italian and presumably the provincial commands also had been given.

p.note: . See B. C. 1. 17-23; R. Holmes, R. R. iii, ch. 14; Veith, Klio (1913), pp. 1-26.
. Along the Adriatic coast.
. The consuls and the bulk of the Pompeian army sailed on Mar. 4 (R. Holmes, R. R. iii, p. 379). ...

div.p: § 2. Romam patribus. The senate refused to negotiate (Caes. B. C. 1. 32-3; Plut. Caes. 35.2; Dio 41. 15-16); Caesar plundered the aerarium and marched to Spain (Cic. Att. 10. 4. 8; 10. 8.6; Plut. Caes. 35. 3; Dio 41. 17-18; App. 2.41; Luc. 3. 113; Flor. 2. 13. 21).

p.note: . Governor of portion of Hispania ulterior for Pompey (Caes. B. C. 1. 38. 1). After his defeat at Ilerda he joined Pompey in Greece, fought at Pharsalus and then crossed to Africa and fought at Thapsus (B. Afr. 18.91); after the battle he and Juba fought together seeking to escape Caesar by death; both perished, though the details of their deaths vary slightly (Bell. Afr. 94; Dio 43. 8.4; App. 2. 100). He is probably identical with the Petreius who, as legatus of C. Antonius, crushed Catiline (Sall. Cat. 59-60; Cic. Sest. 12; Dio 37.39-40). The dates of his magistracies are unknown; he was an ex-praetor when in command in Spain (Vell. Pat. 2. 48. 1) and a senator in 59 B. C., if he is identical with the M. Petreius who, when Cato was threatened with imprisonment by Caesar, offered to go to prison with him (Dio 38. 3. 2).

. Served under Pompey in the Sertorian war (Plut. Sert. 19. 3) and was one of his legati in the East (Plut. Pomp. 34. 1). Consul in 60 B. C. Governor of Hispania Citerior (Caes. B. C. 1. 38. 1; Vell. Pat. 2.48.1). Joined Pompey and fought at Pharsalus (B. C. 3. 88), and afterwards at Thapsus; for his death after that battle see 75.3.

. M. Terentius Varro, the 'learned Varro', legatus of Pompey in Spain, and governor of a portion of Hispania ulterior, but took over the entire command of the province when Petreius marched to join Afranius (Caes. B. C. 1. 38. 1-2). He played but a small part in the fighting in 49 B. C., and surrendered his legions to Caesar (B. C. 2. 17 sqq.); but, remaining in Spain, was later forced to take some part in the second Spanish war of 45 B. C. (Сіс. Fam. 9. 13. 1); he was, however, pardoned by Caesar (Phil. 2. 104) and held in honour by him (see 44. 2).
. For the Spanish campaign see Caes. B. C. 1. 38-55, 59-87; 2. 17-21 (June 23-Aug. 2); R. Holmes, R. R. iii, ch. 16, and pp. 388-408.
, etc. Both statements proved false, as the narrative of the Bellum Civile shows.
. See B. C. 1. 34-6, 56-8; 2.1-16. 22; R. Holmes, R. R. iii, ch. 17, and pp. 409-21; M. Clerc (Musée Belge, 1923, pp. 145-56) tells the story from the Massilian point of view.
. See B. C. 1. 51-55 (especially 52; corn was at 200 sesterces a modius instead of 3 or 4).

div.p: § 1. quattuor menses. See B. Civ. 3.6-19, 23-30. The entire campaign lasted from Jan. 4-Aug. 9, the siege of Dyrrhachium from March-July, 48 В. С. See R. Holmes, R. R. iii, pp. 477-81. For the whole campaign see ib. ch. 19 and pp. 430-81; G. Veith, Der Feldzug von Dyrrh. zwischen Caesar und Pompeius, pp. 132-90.

p.note: . See B. Civ. 3. 84-99; R. Holmes, R. R. iii, pp. 452-76. F. L. Lucas, B. S. A. 24 (1919-21), pp. 34-53, places the battlefield NW. of Pharsalus, N. of the Enipeus and at right angles to it (J. P. Postgate, J. R. S. xii, pp. 187-91, and R. Holmes (p. 467) concur). The date was Aug. 9 (old style); cp. C. I. L. (ed. 2) i, p. 244 (Fast. Amitern.) EO DIE C. CAES.C. F·PHARSALI DEVICIT: p. 248 (Fast. Ant.) DIVVS IVL· PHARS VICIT.

. The eldest son of Ptolemy Auletor, the rex Alexandrinus of 11. 1, who died in 51 B.C. The war lasted Oct.- March, 48-47 B.C. See Caes. B. C. 3. 103-12; B. Alex. 1-33; R. Holmes, R. R. iii, pp. 173-204, 483-506; J. P. Mahaffy, Empire of the Ptolemies, pp. 445-63.
. She was the elder sister of the reigning Ptolemy and at this time about twenty years old.

div.p: § 2. Pontum... Pharnace. See B. Alex. 65-78; R. Holmes, R. R. iii, pp. 210-15, 509-14. Pharnaces was left in charge of the Tauric Chersonese by Pompey, as a reward for revolting against Mithridates and so bringing about his death. See App. Mithr. 110, 111, 113. In 47 B. C. he sought to recover part of the territory of his father.

p.note: . Cp. 37.2 veni vidi vici.
. Lucullus had broken the back of the Mithridatic war before Pompey took over the command. Cp. Lucullus' recriminations against Pompey in Plutarch (Pomp. 31. 6-7. Pompey a 'carrion-bird').
. See B. Africanum: R. Holmes, R. R. iii, ch. 22 and pp. 516-40: Kromayer-Veith, Ant. Schlachtf. iii,

div.p: pp. 761-897. The campaign lasted Dec.-Apr. 47-46 B. C. Thapsus was fought on Apr. 6; cp. C. I. L. (ed. 2) i, p. 235 (Fast. Praenest.) = Dessau, Inscr. R. Sel. 8744 a, LVDI F. Q·E·D·C·CAESAR C.F. IN AFRICA REGEM iubam Vicit.

p.note: . Quintus Caecilius Metellus Scipio gave information to Cicero of Catiline's plans (Plut. Cic. 15. 1); trib. pleb. in 59 B.C. (Cic. Att. 2. 1.9-Cicero defends him successfully in 60 B. C. against charge of bribery at his election); Consul in 52 B.C.; father of Pompey's fifth wife and a staunch optimate. In 49 B.C. he was sent to command in Syria by Pompey (Caes. B. C. 1. 6. 5), but was summoned to Macedonia during the siege of Dyrrhachium (B. C. 3. 33. 1), and later commanded the centre at Pharsalus (B. C. 3. 88. 3); he escaped to Africa and was in command of the Pompeian army in Africa; after Thapsus he escaped with a small fleet and sailed for Spain, but was intercepted by Sittius and committed suicide (B. Afr. 96).

. Son of Hiempsal, king of Numidia (see on c. 71), sided with Pompey on the outbreak of war, annihilated Curio and his army in 49 B.С. (В. С. 2. 25. 4; 38-44), and received the title of king from Pompey. In the Thapsus campaign he supported Scipio and suffered defeat with him. For his death see on M. Petreio above. His hostility to Caesar may well have been determined by an early quarrel with Caesar recorded by Suetonius in c. 71.

. (i) Gnaeus, son of Pompey's third wife, Mucia (born 80-76 B.C.) was sent to get ships from Egypt in 49 B. C. (Caes. B. C. 3. 4. 4); returning with these he did some damage to Caesar's ships at Oricum and Lissus (B. C. 3. 40; Dio 42. 12); after Pharsalus the Egyptian fleet returned home, and he went to Corcyra, where he urged the Pompeians to stand fast, as they held command of the sea, and nearly killed Cicero because he advised peace (Plut. Cic. 39. 1-2; Cat. 55. 2). He later went by way of Africa to Spain (App. 2. 87; B. Afr. 22-3), where after Thapsus he was joined by his brother Sextus and collected a force of thirteen legions. Defeated at Munda, he attempted to escape by sea, but was forced to return to Spain and there killed (B. Hisp. passim ; Dio 43. 28-40. (ii) Sextus, younger son of Mucia (born 75 B.C.; see App. 5. 144), was with his stepmother Cornelia at Mytilene during the Pharsalus campaign, and witnessed his father's death in Egypt (Dio 42. 2. 3 and 5. 7). He took part in the campaign of Thapsus (Dio 42. 5. 7), then joined Gnaeus in Spain, where he held Corduba till news of the disaster at Munda reached him (B. Hisp. 3. 1; 32.4; 34.2). He then fled and took refuge among the Lacetani for a while, then collecting an army defeated Asinius Pollio and made himself master of the south of Spain (Dio 45. 10). Subsequently during the second triumvirate he waged war with the triumvirs, was finally defeated off Naulochus in 35 B. C. by Agrippa (App. 5. 118 sqq.), and fled to the East, where he was captured and

div.p: put to death by orders from Antony (App. 5. 137-44). For the latter part of his career see also Dio 46-9; Vell. Pat. 2. 73-87.

p.note: . The second Spanish campaign is imperfectly known. See Bellum Hispaniense and Dio 43. 28-40; R. Holmes, R. R. iii, ch. 24 and pp. 541-52. It lasted from Dec. 46 to March 45 B. C. (new style). Munda was fought on March 17; see C. I. L. (ed. 2) i, p. 212 FER.QVOD E·D·CAES•VIC.IN HISP. VLT. p. 250 CAESAR Hispania devicit.
. See 29. I n. and on lubam above (35. 2).

. Brother of Marcus; praetor in 44 B. C. (Plut. Ant. 15; Dio 45. 9. 2; App. 3. 14). He was defeated in 49 B. C. in an attempt to retrieve Dolabella's defeat in the Adriatic, and capitulated at Curicte (or at Corcyra Nigra, not Curicte, according to R. Holmes, R. R. iii, p. 110, n. 2). The narrative of this reverse has dropped out between chs. 8 and 9 of the Bellum Civile; but there are references to it in 3. 10.5 and 3. 67. 5 (Antonius the victim of treason); cp. also Dio 41. 40. 2; App. 2. 47; Cic. Att. 10. 7. 1; Liv. Epit. 110; Flor. 2. 13. 31; Luc. 4. 401-580; Veith, Gesch. d. Feldz. C. Julius Caesars, ii, pp. 349-51). He was eventually put to death by command of Brutus in Macedonia (42 B. C.); see Liv. Epit. 121; App. 3. 79; Plut. Brut. 28; Dio 47. 2. 4.

. Tr. pl. in 59 B.C. (Cic. Sest. 113); praetor in 56 B. c. (ibid.). Involved in the bribery scandal of 54 B. C., when he stood for the consulship (Cic. Q. F. 2. 14. 4, &c.), he was elected consul in July 53 B. C. (cp. Dio 40. 17. 1; Plut. Pomp. 54.3; App. 2. 19). He fought on Caesar's side in the Civil War (i) in the Pharsalus campaign (Bell. Civ. 3 passim), and (ii) in 47 B.C. held command in Asia, and, attempting to drive Pharnaces from Armenia and Cappadocia, was defeated near Nicopolis owing to the desertion of his Galatian allies (B. Alex. 34-41; R. Holmes, R. R. iii, pp. 205-9 and 506).
. Cp. Plut. Caes. 39. 3 σήμερον ἂν ἡ νίκη παρὰ τοῖς πολεμίοις ἦν, εἰ τὸν νικῶντα εἶχον; App. 2. 62. Caesar himself and Dio make no mention of this. 37.5)

. So, too, Flor. 2. 13. 83; Eutrop. 6. 24. Plutarch (Caes, 56. 2) says that Caesar actually took part in the battle (so, too, Dio 43. 37. 5) and cried, 'Shame ' on you! ! Why do you not take me and yield me up into the hands of those boys?', while after the battle he stated that he had often before fought for victory, but on that day for the first time he had fought for his life. Appian (2. 104) asserts that he ran out in front of the line of battle crying, 'This shall be the end of my life and of your soldiering!' Cp. also Vell. Pat. 2. 55 for a somewhat similar story. The author

div.p: of the Bellum Hispaniense makes no mention of such a crisis, but that is far from proving that it did not occur.

§ 1. quinquiens triumphavit. (i) Four triumphs in 46 в. с. after his return from Thapsus, i. e. Gallic, Egyptian, Pontic, and African (Plut. Caes. 55. 1-2; App. 2. 101; Dio 43. 19). In these triumphs were led Vercingetorix (Plut. Caes. 27. 3; Dio l. c.), the younger Juba (Plut. Caes. 55; App. 1. c.), and Arsinoe, sister of Cleopatra (Dio, 1. c.). Although none of these triumphs were for victories over Roman citizens, since the African triumph was nominally for the overthrow of Juba the elder, this last triumph, according to Appian, contained pictures representing the suicides of Scipio and Cato, and gave great offence (see, however, next note). (ii) The fifth triumph was after Munda in 45 B. C. (Plut. Caes. 56. 3-4; Dio 43. 42), a triumph over Roman citizens, which was much resented (Plut., 1. c.). See also Vell. Pat. 2. 56. 2; Flor. 2. 13. 88; Liv. Epit. 115. There is a gap in the Fasti Triumphales at this point. For the evidence of coins, see Grueber, Coins of R. Rep. in B. M., pl. 49, nos. 12-16. (There had been no triumph for victory over Roman citizens before 45 В.С.; ср. В. С. 3. 71. 3, where Caesar records Pompey's refusal to make official use of the title of imperator conferred on him by the troops after his victory at Dyrrhachium, or to wear the laurel wreath of the victor.)

p.note: . Velleius (2. 56. 2) mentions citrus wood from Gaul, acanthus from Pontus, tortoise shell from Alexandria, ivory from Africa, silver from Spain, as forming the material of the apparatus in these five triumphs. For other features of these triumphs not recorded by Suetonius cp. Florus, 1. c. (pictures of scenes in the four campaigns, but none of Thapsus; contrast with Appian's statement quoted in previous note); Cic. Off. 2. 28 (an effigy of Massilia); App. 2. 102 (65,000 talents and 2,822 gold crowns displayed); Vell. Pat. 2. 56.2 (600 million sesterces displayed).

div.p: § 2. Velabrum. The triumphal procession started on the Campus Martius near the temple of Isis (Jos. B. Iud. 7. 5. 4), then passed through the Circus Flaminius (Plut. Luc. 37), the Velabrum (Suet.), and the Forum Boarium to the Circus Maximus (Cic. Verr. 2. 1. 154; Plut. Aem. Paul. 32), whence it made its way by the Via Sacra to the Capitol (Hor. Epod. 7.8; Od. 4.2.35). The Velabrum was low ground lying between the Forum, Capitoline, and Palatine. See Platner, Topogr., pp. 393-4.

p.note: . Dio (43.21. 1) states that the accident occurred as he was passing the Temple of Fortune dedicated by Lucullus (the site of which is unknown, though there was a temple of Fortune in the Forum Boarium close to the Velabrum; Platner, p. 398).

div.p: Caesar got into a fresh chariot which took him to the foot of the Capitoline steps which he ascended on his knees. Pliny (28. 21) asserts that after a certain carriage accident Caesar always muttered a charm when he got into a chariot; but there is no reason to connect the story with the present incident.

p.note: . Dio (43.22. 1) describes this escort as taking place at the fourth triumph after the banquet. A torchlight procession would naturally take place in the evening, and elephants would be specially appropriate to the African triumph. They may even have been captured from Juba, who employed elephants in the Thapsus campaign.

. Cp. 35. 2 (a four days' campaign). Plutarch (Caes. 50. 2) says that Caesar employed the words in a letter to a friend, Appian (2.91) in a letter 'to Rome' (es Ρώμην), presumably a public dispatch. Cp. also Dio 44. 46 (Antony's funeral oration) and Flor. 2. 13. 63, venit percussit abscessit.

div.p: § 1. bina sestertia. 2,000 sesterces.

p.note: . 24,000 sesterces. Dio (43. 21. 3) and Appian (2. 102) say 5,000 drachmae = 20,000 sesterces. Appian adds that centurions received double, military tribunes and prefects of cavalry fourfold.

. Cp. 81. 1. For assignations of lands in 46-45 B. C. cp. Cic. Fam. 13. 4-5 (Volaterrae); 13.7 (Regium Lepidum); 9. 17. 2 (Veientem quidem agrum et Capenatem metiuntur). Dio (42. 54. 1) mentions assignment of land to all in 47 B. C. and adds that the lands were widely separated to prevent seditious movements (they had just mutinied); whereas here Suetonius merely says that they were separated to prevent wholesale dispossession of actual occupiers. The motives alleged are not incompatible; but Dio probably exaggerates the distance between the settlements, as Antony and Octavian succeeded in mobilizing the veterans in 44 B. C. with great rapidity. There were large numbers who had not yet received their lands at the time of Caesar's death (cp. App. 2. 133). There are copious allusions to the Campanian settlements in 44-43 в. с. (Сіс. Att. 14. 21; 16.8; Phil. 2. 102; Vell. Pat. 2. 61. 1; App. 3. 40; Nic. Dam. 31).

. There was a smilar provision in the first agrarian law of 59 B. C. (Dio 38. 1. 4). On the other hand, hardship was probably caused by the second law of the same date, which called in the Campanian leases.

. Slightly under ten pecks = two months' rations on the usual scale of distribution (cp. Sall. H. 3. 48, 1. 19; Licinianus 34. 4). Dio (43.21. 3) says 'grain beyond the usual amount and olive oil'; and adds that he struck out half the names of

div.p: recipients of the dole, their numbers having increased enormously during the Civil Wars. Cp. Plut. Caes. 55. 1, where Caesar boasts that his victory in Africa had vastly increased the public revenue in corn and oil.

p.note: . This had been promised at the beginning of the Civil War (Dio 41. 16. 1). For the present distribution cp. Dio 43. 21. 3, agreeing with Suetonius, but adding that it was given only to recipients of the corn-dole.

div.p: § 2. habitationem, 'rent'. House-rents had risen enormously (cp. Vell. Pat. 2. 10; Plut. Sull. 1. 6; Crass. 2. 5). For this remission cp. Cic. Off. 2. 83-4, where Cicero denounces Caesar's measures dealing with house-rent and indebtedness; Caes. B. C. 3. 21; Dio 42. 22. 3 (remission of rent promised by Caelius in Caesar's absence); 42. 51. 1 (granted by Caesar in 47 B. C.). For a similar remission by Octavian cp. Dio 48. 9. 3.

p.note: , 'a banquet and a dole of meat'. Plutarch mentions 22,000 triclinia (Caes. 55. 1); cp. Vell. Pat. 2. 56. 1; Liv. Epit. 115; Dio 43. 21. 3; Pliny 9. 171 (6,000 murenae); 14. 97 (Lesbian, Mamertine, Chian, and Falernian wine). For feasts in the Forum cp. Livy 39. 46. 2-3.

div.p: § 1. spectacula, etc. Cp. Plut. Caes. 55.3; App. 2. 102; Dio 43. 22-3; Liv. Epit. 115; Plin. 8. 16-22; Vell. Pat. 2. 56. 1; also C. I. L. (ed. 2) i, p. 225 (Fast. Maff. July 20) LVDI VICT· CAESAR; p. 244 (Fast. Amitern.) LVD. VICTOR.CAES·DIVI IVL COMMITtuntur. Cp. the account of the shows given by Augustus (Suet. Aug. 43).

p.note: . In the Forum (see below), over which silken awnings were hung to protect the spectators from the sun (Plin. 19. 23; Dio 43. 24. 2). Dio (43.24. 1) says that the slaughter was so great that Caesar was blamed because he himself was glutted with slaughter, and displayed to the people an image of their own woes.

, in the four wards of Rome'. The Suburana, Esquilina, Collina, and Palatina, the establishment of which was attributed to Servius Tullius (Varro L. L. 5.45-54). The division of the city into fourteen regiones dates from the principate of Augustus.

. His example was followed by Augustus (cp. Suet. Aug. 43. 1). It would be interesting to know what languages are meant beside Greek and Latin. On ludi theatri in general see Friedlaender (Eng. Tr.) ii, pp. 90-117.
. See below. :
. A trestle amphitheatre was erected (Dio 43. 22-3).

div.p: For similar displays in the Forum cp. Suet. Aug. 43; Liv. 31. 50.4; 39. 46. 2-3, &c.

p.note: . Cp. Dio 43. 23. 5 (Fulvius Sepinus, a senator, offered to fight but was forbidden: equites, however, were allowed to fight). Gladiators and actors were infames under normal circumstances (Lex. Iul. Mun. 113; Dig. 3. 2. 2. 5).
. A war-dance in armour (Dion. Hal. Ant. 7.72; Plin. 7. 204; 8.5). Cp. also Suet. Ner. 12. 2 and Ael. Spart. vit. Hadr. 19 for such displays at Rome. ..

div.p: §2. D. Laberius. A famous writer of Mimes. Laberius showed his resentment in the prologue to his play, which is preserved in Macrob. 2. 7. 3 (cp. especially 11. 10-15: et enim ipse di negare cui nihil potuerunt | hominem me denegare quis posset pati? \ ego bis tricenis annis actis sine nota | eques_Romanus e Lare egressus meo | domum revertar mimus ; nimirum hoc die | uno plus vixi mihi quam vivendum fuit. et ipse quoque actione subinde se... ulciscebatur inducto habitu Syri, qui ... exclamabat 'porro Quirites libertatem perdimus' et paulo post adiecit 'necesse est multos timeat quem multi timent'). Laberius competed against the still more famous mime-writer, Publilius Syrus, who gained the prize. T. Munatius Plancus also performed (Cic. Fam. 12. 18. 2; Gell. 17. 14. 2). For further references to Laberius see Sen. Contr. 7. 3. 9 and the younger Seneca, de Ira 2. 11. 3.

p.note: . 500,000 sesterces, the sum offered in advance by Caesar as a fee (Macrob. 1. c.).

. Actors were infames, and Laberius had forfeited his position as a knight (cp. quotation from his prologue-above). For the golden ring as the badge of knighthood see note on ins anulorum above, ch. 33.
, sc. ordines. The fourteen rows immediately behind the orchestra were assigned to the equestrian order by the lex Roscia of 67 B. C. (Liv. Epit. 99; Vell. Pat. 2. 32. 3; Cic. Mur. 40, etc.).
. See note on 76. I suggestum in orchestra.

. It is not clear whether these were the ordinary ludi Circenses or special performances at the ludi Victoriae Caesaris; the latter seems most likely. The Circus Maximus, originally laid out by Tarquinius Priscus (Liv. 1. 35. 8), was not completed with stone seats till the empire (Platner, Topogr., pp. 403-9); Pliny (36. 102) gives the dimensions.

. A ditch ten feet wide (Dion. Hal. Ant. 3. 68); Pliny (8.21) explains that it was designed to prevent the wild beasts (especially elephants) from breaking out. It was so called from the narrow strait separating Euboea from the mainland.
. A spectacular ride with elaborate manœuvres, described by Virgil (Aen. 5. 545-603); note especially the concluding lines:

div.p: Ascanius... priscos docuit celebrare Latinos, | quo puer ipse modo, secum quo Troia pubes; | Albani docuere suos; hinc maxima porro accepit Roma, et patrium servavit honorem ; | Troiaque nunc pueri, Troianum dicitur agmen. Despite its name it is probably an old Italic or Etruscan institution. Dio (43.23. 6) states that it was first publicly performed at Rome on this occasion, Plutarch (Cat. 3. 1) that it was first given at the public games by Sulla. It became frequent under Augustus (Suet. Aug. 43. 2.). See Prof. Lily Taylor in J. R. S. (1924), pp. 159–67. It is to be noted that according to Servius (ad Aen. 5. 602) the origin of the sport was described by Suetonius in libro de puerorum lusibus, possibly identical with his 'Games of the Greeks', possibly contained in his 'Roman festivals', or his 'Rome and Roman Customs'. See p. vii.

p.note: . Virgil (Aen. 5. 560) says that there were three turmae, each consisting of a leader followed by twelve boys; but the evolutions which ensue are carried out agmine partito (562); ср. also 580 olli discurrere pares. It is to this aspect of their evolutions that Suetonius here alludes.

div.p: §3. venationes. Hunts in the arena and fights with wild beasts. Caesar sought to outdo the great venatio given by Pompey in 55 B. C. (for which see Cic. Fam. 7. 1. 3; Dio 39. 38. 2) and built a hunting amphitheatre of wood for the purpose (Dio 43. 22. 3). For a record of slaughter at venationes see Mon. Anc. ch. 22 (about 3,500 beasts killed in 26 shows under Augustus). For venationes in general see Friedlaender (Eng. Tr.) ii, pp. 62-74). The first venatio at Rome was given by M. Fulvius Nobilior in 186 B. C. (Liv. 39. 22. 2).

p.note: . Cp. Dio 43. 23. 3 (number of elephants given as 40).

. The show took place in the Circus Maximus (Dio, l. c.), and the spina or barrier dividing the race course was removed, together with the erections, known as metae, at either end of it. These consisted each of three cones (metae) of gilded bronze. See Platner, Topogr., pp. 406 sqq.

. Greek athletic games first found a place in Roman shows in 186 B. C. at the games given by M. Fulvius Nobilior (Livy 39. 22. 2), when the performers were entirely Greek. The next athletic games of which we have any record at Rome were given by Sulla (App. 1. 99). By the time of Caesar they were acclimatized at Rome, though probably many of the competitors were Greek. The games given by Sulla drew so many competitors from Greece as to spoil the Olympic games. See Friedlaender (Eng. Tr.) ii, pp. 117-30.

div.p: § 4. navali proelio. The naumachia mentioned above, the first ever publicly shown at Rome. Cp. Vell. Pat. 2. 56. 1; Dio 43. 23. 4; Plut. Caes. 55. 3; App. 2. 102 (4,000 oarsmen and 2,000 marines). Cp. Mon. Anc. 23. A private naumachia is mentioned in Lucilius (14. 10, L. Mueller). See Friedlaender (Eng. Tr.) ii, pp. 74-6.

p.note: . The Codeta Minor on the Campus Martius (Dio 43.23. 4). The Codeta Maior was on the right bank of the Tiber (Festus, pp. 34 and 50, Linds.). The name describes marshy spots, so called from the abundance of mares-tails (equisetum) growing there (= caudeta).

div.p: § 1. fastos. The Roman year under the Republic had consisted of 355 days (based on a rough calculation of twelve lunar months). March, May, July (Quintilis), October had 31 days, February 28, and the remainder 29. To bring the Calendar into conformity with the solar year, every other year an intercalary month, alternately of 22 and 23 days, was inserted after Feb. 23. This, however, gave an average year of 366 days, and, although attempts were made at an early date to ensure correction of the error, the calendar fell into confusion, and in 191 B. C. the lex Acilia (Censorinus, de die natali, 20. 4-6; Solin. 1.43; Macrob. 1. 13. 31) gave the pontifices full control of the Calendar with power to make or omit intercalary months as they thought fit. While this inevitably gave rise to confusion and even to corruption (for an intercalary month might be inserted to suit private or political ends; cp. Censor. 20. 7; Plut. Caes. 59. 1; Macrob. I. 14. I; Dio 40. 62. 1; Cic. Fam. 8. 6. 5), the confusion became worse after 59 B. C. Between 54 and 46 B. C. only one intercalary month was inserted. On his return from Thapsus Caesar proceeded to the reform of the Calendar. The year was fixed at 365 days with an intercalary day at the end of February every fourth year. January, August (Sextilis) and December were lengthened from 29 to 31 days; April, June, September and November from 29 to 30 days. To adjust the confusion of the current Calendar, the year 46 B. C. had three intercalary months: (i) the usual month inserted after Feb. 23 (23 days), (ii) two abnormal intercalaries of 22 days inserted between November and December; an addition of 67 days in all. Macrobius styles the year annus confusionis. Pliny (18. 211-12) says that ✓ Caesar employed an Alexandrian astronomer named Sosigenes to devise the reform. Appian (2.154) and Macrobius (1. 14. 3) say that he adopted the Egyptian solar year; Plutarch (Caes. 59. 2) that he consulted the best experts; Dio (43. 26. 2) that he got his idea from his stay in Alexandria, adding that the error in the system amounts to I day in 1,461 years actually it is I day in 128 years. Full detail as to the Julian Calendar is to be found in Censorinus, 20. 8-10; Macrobius, 1. 14. For full modern discussions see Groebe in Drumann-Groebe, iii, pp. 755-827; R. Holmes, R. R. i, pp. 339-44, and iii, pp. 285-7; Anc. Britain, pp. 706-26; Class. Qu. (1912), pp. 74-81. It is to be noted that Suetonius himself wrote a work on the Roman Year, which not improbably was the
main source from which Censorinus, Macrobius, and Solinus (1. 34-48) derived their information. See p. vii.

p.note: : e.g. Pharsalus was fought on Aug. 9 (C. I. L. (ed. 2) I, pp. 244 and 248), yet the corn was barely ripe, the Calendar having got two months in advance of the sun.

. The words might by ancient methods of reckoning mean either every third year or every fourth. The meaning was mistaken almost at once, and in the first 34 years of the Julian Calendar there were 12 leap-years instead of 9 (Solin. 1. 44; Macrob. I. 14. 13-14). The error was rectified by Augustus, who stopped the observance of leap-years from 8 B. C. to A. D. 8.

div.p: § 2. cum intercalario, 'including the intercalary month'.

§ 1. senatum supplevit. In 47 B. C. he added certain knights, centurions, and subordinate officers to replace senators who had fallen in the war (Dio 42. 51. 5; cp. Cic. Phil. 8. 26 (Decidius Saxa)). In 46 B. C. he restored to the roll of the senate persons unworthy of it (Dio 43. 27. 2-an unpopular step). In 45 B. C. he raised the number of senators to 900 (Dio 43.47.2). Cp. also Cic. de Div. 2. 23 senatu quem maiore ex parte ipse cooptasset. For the admission of haruspices cp. Cic. Fam. 6. 18.2; of Spaniards cp. B. Afr. 28. 2; Cic. Phil. 11. 2; of Gauls see 80. 2n. Finally, by doubling the number of quaestors he automatically raised the annual accession of fresh members; see on quaestorum below. See Willems, Le Sénat, i, pp. 581-97.

p.note: , 'admitted fresh persons to the ranks of the patricians'. Cp. Dio 43. 47. 3. This was done by a lex Cassia (probably named after L. Cassius, tr. pl. 45-44 B. C.; see Cic. Phil. 3.23). Cp. also Suet. Aug. 2 (The Octavii restored to the patriciate from which they had lapsed). For similar action under the principate cp. Mon. Anc., ch. 8 (ad init.). This honour was conferred partly as a social distinction, partly to recruit the depleted ranks of the patriciate; cp. Tac. Ann. 11. 25, where the admission of fresh families to the patriciate is explained by the words exhaustis (gentibus) quas dictator Caesar lege Cassia, princeps Augustus lege Saenia sublegere.

. There were ten praetors in 46 B. c. (Dio 42.51. 3); fourteen in 45 B. C. (Dio 43.47.2); sixteen in 44 B. C. (Dio 43. 49. 1; 51.4). The increase was due to the rise in the number of provinces. For Caesar's purpose in the increase of the number of magistrates see F. B. Marsh, Class. Journal, xx (May, 1925), pp. 451-64.
. Two new plebeian aediles were appointed to take charge of the corn supply (cp. Dio 43. 51. 3); they were known as aediles cereales (Gell. 16. 7. 12; Dig. 1. 2. 2. 32). 3333 H
. The number was raised to forty in 45 B. с. (Dio 43. 47. 2). As in the case of the praetors this increase was to meet the demands of the new provinces.

. A fourth tresvir capitalis (C. I. L. 9. 2845), and a fourth tresvir monetalis were appointed (Grueber, Coins R. Rep. in B. M. i, p. 542, 44 B. C.). The colleges of pontifices, augures, and quindecimviri sacris faciundis were each increased by one in 47 B. C. (Dio 42. 51. 4).

, 'deprived of their rank'. Probably with special reference to the action of Appius Claudius, censor in 50 B. C., who (cp. Dio 40. 63. 3) struck a large number of senators off the roll, thereby converting them into Caesarians. Sallust was one of the victims (Dio, 1. c., and Invect. in Sall. 6. 16).

. More especially the victims of Pompey's new law de ambitu of 52 B. C. (Caes. B. C. 3. 1. 4; Cic. Att. 10. 4. 8). For the restoration of such persons by tribunicial action, cp. Cic. Phil. 13. 27 (T. Plancus).

div.p: § 2. comitia partitus est. This seems to date from the last year of Caesar's life. A bill was brought in by L. Antonius (tr. pl. Dec. 45-44 B. C.) by which 'he and Caesar shared the elections', as Cicero rhetorically expresses it (Phil. 7. 16). Dio (43.51. 3) bears this out; he states that in 44 B. C., when the magistrates were appointed for three years in advance, owing to Caesar's prospective absence from Rome on his Parthian campaign, half were chosen by Caesar, as he was legally entitled to do, though in actual fact he chose the whole of them. Similarly under the principate Augustus shares the elections with the comitia (Tac. Ann. 1. 15. 1), Tiberius with the senate (ib. 15. 2). Our knowledge as to the earlier elections during the Civil War is derived from Dio and is somewhat vague. In 48 (for 47 B. C.) all the elections, except to the plebeian magistracies, fell into his hands; by the decree of the people he appointed the pro-praetors without sortitio, while in the case of the pro-consuls the sortitio was merely nominal (Dio 42. 20. 4). In 47 (for 46 B. C.) the ten praetors were appointed by Caesar (and probably all the non-plebeian magistracies as well); cp. Dio 42. 51. 3. In 46 (for 45 B. C.) the appointment of all magistrates was voted to him by the senate (Dio 43. 14. 5). In 45 (for 44 B. C.) the consuls were appointed by Caesar, the remaining magistrates nominally elected 'since Caesar would not accept the appointment of them', but in reality all were appointed by him. The pro-magistrates were appointed without sortitio (Dio 43. 47. 1).

p.note: , etc. For this extension of the Republican practice of commendatio by distinguished persons, as further developed under the principate cp. Tac. Ann. 1. 15. 2, where Tiberius commends candidates sine repulsa et ambitu designandos.
. The terms for which Caesar received his successive dictatorships, and the length of time during which he actually held

div.p: them, are matters of dispute. The following is a brief statement of the case. Dict. I. From June or July to December 49 B. C. (Caes. B. C. 2. 21.5). Dict. II. After Pharsalus, i. e. from late in 48 B. C. or early in 47 B. C., until early in 46 B. C.; possibly for one year (so Plut. Caes. 51. 1; Dio 42. 20. 3). Dict. III. After Thapsus (April, 46 B. C.) for a term of ten years (Dio 43. 1. 1; Grueber, Coins R. Rep. in B.M., i, pp. 537-9). Dict. IV. Caesar assumed this style on completion of the first year of his third dictatorship, and maintained it to some point not later than Feb. 15 in 44 B. C. (Bell. Hisp. 2.1; Grueber, i, pp. 540-2; C. I. L. (ed. 2), i, p. 50). Dict. perpet. Caesar received this new title not later than Feb. 15 (44 в. с.); Сіс. Phil. 2. 87; Liv. Epit. 116; Plut. Caes. 57. 1; App. 2. 106; Dio 44. 8.4; Grueber, Coins R. Rep. i, pp. 545-6. See also 76. I below. For fuller discussion cp. R. Holmes, R. R., iii, pp. 564-7; Drumann-Groebe, iii, pp. 735-9; P. Schnabel, Klio, xix, pp. 354-5.

p.note: . Sulla had made a law debarring the children of the persons whom he had proscribed from holding public office. An attempt was made in 63 B. C. to get the disqualification removed (cp. Quint. II. 1. 85 for Cicero's arguments against it). For Caesar's action (49 B. C. on return from Spain) see Dio 41. 18.2; Plut. Caes. 37. 1; Vell. Pat. 2. 43.

. These had provided a third of the juries since 70 B. C. (Ascon., p. 67, Cl.; Cic. Att. 1. 16. 3). They were once genuine officials (paymasters to the troops; cp. Cat. ap. Gell. 6 (7). 10; Varr. L. L. 5. 180). The iudices bearing this name have been held to be citizens whose census ranked next below that of the equites (i. e. which fell between 300,000 and 400,000 sesterces), a not improbable hypothesis, but unsupported by direct evidence. For their abolition by Caesar cp. Phil. 1. 19-20; Dio 43. 25. 1 (46 B. C.), where the motive is said to have been the removal of the most corruptible portion of the juries. For a discussion of their status cp. R. Holmes, R. R., i, pp. 391-5; Denniston, Cic. Phil. i, ii, pp. 176-8.

div.p: § 3. recensum. This, as Suetonius recognizes, was distinct from the regular census conducted by the censors on the Campus Martius. No regular census was held between the years 70-28 B. C. (see Mon. Anc. ch. 8, lustrum post annum alterum et quadragesimum feci). Dio (43. 21. 4) also regards this as a special investigation, in connexion with the corn-dole (46 B.C.). On the other hand (43.25. 2) he speaks of census which Caesar conducted as if he was censor. Similarly Livy (Epit. 115), Plutarch (Caes. 55. 3), and Appian (2. 102) seem to make no distinction. For the whole subject see Hardy, Problems, ch. 8, esp. pp. 296-303.

p.note: , 'street by street'. The vici of this date must not be confounded with the vici forming subdivisions of the fourteen regiones established by Augustus (Suet. Aug. 30. 1). Cp. the κατ' οἰκίαν ἀπογραφή for taxation in Ptolemaic Egypt (Wilcken, Gr. H 2

div.p: Ostraka i. 442). It is scarcely necessary to suppose, however, that Caesar owed the idea to his knowledge of Egypt.

p.note: . The large blocks (insulae) of tenement-houses in which the poorer classes lived. The recensus was, in effect, a poverty test. Recent excavations at Ostia have revealed the nature of these lofty buildings, which seem to have had a strong resemblance to the tenement buildings to be seen in the older quarters of Rome and Naples to-day; Vaglieri, Ostia, plans 2-4; Mau-Kelsey, Pompeii, pp. 33-4-

. Dio (43. 21. 4) states that Caesar reduced by one-half the recipients of the dole (increased enormously by the civil wars, and more especially since the lex Clodia of 58 B. C. (Ascon., p. 8, Cl.; Cic. Sest. 55). Augustus fixed the number at 200,000 after seriously contemplating the abolition of doles (Mon. Anc. ch. 15; Suet. Aug. 42. 2; Dio 55. 10. 1).
, 'that fresh meetings might not be set on foot at any future time for the revision of the roll'.

. From the lex Iulia Municipalis (1-19) it may be inferred that applicants gave in their names (professio) to the praetor urbanus to be placed on a waiting list. The persons thus registered would ballot (subsortitio) for a place on the roll. See Hardy, R. Laws and Charters, pp. 141-2, 150 n.; Problems, p. 246.

div.p: § 1. colonias. Such as Carthage, Corinth, Arelate (Arles), Carthago Nova (Cartagena), and many others. See R. Holmes, R. R., iii, pp. 321-2; Meyer, Caesars Monarchie, pp. 483-96; Kornemann in Pauly-Wissowa, Realenc. iv. 1. 524-34. The lists are not absolutely certain, as the colonies planted by Julius and Augustus cannot always be distinguished.

p.note: , 'that the population might be kept up'.
. The reading of the MSS. is clearly wrong. quadraginta, quinquaginta, and sexaginta have all been conjectured, and any one of them may be right.
, "who was not bound by the oath of allegiance', i. e. who was not on foreign service.
. Italian emigration was at its highest in the first century B. C.; see J. Hatzfeld, Les trafiquants italiens dans l'Orient hellénique, ch. 3.
. See 2. I n.
, were cattle-farmers'.

. Caesar presumably had in mind the danger of slave-herdsmen, who were often armed and might be dangerous. Cp. the shepherd slaves who joined Spartacus (Plut. Crass. 9.4). There is no evidence that this was in any way the beginning of an attack upon slavery. It was no novelty, since

div.p: a similar provision was made in the Licinian Law of 367 B. C. with regard to farm-slaves in general. ...

p.note: . Physicians were in the majority of cases Greeks. There is no parallel for such a wholesale enfranchisement of special professions to be found elsewhere. But Augustus in a general expulsion of peregrini from Rome excepted medicos et praeceptores (Suet. Aug. 42.3). liberalium artium doctores would include grammatici, rhetoricians and philosophers. For the latter cp. Caesar's grant of the citizenship to Cratippus the Peripatetic at the request of Cicero (Plut. Cic. 24). For Caesar's general franchise policy see Meyer, Caesars Monarchie, pp. 483-96. See also Suet. 80. 2 peregrinis...

div.p: §2. de pecuniis mutuis. Cp. Caes. B. C. 3: 1. 2 (48 Б.С.). cum fides tota Italia esset angustior neque creditae pecuniae solverentur, constituit ut arbitri darentur; peress fierent aestimationés possessionum et rerum, quanti quaeque earum ante bellum fuisset, atque eae creditoribus traderentur. Suetonius adds a fresh detail

p.note: , si quid usurae nomine numeratum

. This cancellation of arrears of interest was legal, usury being forbidden by law (Liv. 7. 42. I (342 В.С.); Cato, Pr. R. R.; Tac. Ann. 6. 16. 1; App. 1. 54), although the law had been treated as a dead letter. Further, it is to be noted that property had deteriorated in value since the outbreak of the civil war, and consequently the worth of the piece of property handed over to the creditor would be considerably less than the actual sum owed. Cp. also App. 2 48; Dio 41. 37-8 (Caesar also passes a law against hoarding, forbidding any one to hold more than 60,000 sesterces in silver and gold). There are many references in Cicero's letters to the 'tightness of money' about this period (cp. Att. 7. 18.4; 9.9.4; 10. 11. 2; Fam. 16.5). For reference to Caesar's legislation see Fam. 11. 27. 7; 11. 28. 2 (Matius, Caesar's friend, lost money by it); 13. 8. 2 (praedia in aestimationem). Tacitus (1. c.) alludes to a law of Caesar's de modo credendi possidendique intra Italiam. It is suggested by Nipperdey (ad loc.) that this law was permanent, whereas the measure described here and by Caesar (1. c.) was merely a settlement of the immediate needs of the situation in 48 В. С.

. Cp. note on obaeratorum (27.2). The demand for the cancellation of debts was one of the catchwords of the Catilinarian conspiracy. Caesar (B. C. 3. 1. 3) expressly states that these measures were designed ad timorem novarum tabularum tollendum minuendumque, qui fere bella et civiles dissensiones sequi consuevit. Cicero (Off. 2. 84), writing in 44 B. C., unjustly remarks that Caesar carried out his old Catilinarian design. Caesar did not succeed in crushing the demand for novae tabulae. Not long after his departure for Epirus, M. Caelius Rufus (one of the praetors) promulgated a law for the cancellation of debts;

div.p: rioting ensued and the consul Servilius brought the matter before the Senate, with the result that Caelius was deposed (Caes. B. C. 3. 20-2; Dio 42. 22-5). In the next year (47 B. C.) Dolabella attempted to cancel debts and abolish house-rents; there was further rioting, which Antony managed to suppress (Dio 42.29-33; Plut. Ant. 9. 1; Liv. Epit. 113).

p.note: , 'for which a draft had been given'; cp. Cic. Att. 16. 2. I de Publilio autem, quod perscribi oportet, non puto moram esse faciendam.

div.p: § 3. collegia. A senatus consultum of 64 B.C. had disbanded collegia, which instead of being legitimate guilds or associations were employed for political purposes adversus rempublicam (Ascon., p. 7, Cl.). Cloditis restored these in 58 B. C. (Cic. Sest. 55; Pis. 9). Caesar once more disbanded them, making special exception in the case of the Jewish synagogues (Joseph. Ant. 14. 10. 8. 216). The evil had sprung up again in the principate of Augustus, who once more dissolved all praeter antiqua et legitima (Suet. Aug. 32. 1). Cp. also the lex Ursonensis 106.

p.note: . Apart from the instances quoted in this and the succeeding chapter, the only laws clearly attributable to Caesar which have any definite bearing on Suetonius' statement would seem to be the following: (1) The Lex Iulia de Repetundis of 59 B. C. Cicero, who repeatedly alludes to this statute (Att. 5.16.3; Sest. 135; Pis. 37; Rab. Post. 8) merely states in general terms that its sanctions were sharper than those of its predecessors. The Corpus Iuris mentions the penalties of fourfold restitution with an action against heirs (Cod. Theod. 9. 27; Cod. Just. 9. 27. 1-2), of exile and death (Dig. 48. 11. 7. 3). The death penalty was an aggravation due to a reinforcing decretum of an emperor; the others no doubt were introduced by Caesar; for a fuller discussion see Tyrrell and Purser, Corr. of Cicero (2nd ed.) iii, App. 2, pp. 327-8. (2) A Lex de Maiestate, which made aquae et ignis interdictio compulsory, whereas previously it may have been at the discretion of the court (Cic. Phil. 1. 9. 23). (3) A similar Lex de Vi (ibid.; Dio 44. 49. 3; Dig. 1. 21. 1; 22.5.3.5:48. 2. 3. 4). The Digest further refers to Leges Iuliae de Peculatu and de Residuis (Dig. 22. 5. 13; 48. 13). But it is not certain whether these belong to Caesar or to Augustus (see the contrary statements in Mommsen, Strafr., p. 128, and Botsford, Roman Assemblies, p. 455, n. 9); and in any case we know nothing about their sanctions.

. Murderers of near relatives. This law was probably a modification of the Lex Pompeia of 55 B. C., which prescribed death in cases of murder of parents or grandparents, and interdictio in less heinous cases (Dig. 48. 9. 1 and 9; Greenidge, Legal Proc., p. 506). It is with the latter penalty that Caesar's law is concerned.
. Allusion unknown.
. Presumably those whose fortune fell below a certain level.

div.p: § 1. ius dixit. That the dictator, like all magistrates with imperium, had iurisdictio is clear from Livy (41. 9. 11). For examples cp. Val. Max. 6. 2. 11. A man who had stood security for Pompey in 52 B. C., on the money being demanded after Pompey's death, asked Caesar whether he was bound to pay. Despite the fact that the man taunted Caesar with the sale of Pompey's property, he ordered the money to be paid ex suo fisco (Sen. de Ben. 5. 24. 1). A veteran from Munda brought a dispute concerning his lands before Caesar, who decided in his favour (a delightful story, well told). Dio (43.47.4) says that he released certain persons who were on the point of being condemned for bribery, and was consequently suspected of taking bribes himself. This suggests arbitrary interference with the quaestiones perpetuae rather than iurisdictio in the ordinary sense. Nor again can the abnormal case of the trial of King Deiotarus held in Caesar's house strictly come under this head. Later we find the princeps following Caesar's precedent; cp. Suet. Aug. 33 (so, too, Claudius, Trajan, etc.).

p.note: . See note on poenas facinorum auxit (42. 3).
: i. e. though no previous adultery was suspected.

, 'customs and harbour-dues'; abolished in 60 в. С. after Pompey's new annexations in the East, by a bill proposed by the praetor Metellus Nepos (Dio 37.51.3; Cic. Att. 2. 16. I portoriis Italiae sublatis; Q. F. I. 1. 33, where the abolition is said to have been due to the exactions of the portitores rather than the incidence of the portoria themselves). Caesar's restoration of the portoria on foreign imports must have been due in the main to the needs of the revenue.

. A comparatively late luxury at Rome, though of ancient use in the case of sick persons. Eusebius (Hieron.) Chron., p. 238 (Fotheringham) states that the use of litters was restricted by Caesar to women who had neither husband nor children and were under forty-five.
. This law was reinforced by Augustus, who forbade the wearing of 'purple' (crimson) save by senators and magistrates (Dio 49. 16. 1).

div.p: § 2. sumptuariam. Cp. Dio 43. 25. 2 (expenditure not only regulated by law, but checked by police measures). There are various allusions to the working of the law in Cicero's letters of 46 and 45 B. C., e. g. Fam. 9. 15.5; 9.26.3 (Cicero's expenses on food are well within the provisions of the law). In Att. 12. 35 and 36 he alludes to a law restricting the amount that might be expended

upon tombs. Despite the date (45 B. C.), it has been held that the law alluded to was that passed by Sulla (cp. Plut. Sull. 35.2-3; Tyrrell and Purser on Att. 12. 35. 2). It is doubtful, however, whether Sulla's law would have been maintained in full force till 45 B. C. Caesar's law seems to have proved a failure; cp. Cic. Att. 13.7 (45 В. С.).
