Such was the usual fate of sumptuary laws; for a list of earlier laws see Gell. 2. 24: Macrob. 3. 17. 11. Augustus re-enacted the law of Caesar (Suet. Aug. 34. 1).

§ 1. Martis templum. There were already two temples of Mars in existence, one near the Circus Flaminius, another outside the Porta Capena; see Platner, Topogr., pp. 349 and 432. The site selected by Caesar was the Codeta Minor (see 39. 4). It is conceivable that Cic. Att. 13. 42. 3 (opinor augures velle habere ad templum effandum) may refer to the dedication of the site as a templum. But the site had not yet been filled in in 43 B. C. (Dio 45. 17. 8), and the temple was never built. The temples of Mars erected by Augustus were quite distinct, one being on the Capitol, the other in the Forum Augustum. theatrum. Begun in 44 B. C. (Dio 43. 49. 2-foundations only) and completed by Augustus in 13 or II B. C. (Plin. 8. 65). It was then named after Marcellus, Augustus' adopted son, who died in 23 B. C. (Dio 53.30. 5-6; Suet. Aug. 29.4; Mon. Anc., ch. 21). A large portion of the façade is still visible in the Piazza Montanara, lying between the Tiber and the south-west end of the Capitoline. But Tarpeio monti accubans suggests that Caesar intended that it should be built actually against the Capitoline, whereas there is a considerable distance between the Theatrum Marcelli and the hill. Suetonius further suggests that the theatre was not actually built (cp. destinabat and sect. 4). The alleged identity of the theatres was probably nominal rather than real; it may be noted also that it was smaller than the theatrum Pompei, which is inconsistent with summae magnitudinis. Augustus probably used only a portion of the site.

§ 2. ius civile. The 'judge-made' law, embodied in the formulae of the two praetors. For this design of codification cp. Isidor. Etym. 5. 1. 5, leges autem redigere in libris primus cos. Pompeius instituere voluit, sed non perseveravit obtrectatorum metu. deinde Caesar coepit facere, sed ante interfectus est. Rome had to wait till Justinian for its Code. Probably the work was placed in the hands of C. Trebatius (see 78. 1), who is cited by Dig. 1. 2. 2.45 as an authority and wrote de Iure Civili (Porph. ad Hor. S. 2. 1. 4). For a brief account of the formulae of the praetors see Greenidge, Legal Proc., pp. 83 sqq.

p.note: . Another unfulfilled project. The first library at

div.p: Rome was established in the Atrium Libertatis by Asinius Pollio (Plin. 35. 10; 7. 115; Isid. Etym. 6. 5). Augustus founded two more, one in the Porticus Octaviae (Suet. Gr. 21), the other attached to the temple of Palatine Apollo (Suet. Gr. 20; Aug. 29. 3). After that libraries multiplied both at Rome and in the municipia.

p.note: , 'open to the public'.
. See on 34. 2. A most suitable choice. He was the one living writer whose statue was placed in the library of the Atrium Libertatis (Plin. 7. 115).

div.p: § 3. Pomptinas paludes. The Pontine marshes were still habitable in the fourth century B. C., as the establishment of colonies in that region shows. For Caesar's scheme cp. Dio 44. 5. 1 (44 В. С.); Plut. Caes. 58. 3; Cic. Phil. 5. 7. The task has been many times attempted and is now once more in hand.

p.note: . A large lake in the Abruzzo, drained with only temporary success by Claudius into the Liris (Tac. Ann. 12. 56; Suet. Claud. 20. 1). It was at last drained successfully by Prince Torlonia into the Anio (1865-74).

, 'to build a road'. There were eventually three roads to the Adriatic: (i) the old Via Flaminia to Fanum; (ii) the Salaria to Firmum; (iii) the Valeria to Aternum (see M. Besnier in Daremberg-Saglio, VIA, pp. 794-6). C. I. L. 6. 31603 mentions the prolongation of the Salaria from Reate, probably by Augustus in 17-16 B. C. This probably represents Caesar's design.

. Cp. Plut. Caes. 58. 4; Dio 44. 5. I (44 B. C.); Plin. 4. 10 perfodere navigabili alveo angustias eas tentavere Demetrius rex, dictator Caesar, Gaius princeps, Domitius Nero nefasto, ut omnium patet exitu, incepto; Suet. Calig. 21; Ner. 19. 2. The work was finally accomplished in 1893. This design was probably conceived in connexion with Caesar's foundation of a colony at Corinth (Plut. Caes. 57.3; Strab. 8. 6. 23, p. 381). Plutarch (Caes. 58. 3) mentions two other projects: (i) the diversion of the Tiber to enter the sea at Circeii, (ii) a new port at Ostia. Cicero (Att. 13. 33 a. 1) mentions a plan of diverting the Tiber to run close under the Mons Vaticanus, so that the Campus Vaticanus might be joined to the Campus Martius.

. The Daci and Getae had raided Thrace and Pontus, and continued to cause alarm until 29 B. C. Caesar's measure was probably intended to safeguard communications with the East during his Parthian campaign, and was something more than mere frontier-protection. Cp. App. 2. 110; 3. 25 (also Illyr. 13); Vell. Pat. 2. 59.4; Suet. Aug. 8. 2; Strabo 7.3.5 (p. 298). Plutarch (Caes. 58.2; cp. also Zonar. 10. 11) seems to suggest that the Parthian expedition was to come first; he states that Caesar intended after conquering the Parthians to sweep back by way of the Caspian, Caucasus, Scythia, and Germany to Gaul, thus shortening the frontier of the Roman Empire. Even Caesar can hardly have contemplated this

div.p: as an immediately feasible design, though he may have spoken of it as ideally desirable or as a task that would some day have to be undertaken.

p.note: . A revanche for Carrhae. The Parthians had remained quiet between 49-45 B. C. Pompey had vainly sought their aid in 49 B. C. (Caes. B. C. 3. 82.5; Dio 41.55.3342.2.5 44.45.3). But in 44 B. C. Caecilius Bassus, a Pompeian, had usurped the government of Syria, and a Parthian army had advanced to aid him (Cic. Att. 14. 9. 3 (May 44 B. C.); Deiot. 23-5; Liv. Epit. 114; App. 3.77; 4.58; Dio 47. 26-7; Joseph. Ant. 14. 11. 1; B. Jud. 1. 10. 10). Appian (2. 110) states that Caesar had collected sixteen legions and 10,000 cavalry for the campaign and had actually sent them across the Adriatic. The statement that they had already crossed is probably an exaggeration. Dio (43. 51. 1) says that the project was popular at Rome.
. Territory west of the Upper Euphrates, on the Erzingyan-Erzerum road. This line of advance was used by Corbulo in A.D. 58 (Tac. Ann. 13. 39. 1).
. Caesar intended to avoid the rashness which had involved Crassus in disaster.

div.p: § 1. excelsa statura, colore candido. Cp. Vell. Pat. 2. 41. 3 forma excellentissimus omnium civium; App. 2. 151 εὐφυεῖς ἄμφω (Caesar and Alexander) καὶ καλοί; Plut. Caes. 17. 2 τὴν ἔξιν ἰσχνὸς καὶ τὴν σάρκα λευκὸς καὶ ἁπαλός; Cic. Brut. 261 rationem dicendi tenet voce motu forma etiam magnificam et generosam; Dio 43.43 τό τε ὅλον τῇ τε ᾿Αφροδίτῃ πᾶς ἀνεκεῖτο καὶ πείθειν πάντας ἤθελεν ὅτι καὶ ἄνθος τι ὥρας ἀπ᾿ αὐτῆς ἔχοι. The numerous portraits of Caesar vary so much in character that the conclusions drawn by the critics are of very little value. This applies not merely to the sculptured portraits, but to the coins as well. See Bernoulli, Römische Ikonographie, i, pp. 145-81, pl. 14-15; (coins) pl. 3, nos. 53-71; F. J. Scott, The Portraitures of Julius Caesar; R. Holmes, Ancient Gaul (ed. 2), pp. xix-xxiv (a robust and entertaining piece of criticism).

p.note: , 'rounded', 'shapely'. ...
, 'somewhat large' in proportion to the rest of the face.
. For his physical vigour cp. 57. 1. Plutarch (Caes. 17. 2) holds that this vigour was due to will-power rather than to his constitution.

, 'towards the close of his life'. These fainting-fits are distinguished by Suetonius from his epileptic seizures. See next note. He was apparently indisposed at the time of his visit to Cicero (Att. 13. 52. I-Dec., 45 B.C.); cp. the familiar ἐμετικὴν

div.p: agebat. But from that no real inference as to his general health can be drawn. See also below, 81.4; 86. 1.

p.note: . Epilepsy, so called because such seizures were considered of evil omen and caused the adjournment of public assemblies at which they occurred. Plutarch (Caes. 17. 2) says that his first fit occurred at Corduba in 46 B.C.; but (in 53. 3) states that according to some authorities he was suffering from his usual complaint' at Thapsus, and consequently took no personal part in the battle. Appian (2. 110-44 B. C.) also mentions his liability to epilepsy.
. Three such instances are recorded; at Corduba and Thapsus (see above) and a possible example in Plutarch (Caes. 60. 2), where epilepsy is urged as an excuse for his not rising to greet the Senate.

div.p: § 2. morosior, 'somewhat fastidious'. Cp. Dio 43. 43. 2.

p.note: , with the scissors; raderetur, with the razor.

, 'had superfluous hair plucked out'. A mark of effeminacy; cp. Scip. ap. Gell. 6. 12 nam qui cotidie unguentatus adversum speculum ornetur, cuius supercilia radantur, tur, qui barba volsa feminibusque subvolsis ambulet-eumne quisquam dubitet quin idem fecerit quod cinaedi facere solent? Prop. 4. 8. 23 vulsi ...nepotis; Quint. 8. Pr. 19 corpora si quis vulsa atque fucata muliebriter comat, etc. Cp. Gk. τίλλεσθαι, παρατίλλεσθαι. Hence exprobraverunt in the next clause.
. Cp. 51 moechum calvom adducimus. Dio 43. 43. I gives a similar account.

. Cp. Dio 43. 43. 1; the laurel crown appears on his coins; cp. Hill, Hist. Rom. Coins, pl. 12. 66; Grueber, Coins R. Rep. in B. M., pl. 54. The laurel was worn by triumphatores (Plin. 15. 137). Pompey received the ius laureae (Vell. Pat. 2. 40. 4), and it is a regular imperial attribute as coins of the principate show. For Caesar's corona civica (oak-leaves) cp. 2. 1.

div.p: § 3. lato clavo. On the tunic; two vertical stripes from the neck; cp. Daremberg-Saglio, i, p. 1243.

p.note: . Both the fringes and the length of the tunic-sleeves were marks of effeminacy; cp. Gell. 7. 12. 1 tunicis uti virum prolixis ultra brachia et usque ad primores manus ac prope in digitos Romae atque omni in Latio indecorum fuit. eas tunicas Graeco vocabulo chiridotas appellaverunt, feminisque solis vestem longe lateque diffusam decoram existimaverunt.

. The girdle was not worn with the laticlave tunic as a rule. With the ordinary tunic it was worn, but it was regarded as a mark of effeminacy to wear it loose. Hence Sulla's remark below. Cp. the use of discinctus in Hor. Epod. 1. 34 discinctus... nepos; cp. also Sen. Ep. 114. 4 and 6.
. Dio 43.43.4 tells the same story about

div.p: Sulla and puts a remark on the same subject in the mouth of Cicero : τὸ δ᾽ οὖν χαῦνον τοῦ ζώματος αὐτοῦ ὁ μὲν Σύλλας ὑπετόπησεν ὥστε καὶ ἀποκτεῖναι αὐτὸν ἐθελῆσαι, τοῖς τε ἐξαιτησαμένοις εἰπεῖν ὅτι ἐγὼ μὲν χαριοῦμαι τοῦτον ὑμῖν, ὑμεῖς μέντοι καὶ πάνυ τοῦτον τὸν κακῶς ζωννύμενον φυλάττεσθε. ὁ δὲ δὴ Κικέρων οὐ συνενόησεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ σφαλεὶς ἔφη ὅτι οὐκ ἄν ποτε προσεδόκησα τὸν κακῶς οὕτω ζωννύμενον Πομπηίου κρατήσειν. Plutarch (Caes. 4. 4) says that Caesar's dandified appearance dulled Cicero's suspicions.

p.note: . A street rising from the Forum to the Esquiline; Platner, Topogr., p. 18.
. On Lake Nemi, built in 50 B.C. (Cic. Att. 6. 1. 25). He had other villas at Tibur (Invect. in Sall. 7. 19), at Labici (83. 1), at Baiae (Sen. Ep. 51. 11). ...
: i.e. built with borrowed money and still far from completed.
. He carried materials for constructing these in any place where he made a long stay. sectilia = made of slabs of coloured marble, as opposed to mosaics (tessellata).

. The mussel-pearls still found in Scottish rivers. The pearls on the breastplate dedicated by Caesar in the temple of Venus Genetrix were British. Cp. Pliny (9. 116) who describes them as parvae et discolores; cp. Tac. Agr. 12. 7 subfusca et liventia. Pearls became fashionable at Rome after Pompey's triumph in 61 B. C. (Plin. 37. 12; see Deutsch, Cl. Journ. (1923-4), pp. 503-5). Cp. also the pearl given to Servilia (50. 2). The alleged motive is obviously absurd. For Caesar's real motives see B. G. 4. 20. He was generally criticized for invading a country so poor that nothing was to be gained thereby (Plut. Caes. 23. 3; Cic. Att. 4. 18. 5).
: embossed work in metal.
: of good figure. politiora: well-trained and educated.
, 'forbade these purchases to be entered in his accounts'. On the other hand, in the next chapter Suetonius mentions the strictness of his domestica disciplina.

. Soldiers wearing the sagum (woollen military cloak) or Greeks wearing the pallium (ἱμάτιον). For the size of Caesar's retinue cp. Cic. Att. 13. 52, where he complains of the impossibility of entertaining a man with a retinue of 2,000. But probably the bulk of the 2,000 were troops on the move.
. Romans of good birth.
. Cp. Dio 44. 39. Ι τά τε ἴδια εὐοικότατός τε ἅμα καὶ εὐδαπανώτατος ἐγένετο, ἀκριβὴς μὲν ὢν ἐς τὸ τὰ ὑπάρχοντα διαρκῶς φυλάξαι, δαψιλὴς δὲ ἐς τὸ τὰ προσήκοντα ἀφειδῶς ἀναλῶσαι.
. Contrast the bad manners of the host in Juvenal (5. 67-76), who was guilty of such invidious distinctions.

div.p: § 1. Nicomedis contubernium. Cp. 2. 1 and 22. 2.

p.note: . Fr. Poet. Rom., p. 322. See note on 73, Gaio Calvo.
. See 4. I n.
. See 9. 2 n.

. sponda is commonly used of the outer edge of the bed, pluteus of the interior (cp. Isid. 20. 11. 5; Mart. 3. 91. 9). But here spondam interiorem can only mean the inner edge and is used as a synonym for paelicem.

div.p: § 2. edicta Bibuli. See 9. 2; 20. I. M. Brutus. There is no evidence as to the source of this quotation.

p.note: . Unknown.
. Cp. Cic. Att. 2. 8. 1 (the younger Curio calls the triumvirs reges).
. See 23. I.
. A Ganymede.

div.p: § 3. Cicero. Not in any extant work.

p.note: . Nysa was the daughter of Nicomedes III, Caesar's host. She was named after her mother; cp. Sall. H. 4, fr. 69. 9 (ed. Maurenbrecher, p. 184). Gellius (5. 13. 6) quotes from a speech of Caesar's under the title pro Bithynis. But that speech was apparently delivered before luncus, governor of Bithynia; see note on 4.

div.p: § 4. Gallico triumpho. Cp. 37. 1; 51. 1. For the licence granted on these occasions cp. Dion. Hal. Ant. 7. 72; Liv. 39.7.3; Vell. Pat. 2. 67; Mart. 1. 5, etc. Dio (43. 20. 2) mentions other jibes against his foibles, such as those given by Suetonius in 51. I and 80. 3. He also states that the people admired his good nature,
and that he himself was pleased with their jests, always excepting those dealing with the Nicomedes scandal, which he denied on oath, 'thereby incurring greater ridicule '.

p.note: , etc. Trochaic tetrameter catalectic. The second line is weak and unnecessary, and is omitted in the best MSS.
. Sensu obsceno.

div.p: § 1. Postumiam Servi Sulpici. Wife of the consul Servius Sulpicius mentioned above (29. 1). For another possible amour of hers cp. Cic. Att. 5. 21. 9. ...

p.note: . Probably the daughter of Lollius Palicanus, tr. pl. 71 B.C. Her husband Gabinius was the consul of 58 B. C. He entered Caesar's service in 49 B. C. The most obvious time for this liaison would have been 66-62, when Gabinius was on service with Pompey.
. Described in Cic. Fam. 5. 8. 2 as praestantissimam omnium feminarum, but not above suspicion (cp. Plut. Cic. 25. 2 ad fin.).
. Pompey's third wife; unfaithful to him during his absence and divorced by him (Cic. Att. 1. 12. 3-Jan. 61 в.с.). Ср. also Plut. Pomp. 42. 6; Ascon. Scaur. 20.
. For the elder see 9. 2; 52. 3. For the younger see 29. 2.
. Iulia the daughter of Caesar (married 59 B. C., see 21. I).

div.p: §2. Serviliam. Niece of Drusus, tr. pl. 91 B. C.; married (i) M. Brutus the elder, (ii) Silanus, cos. 62 B. C.; left a widow soon after 62 B. C. For her amorous correspondence with Caesar see Plut. Cat. 24. 1; Brut. 5. 2. For the rumour that Brutus was Caesar's son cp. 82.2; Plut. Brut. 5. 1; App. 2. 112. But Brutus was too old, being born in 85 в. с. (Cic. Brut. 230, 324; Gelzer in Pauly-Wissowa, 10. 1, col. 974).

p.note: . 6,000,000 sesterces. Cp. Metella's pearl in Hor. S. 2. 3. 239 (1,000,000) and Cleopatra's (Plin. 9. 119-text doubtful); Macrob. 3. 17.5 (10,000,000); both stories are, however, probably mythical.
. Cicero (Att. 14. 21. 3) speaks of her as being in possession of the estate of Pontius Aquila at Naples: cp. 78.2.

, 'since there is a third knocked off', i. e. nothing is charged for Tertia! and yet again with a second double entendre ='since Tertia has been made his mistress', since the verb may be used in matrimonium or in stuprum.
, etc. Troch. tetram. catal. with dactyl in third foot of second line.
, 'squandered in harlotry'.

div.p: § 1. Bogudis. Bocchus and Bogud (Dio 41. 42. 7-49 B. C.) were proclaimed kings by Caesar in opposition to Juba, who sided with Pompey. Bogud helped Caesar in 46 B. C. (B. Afr. 23) and 45 B. C. (Dio 43. 36. 1) and helped to decide the battle of Munda (Dio 43. 38. 2).

p.note: . M. Actorius Naso (9. 3).
. Cp. Plut. Caes. 49. 1; App. 2. 90; Strabo 17. 1. II (p. 796); a cause of reproach to Caesar (Dio 43. 20. 2; 43.27. 3); see also references to Cic. Att. below-in urbem.
. A state-barge fitted with cabins. See Torr, Ancient Ships, pp. 123-4. Appian (2.90) says that they had a retinue of 400 vessels.

. The army can scarcely have been required to follow them up the Nile, and Caesar can hardly, at this moment, have contemplated a serious invasion of Ethiopia. Probably Caesar turned back on hearing of insubordination at Alexandria, where the troops were discontented over their rations (Plut. Caes. 48.4). See R. Holmes, R. R., iii, p. 203. n. 3.

. Both Dio (43.27. 3) and Eusebius (Hieron.) (Chron. ed. Fotheringham, p. 238) make her come to Rome in 46 B. C. Dio says that she lived in Caesar's house. Cicero (Att. 14. 8. 1; 14.20. 2; 15. 1.5; 15.4.4; 15.15. 2; 15. 17. 2) refers to a regina, living trans Tiberim in hortis (sc. Caesaris). She is generally identified with Cleopatra, who must, therefore, have made a long stay in Rome, since these letters were written shortly after Caesar's death. See R. Holmes, R. R., iii, pp. 503-6.

, Caesarion. There is a strong prima facie case for Caesar's paternity. Cleopatra asserted it (Suet. Aug. 17. 5; Dio 47.31.5; 49. 41. 1); so did Antony (below and Dio 50. 3. 5); cp. also Nic. Dam. 20. Plutarch (Caes. 49.4; Ant. 54. 3) does no more than recognize the wide-spread belief as to Caesar's paternity. Against this testimony must be set that of Oppius mentioned below. Further, the evidence on both sides is interested. It was obviously to the interest of Cleopatra to affirm that Caesar was the father; not less was it to the interest of Antony to do the same at such times as he was the opponent of Octavian. Caesarion was a useful pawn, who could be played off against the adopted son of Caesar.

div.p: Consequently it was natural that Antony should tell the senate that Caesarion was Caesar's son as soon as Octavian put in an appearance at Rome and began to assert his position as Caesar's heir. The same attitude was no less natural during the later period of hostility which ended at Actium; hence Antony asserts in his will that Caesar was the father (Dio 50. 3. 3), and hence Octavian puts Caesarion to death (Suet. Aug. 17. 5). Oppius, who denies the paternity of Caesar, is supporting the claims of Octavian, the heir of his friend. Many historical parallels might be quoted; e.g. the game played with Heracles the reputed son of Alexander; see Tarn, J. H. S., 1921, pp. 18 sqq. The problem scarcely admits of a positive answer.
§ 2. M. Antonius. It is perhaps worth noting that Antony was not in Egypt in 48-47 B. C., having returned to govern Italy as Caesar's magister equitum.

p.note: . An eques, taking no overt part in politics; a loyal and devoted friend to Caesar; see especially Cic. Fam. 11. 27 and 28, written towards the end of August, 44 B. C. He reconciled Caesar and Cicero in 47-46 B. C. (see Fam. 11. 27. 5).

. C. Oppius, an eques, one of Caesar's confidential agents; see Cicero's letters passim from 54 B. C. Like Matius he befriended Cicero (Fam. 11. 29). Besides the work here mentioned he wrote memoirs (or possibly an actual biography of Caesar) to which Caesar's biographers refer (e. g. Plut. Pomp. 10. 4-Oppius must be read with caution when speaking of Caesar's enemies or friends; Caes. 17.5; Suet. 53). He also wrote the lives of Cassius (Charis. G. L. i, p. 147. 3) and Scipio Africanus the Elder (Charis. 1. c.; Gell. 6. 1. 2).

div.p: § 3. Helvius Cinna. Tr. pl. 44 B. C.; see 85. 1. Cp. Dio 44. 7. 3 for this amazing proposal (there attributed to persons unnamed and cited as an example of proposals made either in a spirit of exaggerated flattery or to make Caesar ridiculous). It is possible that the lines quoted from Laberius by Gellius (16. 7. 12) may refer to this proposal: duas uxores? hercle hoc plus negoti est, inquit cocio; \ sex aediles viderat. The reference to six aediles is a hit at Caesar's increase of the number of aediles; see 41. I aedilium.

p.note: . Cp. Vell. Pat. 2. 41. 2 Alexandro, sed sobrio neque iracundo simillimus.
. The fact that he called Caesar 'Drunkard!' in an altercation is not evidence to the contrary (Plut. Cat. 24. 1; Brut. 5. 2).
. From condire, 'perfumed oil'; cp. Plut. Caes. 17.5.

: i. e. 61-60 B. C.; pro consule is a courtesy title given to propraetors 81-52 B. C.; see Willems, Le Sénat, ii, p. 571, n. 5. Plutarch (Caes. 12) merely says that Caesar became rich, but gives no detail. For confiscations in 49 B. C. see Dio 41. 24. I.
. Probably the sacking of villages evacuated by inhabitants who fled across the Douro (Dio 37. 52. 4; Meyer, Caesars Monarchie, p. 56, n. 4).

div.p: § 2. in Gallia fana. For the plunder of Tolosa in 106 B. C. as showing the possibilities of sacrilege in Gaul, cp. Dio fr. 90 (ed. Boissevain; Strab. 4. 1. 13, p. 188; Orosius 5.15. 25 (100,000 lb. of gold and 1,000,000 lb. of silver plundered by Servilius Caepio from the temple of Apollo). But in general Gallic temples were merely groves and pres presumably not worth looting; see R. Holmes, Conquest of Gaul (ed. 2), pp. 31-2. There is no other mention of sacrilege in Gaul. ternis milibus, 'offered it for sale at 3,000 sesterces a pound'. Probably below the usual price. Presumably he desired to coin silver denarii, gold not being used for coinage as yet. For the wealth acquired by Caesar in Gaul as early as 54 B. C. cp. note on 26. 2 forum...incohavit, cuius area super sestertium milies constitit.

p.note: . Post-Augustan, 'for sale '.

div.p: § 3. furatus e Capitolio. There is no other record of any such raid on the state treasure in 59 B. C.; the treasure in question is presumably that deposited by Camillus on the Capitol in 389 B. C. to keep it safe from Gallic invaders (Livy 5. 50. 6). It was apparently still housed there as late as 52 B. C., when according to Pliny (33. 14) 2,000 lbs. of gold mysteriously disappeared from the treasure-house of Capitoline Jupiter. But the scandal here recorded is scarcely credible in view of the silence of all other authorities, contemporary and later writers alike. It is conceivable that Suetonius is citing a scandalous interpretation of the loss mentioned by Pliny. On the other hand Appian (2.41), when describing 3333 I

Caesar's raid on the aerarium Saturni in 49 B. C., makes him seize a treasure deposited at the time of the Gallic invasion, with a curse on any who used it save for a Gallic war. He receives confirmation from Lucan (3.156), who says that the treasure was multis non tactus ab annis. There is no record of the transference of this treasure from the Capitol to the aerarium Saturni; but it is conceivable that it was transferred after the discovery of the loss in 52 B. C. Of the plunder of the aerarium Saturni in 49 B. C. there is no reasonable doubt (cp. Pomp. 62. 1-2; Caes. 35.3; Dio 41. 17. 1-2; Flor. 2. 13.21; Plin. 33.56; Oros. 6. 15.5).

p.note: . For a similar fraud cp. Suet. Vit. 5.

. The only definitely recorded instance is the case of Ptolemy. See below. But Cicero, referring apparently to the confirmation of Pompey's acta, speaks (Att. 2. 9. 1-59 В. С.) of those qui regna, qui praedia tetrarchis, qui immanis pecunias paucis dederunt, and again again at a later date (54 B. C.) alludes in connexion with events of 59 B. C. to the donatio regnorum. Cp. also his In Vatinium (29) where he asks Vatinius fecerisne foedera tribunus plebis cum civitatibus, cum regibus, cum tetrarchis?-a passage which Pocock (In Vat., pp. 173-5) interprets as an allusion to the acta Pompei, which he holds were ratified not by a lex Iulia, but by a lex Vatinia, Vatinius acting as Caesar's agent. The details of the scandal are lacking. But it must be assumed that Caesar made money out of the proceedings, and that perhaps he went somewhat further than the original acta Pompei in making arrangements with subject-princes.

. The debt was contracted by Ptolemy Auletes, probably in 59 B. C.; he was expelled from Egypt in 57 B. C. for trying to collect money from his subjects to pay his debt (Dio 39. 12-13). In 55 B. C. Gabinius got 10-11,000 talents from Ptolemy for restoring him to his throne (Dio 39. 55.4; App. Syr. 51; Plut. Ant. 3. 2; Cic. Rab. Post. 30). Dio (l. c.) says that this was the doing of Gabinius; but it is not improbable that some of it found its way into Caesar's pockets. Later, according to Plutarch (Caes. 48. 5), Caesar got 10,000,000 drachmae out of the younger Ptolemy in settlement of the debt of the elder Ptolemy, alleged to have been 17,500,000 drachmae.

. This would specially apply to the plunder of the aerarium sanctius in the Temple of Saturn, or to the alleged plunder of the Capitol. See note on furatus e Capitolio (above), where references are given.

div.p: § 1. eloquentia. Cp. Cic. Brut. 252 sed tamen, Brute, inquit Atticus, de Caesare et ipse ita iudico, illum omnium fere oratorum Latine loqui elegantissime; nec id solum domestica consuetudine...

sed multis litteris et iis quidem reconditis et exquisitis summoque studio et diligentia est consecutus ; 258; 261 splendidam quandam et minime veteratoriam rationem dicendi tenet, voce motu forma etiam magnificam et generosam quodammodo; Quint. 10. 114 С. Caesar si foro tantum vacasset, non alius ex nostris contra Ciceronem nominaretur. tanta in eo vis est, id acumen, ea concitatio ut illum eodem animo dixisse quo bellavit appareat; exornat tamen haec omnia mira sermonis cuius proprie studiosus fuit elegantia. Tac. Ann. 13. 3. 4 dictator Caesar summis oratoribus aemulus; Dial. 21. 5 and 25.3; Fronto, p. 181 (ed. Rom.) Caesari facultatem dicendi video imperatoriam fuisse; Plut. Caes. 3.2 λέγεται δὲ καὶ φῦναι πρὸς λόγους πολιτικοὺς ὁ Κ. ἄριστα καὶ διαπονῆσαι φιλοτιμότατα τὴν φύσιν, ὡς τὰ δευτερεῖα μὲν ἀδηρίτως ἔχειν, τὸ δὲ πρωτεῖον, ὅπως τῇ δυνάμει καὶ τοῖς ὅπλοις πρῶτος εἴη μᾶλλον ἀσχοληθεὶς ἀφεῖναι, πρὸς ὅπερ ἡ φύσις ὑφηγεῖτο τῆς ἐν τῷ λέγειν δεινότητος ὑπὸ στρατειῶν καὶ πολιτείας, ᾗ κατεκτήσατο τὴν ἡγεμονίαν, οὐκ ἐξικόμενος. Speeches not recorded in this chapter are as follows: in C. Antonium (see 4. 1, note on Dolabellam); pro Plautia Rogatione (Gell. 13. 3. 5; Suet. 5. 1 n.); in Memmium et Domitium (Schol. Bob. Sest., p. 89; Vat., p. 116H); pro Bithynis (Gell. 5. 13.6; Suet. 4. 2, note on supplicio ; pro Decio Samnite (Tac. Dial. 21. 6).

p.note: . See on 4. I.

. Cicero's letters to Cornelius Nepos were published in a collection consisting of at least two books (Macr. 2. 1. 14). None survive, though they were in existence as late as the time of Lactantius (Inst. Div. 3. 15. 10).

div.p: § 2. Strabonis Caesaris. Consul in 86 B. C., and put to death by Sulpicius in 85 B. C. (Cic. Brut. 307; Phil. 11. 5. 11). He was famous as an orator and tragic poet. For his oratory cp. Cic. Brut. 177 festivitate et facetiis C. Iulius L. f. et superioribus et aequalibus suis omnibus praestitit oratorque fuit minime ille quidem vehemens, sed nemo unquam urbanitate, nemo lepore, nemo suavitate conditior; 207; 305; De Or. 3. 8. 30 quid, noster hic Caesar nonne novam rationem attulit orationis et dicendi genus induxit prope singulare? quis unquam res praeter hunc tragicas paene comice comice, tristes remisse, severas hilare, forenses scenica prope venustate tractavit atque ita ut neque iocus magnitudine rerum excluderetur nec gravitas facetiis minueretur. He was second cousin once removed of the dictator. His full name was C. Iulius Caesar Strabo Vopiscus Sesquiculus (C. I. L. (ed. 2), i, p. 198; Victorinus, G. L., vi, p. 8. 8). For fragments of speeches see Meyer, Or. Rom. Fragm. (ed. 2), p. 330; for fragments of plays see Ribbeck, Trag. Rom. Fragm. (ed. 2), p. 263.

p.note: . In 103 B. C. he prosecuted T. Albucius, governor of Sardinia, on a charge of extortion; cp. Cic. Off. 2. 50 ut nos pro Siculis, pro Sardis Iulius.

div.p: § 3. pro Quinto Metello. Q. Metellus Nepos, who in 62 B. C. 12
as tr. pl. brought forward a bill proposing that Pompey should be recalled to Rome to crush Catiline. Caesar supported Metellus, and was involved in the senate's displeasure. See note on c. 16.

p.note: , 'shorthand writers'. From the adj. actuarius, 'agile', 'rapid'. The great debate on the arrested Catilinarians was taken down by stenographers in 63 B. C.; according to Plut. Cat. 23. 2, the first occasion on which a debate was thus reported, the innovation being due to Cicero, who had stenographers trained for the purpose.
, which he wrote for Metellus'. Suetonius goes on to show that this title is inapplicable, adding 'although Caesar speaks in person, defending himself and Metellus'.

div.p: § 4. apud milites. Probably distinct from the speech cited by Diomedes, de Art. Gramm., p. 395 (G. L. 1. 400. 20) frustro ait Caesar apud milites de commodis eorum.

p.note: , 'however this may be '.

. The campaign must have been the second Spanish campaign in which Asinius Pollio took part (see note on 30. 4). It is possible that the first fight may have been that described in B. Hisp. 24, and the second Munda. But our knowledge of the campaign is so scanty that no conclusion is possible.

div.p: § 1. commentarios. The Gallic War was written some time before the final break with Pompey; cp. 7. 6. I where Pompey is praised. The view generally held is that it was composed en bloc (cp. R. Holmes, Conquest of Gaul (ed. 2), pp. 202-9), on the strength of 8. praef. 6 ceteri enim quam bene atque emendate, nos etiam quam facile atque celeriter eos perfecerit scimus. Cp. also sect. 3 (below) celeriter. Cp. on the other hand M. Radin (Class. Phil. 1918, pp. 283 sqq.; Class. Journ., Dec. 1924, pp. 170-2), who argues that they were written in instalments. The Civil War was written after Munda; cp. 3. 18 bello perfecto ab iis Caesar haec facta cognovit ; 3.57.5 and 60. 4.

p.note: . Hirtius, the author of Bell. Gall. 8, states that he continued the Bellum Civile to the death of Caesar, but that he did not actually take part in the Alexandrian and African campaigns, deriving, however, much of his information from conversations with Caesar. There is no evidence that the author of B. Alex. took any part in the campaign, and there is a general resemblance between its style and that of B. Gall. 8 (see Klotz, Caesar-studien, pp. 180-204). Failing definite evidence to the contrary

div.p: the B. Alexandrinum must be attributed to Hirtius; cp. R. Holmes, R. R. iii, p. 483. On the other hand the Bellum Africanum stands on a different footing. The author was clearly present in the field. Therefore he was not Hirtius. Differences in style have also been detected, but would not, perhaps, be in themselves conclusive. There is no indication as to the identity of the author. The B. Hispaniense was written by an eye-witness, and Hirtius was not actually with Caesar in Spain; nor could he be accused of writing a book not unjustly described by R. Holmes as the 'worst book in Latin literature'. The style is childish and incompetent, though the book has some value in view of the very scanty information concerning the campaign which has survived elsewhere. Nipperdey's discussion of the problem in the Introduction to his edition of the Commentaries is still the most important contribution to the subject. For good summaries of the discussion see Schanz, Gesch. Röm. Litt. (3rd ed.) i, pt. 2, pp. 135 sqq., and Klotz in Pauly-Wissowa, x. 1. 272 sqq.

p.note: . See note on 52. 2. There is no reason to suppose that Oppius was a soldier, and the attribution does not seem specially probable.

. Of plebeian stock and obscure antecedents, A. Hirtius owed his rise to the patronage of Caesar; tr. pl. in 48; praet. 47; cos. 43. He was with Caesar in Gaul, but is nowhere mentioned as legatus. He was a loyal friend to Caesar, who employed him as a negotiator. Q. Cicero (Fam. 9. 16. 27) speaks slightingly of him as a debauchee, while M. Cicero describes him as luxurious and an epicure (Att. 12.2.2; Fam. 16. 7), but is on friendly terms with him on the whole, giving him the benefit of his instructions in the technique of rhetoric (Fam. 1. c.; Suet. de rhet. 25. 3). In 43 B. C., during the campaign of Mutina, Cicero does his best to support him and speaks of him in high terms (e. g. Fam. 12. 5. 2). Cicero's correspondence with Hirtius seems to have been voluminous, as many as nine books having been published (Nonius, p. 450 M). For further literary activities of Hirtius see below, note on Anticatones.

. This should strictly mean that he completed Bk. VII, but must be regarded as a loose description of the supplementary Bk. VIII. Suetonius ignores Hirtius' statement (B. G. 8 praef.) that he completed the Civil War as well.

div.p: §2. Cicero. Brut. 262.

p.note: , 'plain... direct... elegant'.

, 'crimp and curl'. calamistri are curling-tongs. Similar metaphors are used by Cicero elsewhere (Brut. 78 and 162; Orat. 78; De Or. 3. 100). Cp. also Suet. Aug. 86. 2 myrobrechis cincinnos and Dion. Hal. de comp. verb. 25 Πλάτων τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ διαλόγους κτενίζων καὶ βοστρυχίζων καὶ πάντα τρόπον ἀναπλέκων οὐ διέλιπεν.

div.p: § 3. Hirtius. B. Gall. 8 praef.

§4. Pollio Asinius. See note on 30.4. The quotation is presumably from his history of the Civil War. The cognomen is placed before the gentile name in accordance with the common practice of post-Augustan writers (cp. Tac. H. 2. 86 (Primus Antonius; 91.4 Priscus Helvidius); and Cimber Tillius (82. 1, below).

p.note: . A specific instance of this criticism is cited by Appian (2. 82), who states that Pollio counted 6,000 Pompeian dead on the field of Pharsalus, whereas Caesar (B. C. 3. 99. 4) puts the number at about 15,000. This general criticism of Caesar has often been repeated (see especially the remarks of Meyer (Caesars Monarchie), who gives references to his critical discussions on p. 620, n. 2). But in general Caesar's accuracy and, still more, his good faith has been vindicated. See R. Holmes, Conquest of Gaul (ed. 2), pp. 211-56; R. R. ii, pp. 334-7, and iii, pp. 382-3.
. This is possible. Great as Caesar's work is, it naturally bears the marks of hasty composition here and there. The

div.p: §5. de analogia duos libros. Cp. Fronto (Naber) 221. work was dedicated to Cicero (Gell. 19. 8. 3; Cic. Brut. 253) and it was probably in the dedication that he paid Cicero the fine, if somewhat ironical, compliment cited by Pliny (7. 117) quanto plus est ingeni Romani terminos in tantum promovisse quam imperi. Broadly stated, the aim of the analogist was to bring all irregularities of language into agreement with the normal, to standardize grammar and reduce it to rule. The anomalist on the other hand laid stress on the importance of custom and usage in the development of language. Caesar, while championing the cause of analogia, was not blind to the claims of consuetudo; ; cp. the famous ous saying cited by Gellius (1. 10. 4) ut tanquam scopulum sic fugias inauditum atque insolens verbum; also Cic. Brut. 261 Caesar autem rationem adhibens consuetudinem vitiosam et corruptam pura et incorrupta consuetudine emendat. For a brief statement of the analogist controversy at Rome see Sandys, Hist. Class. Scholarship, i, pp. 175-7; also F. H. Colson, in Class. Quart. xiii, p. 24 (1919). The scanty fragments of the de Analogia are to be found in Kuebler's ed. of Caesar, iii, p. 140. The work was probably composed early in 54 B. C. or 52 B. C. See below on conventibus

p.note: . After the death of Cato at Utica Cicero wrote a laudatio Catonis (Att. 12. 5. 2; 13.27. 1; 13. 46. 2; Plut. Caes. 54.3; Tac. Ann. 4.34.7). Caesar, although he admired the style (Att. 13. 27), took exception to the matter and published his Anticato as a counterblast. That there were two Anticatones is borne out by Juvenal (6. 338 duo Caesaris Anticatones), Priscian (G. L. 2. 227. 2 Caesar in Anticatone priore), and Cicero

div.p: (Att. 13. 50 and 51, where the work is spoken of as libri). The fact that Tacitus (1. c.) and Plutarch (Cic. 39. 2; Cato 36. 3), and Appian (2. 99) do not explicitly recognize two Anticatones proves nothing. It has been suggested that one of these was written by Hirtius, who sent a denunciation of Cato to Cicero about the same time (probably from Narbo); cp. Cic. Att. 12. 40. 1. But there is no reason why Caesar should not have written his work in two books. (For the contrary view see Dyroff, Rhein. Mus. i, pp. 481-4 (1895); Kalinka, Philol. lxix (1910), pp. 479-82; R. Holmes, R. R. iii, pp. 311, n. 14.) More than one laudatio Catonis was written on the other side; e.g. by Brutus (Cic. Att. 13. 46) and by M. Fadius Gallus (Fam. 7. 24 and 25). The Anticatones of Caesar were apparently in the form of a declamation (Tac., 1. c., speaks of the work as an oratio). Only a few fragments survive, for which see Kuebler. The work was violent in tone and assailed Cato's private life, but was courteous as far as Cicero was concerned (Plut. Cic. 39. 2).

p.note: . Nothing is known of the poem beyond what is stated here. It was perhaps suggested by Lucilius's poem describing his journey from Rome to Capua, and thence to Sicily (Bk. 3); cp. Horace's journey to Brundisium (S. 1. 5). which according to Porphyrion was similarly inspired.

, 'after the completion of his assize circuits'. Provinces were divided into juridical conventus (cp. Cic. Fam. 3. 8. 4-6; Att. 5. 20. 1; 21.9). The precise date is uncertain. The passage from the de Analogia in Cic. Brut. 253 seems to refer to the de Oratore (3. 10. 37), which was published in 55 B. C., from which Hendrickson (Class. Phil. i, 110-16 (1906)) infers that Caesar wrote his work soon after reading Cicero's dialogue, i. e. early in 54 B. C. But it may have been in 52 B. C. Caesar refers to his conventus in B. G. 1. 54. 3 (58-57 В. С.), 2. 35. 3 (57-56 в. с.), 5. 1.5 (55-54 B. C.), 7. 1. I (53-52 B. C.). He remained in Transalpine Gaul during the winter of 54-53 B. С.
. March 17, 45 B. C. Cp. 35 (end).

. Caesar was in Rome as late as Sept. 24, 46 в. с.; ср. Cic. Fam. 6. 14. 2. He set out for Spain soon after, and reached Saguntum in 17 days (Oros. 6. 16. 6), Obulco (35 m. from Corduba) in 27 (Strabo 3.4.9; App. 2. 103; cp. also Dio 43. 32; B. Hisp. 2. 1). Suetonius does not mention the actual locality, so that quarto et vicensimo die is not necessarily inconsistent. Corduba is about 1,550 miles from Rome, which would make his rate of travel about 55 miles a day (taking the estimate of 27 days). Cp. the journey from Rome to Geneva in 8 days (about 600 miles) recorded by Plutarch (Caes. 17. 3); the elder Cato's journey from Hydrus to Rome in 5 days (Liv. 36. 21. 6); Peel's journey from Rome to London in 1834 at the rate of 75 miles a day. The normal daily stage in ancient times was 30-40 miles; see

div.p: Riepl, Das Nachrichtenwesen, pp. 129-57; also note on 57 1. celeritate.
§ 6. epistulae. All are lost except those mentioned below (note on ad Ciceronem) and some fragments in Greek found at Mytilene (Kuebler, iii, p. 214).

p.note: . The exact nature of the innovation is not certain. The most probable explanation is that given by Maunde Thompson (Palaeography, p. 46, n. 3) : 'Before the time of Julius Caesar official dispatches appear to have been written

, that is with lines parallel with the height of the roll. He wrote in the book style, the lines parallel with the length of the roll.' In that case the paginae will be columns (σελίδες). The passage is, however, capable of another interpretation, viz. that Caesar adopted the codex form, i. e. the paginated book that we use to-day. This is not, however, probable, as will be clear from the following comment, for which we are indebted to Sir Frederick Kenyon: 'I think transversa charta must certainly mean that they wrote in one broad column all across the width of the papyrus -no doubt on the horizontal fibres. That would be the form of a letter or official rescript; and the point of Suetonius' remark must be that Caesar was the first to put his dispatches in the form of a book. Memorialis liber might be a note-book; but that would be a less ceremonious way of addressing the Senate, and even, I should imagine, an insulting one. I should therefore be disposed to translate pagina 'column', a well-known use of it, and to take the meaning to be that Caesar put his dispatches in the form of a small book (hence libellus rather than liber), in columns of three or four inches width on a roll of papyrus. All the evidence goes to show that the codex-form at that time existed only for note-books; and the point of the passage must be that Caesar's dispatches to the Senate were in such a form that they could be enumerated among his literary works. Memorialis I take to mean that the dispatch was not regarded as an ephemeral letter, but as a more or less permanent record, a permanent mémoire à servir.

. At least three books of these were known to Servius (see ad Georg. 3. 204). Cicero mentions uberrimae litterae from Caesar in Britain (Att. 4. 17.6; cp. also Att. 4. 18. 5; Q. F. 2. 13.1; 3.1.25; 3.5.3; Att. 7.2.7). Actual letters from Caesar will be found in Att. 9.6a; 9.7c; 9. 132; 9. 14. 1; 9. 16.2; 10. 8b.
. Cp. Gell. 17.9 libri sunt epistularum C. Caesaris ad C. Oppium et Balbum Cornelium, qui rebus eius absentis curabant.
, 'in cipher'. notae also is used in the sense of shorthand

div.p: , which is in a sense a sort of cipher. It is indeed more strictly accurate in that sense, since signs are used for letters or groups of letters (e. g. notae Tironianae). ...

p.note: . A cipher of the simplest kind; D=A, E=B, F=C, etc. A similar form was employed by Augustus (Suet. Aug. 88 quotiens scribit, B pro A, C pro B, ac deinceps eadem ratione sequentes literas ponit; Isid. 1.25). Gellius (17. 9. 1) states that Caesar used a cipher of this character in his letters to Oppius and Balbus, but seems to indicate that the key was not always the same: quaenam vero littera pro qua scriberetur, ante iis, sicut dixi, complacebat, qui hanc scribendi latebram parabant. More complicated ciphers were also sometimes employed by Caesar, for Gellius goes on to say est adeo Probi grammatici commentarius satis curiose factus de occulta litterarum significatione in epistularum C. Caesaris scriptura. For an account of the use of cipher in antiquity see Gardthausen, Gr. Palaeogr., pp. 231-42. Suetonius himself may have dealt with the subject in his 'Signs used in writing' (cp. p. vii); see Reifferscheid, Suet. Rel., p. 419.

, 'letters of the alphabet'. While the use of elementa in this sense was doubtless common enough (cp. Gk. στοιχεῖα), the nearest parallel in literature is Lucr. 1. 824 multa elementa vides multis communia verbis, | cum tamen inter se versus ac verba necesse est | confiteare et re et sonitu distare sonanti. | tantum elementa queunt permutato ordine solo. elementa literarum is common enough, but Varro in his de Gramm. (p. 228, 8 Goetz and Schoell, Varr. de Lingu. Lat.) sharply distinguishes between elementa (elementary sounds) and literae (actual letters); e. g. artis grammaticae initia ab elementis surgunt, elementa figurantur in literas. Varro is followed generally by the grammarians (see G. L. 1. 426. 32 and 7.377. 1). The attempt to derive the word from LMN has little to recommend it (see Walde, Lat. etym. Wörterb., s. v.).

div.p: § 7. et a puero. This reading is found in some of the better MSS., and is not far removed from that of the cod. Memmianus (et aitvero ab). Bentley's ut ait Varro, ab adulescentulo is attractive, but needs further support.

p.note: . Nothing further is known of these works. The only lines by Caesar which have survived are the well-known lines cited by Suetonius in his life of Terence, where Caesar hails the poet as O dimidiate Menander. Pliny the younger (5.3.5) mentions him as a writer of erotic verse. Tacitus (Dialog. 21. 6) speaks slightingly of his verse: fecerunt enim (sc. Caesar and Brutus) et carmina et in bibliothecas rettulerunt, non melius quam Cicero, sed felicius, quia illos fecisse pauciores sciunt.
. Probably a collection of brilliant sayings, which Cicero (Fam. 9. 16. 4) seems to indicate were actually circulated

div.p: (audio Caesarem, cum volumina iam confecerit ᾿Αποφθεγ μάτων, si quid adferatur ad eum pro meo quod meum non sit reicere solere.

p.note: . For the letters of Augustus, of which a collection seems to have been published, cp. Suet. Aug. 71. 76.86; Claud. 3; Rel. (ed. Reifferscheid), pp. 45, 46, 47; Tac. Dial. 13. 2; Quint. I. 6. 19; 1.7.22; Gell. 15.7.3.

. Son of a Greek, Theophanes of Mytilene, friend of Pompey the great. Tac. Ann. 6.18.4; Strabo 12. 618 C (procurator of Asia). Stobaeus (Florileg. 78. 7) has preserved a fragment of a Greek tragedy (Medea) by Pompeius Macer, and there are two epigrams under the same name in Anth. Pal. 7. 219 and 9. 28. Whether these poems are by this Pompeius Macer or by his son or grandson (cp. Tac., 1. c.) is uncertain. Equally uncertain is it whether the Macer who was Ovid's friend (Am. 2. 18; ex Pont. 2. 10. 13) is to be identified with any of this family.

. Augustus founded two libraries: (i) in the Porticus Octaviae (Suet. Gr. 21); (ii) in the precinct of Palatine Apollo (Suet. Gr. 20 and Aug. 29. 3). To these must be added the first public library at Rome founded by Asinius Pollio in the Atrium Libertatis Libertatis; see above 44. 2.
. Cp. Plut. Caesar, 17, especially sect. 4 τὸ μὲν οὖν ἱππεύειν ἐκ παιδὸς ἦν αὐτῷ ῥάδιον. εἴθιστο γὰρ εἰς τοὐπίσω τὰς χεῖρας ἀπάγων καὶ τῷ νώτῳ περιπλέκων ἀνὰ κράτος ἐλαύνειν τὸν ἵππον.

. See Plut., 1. c., especially sect. 2 ἡ δὲ τῶν πόνων ὑπομονὴ παρὰ τὴν τοῦ σώματος δύναμιν ἐγκαρτερεῖν δοκοῦντος ἐξέπληττεν. Also more generally Luc. 2. 657 nil actum credens dum quid superesset agendum; Dio 44. 38. 2.

, etc. Cp. Plut., 1. c., θεράπειαν τῆς ἀρρωστίας τὴν στρατείαν, ταῖς ἀτρύτοις ὁδοιπορίαις καὶ ταῖς εὐτέλεσι διαίταις καὶ τῷ θυραυλεῖν ἐνδελεχῶς καὶ ταλαιπωρεῖν ἀπομαχόμενος τῷ πάθει καὶ τὸ σῶμα φρουρῶν δυσάλωτον.

. See note on Hispaniam ulteriorem (56.5) and on nuntios praevenerit (below). For other examples see B. G. 3. 29. 2; 5.48. 1; 7.40.2 (4 legions cover 45 miles in 28 hours with three hours' rest); B. C. 3.75-6. Cp. also Drumann-Groebe, iii, p.723; and for the impression produced by such speed Cic. Att. 7. 22. I o celeritatem incredibilem ; 8. 9. 4 τέρας horribili celeritate; 10. 9. I volare dicitur.

. Cp. Suet. 31.2; Plut. Caes. 32. 3 (he rides in a miller's cart on the way to the Rubicon). There was no state post till the principate of Augustus (Suet. Aug. 49. 3), and probably no guilds of vehicularii or iumentarii.
. A little under 95 English miles. There is no other record of such a distance being covered in a day by Caesar or any other Roman before the institution of the Imperial post.

div.p: § 1. perspeculatus. Cp. the frequent recurrence of phrases such as exploratoribus missis in B. Gall. (more than forty cases in Meusel, Lex. Caes. s. v. exploratores and exploro).

p.note: . Caesar not only makes no mention of the fact, but (B. G. 4. 21. 1) states that he sent one Volusenus to reconnoitre. Lipsius conjectured per suos. But the words may be a slip on the part of Suetonius, or he may be following some Caesar-legend; many must have sprung up, as for instance possibly the story dealt with in the next note.

. Cp. 25 in Germanorum finibus, where he refers to the disaster at Atuatuca in the country of the Eburones (generally identified with Tongres and in any case lying well within the imperial province of Lower Germany). Here the allusion appears to be to the siege of Q. Cicero's camp near Namur, likewise in Germania Inferior. But Caesar makes no mention of this romantic adventure, though the story of the relief of the garrison is thrilling enough (B. G. 5.45 sqq.). Probably another legend.

div.p: § 2. Dyrrhachium. On Jan. 4, 48 B. C., Caesar crossed the Adriatic with 15,600 men. Pompey forestalled him in seizing the important harbour of Dyrrhachium (Durazzo), and Caesar encamped on the river Apsus.

p.note: . Bibulus with 110 ships was at Corcyra, fifty miles south of Palaeste, where Caesar landed; but his ships were not ready for sea, and he was unaware that Caesar had sailed. Lucretius Vespillo and Minucius Rufus with eighteen ships were nearer at Oricum, but did not venture to attack (B. C. 3. 7).

. Caesar was vastly outnumbered and in sore need of reinforcements. Thirty of his transports which he had sent back for fresh troops were captured by Bibulus, who for some time blockaded the coast of Epirus. Bibulus died, and Libo, one of his two successors, made a bold attempt to seal up the harbour of Brundisium where Antony was waiting with reinforcements. The attempt failed, but the Pompeian naval forces were still strong enough to prevent Antony from venturing to cross. At length, on receipt of urgent orders from Caesar, he sailed (end of March). Cp. В. С. 3. 18-30.
. Caesar, almost alone, is silent as to this exploit, perhaps because it failed. If the story is true and it is difficult to reject it-the date must have been some time in the

div.p: middle or latter half of March. Plutarch (Caes. 38. 3) gives full details: 'Caesar, disguised as a slave, embarked on a pinnace with twelve oars at the mouth of the R. Aous; a strong W. wind made it impossible to get out of the river, and after two attempts he desisted; it was after the first failure that he is said to have made his famous remark, “Be of good cheer, you carry Caesar and his fortunes."" Appian (2. 56-8) adds that Caesar then sent Postumius in his place; he reached Dyrrhachium in safety. Gabinius with volunteers sought to reach Caesar by the land route, but his troops were cut to pieces by the Illyrians. Antony then set sail, and reached Nymphaeum with the loss of but two ships. Cp. also Dio 41.46.2; Val. Max. 9.8.2; Florus 2. 13. 37; Zon. 10.8; Lucan 5. 476-677 (amazing bombast).
..castris ...

p.note: . There is no mention of omens in the Commentaries, only of Fortune (B. C. 3. 68. 1). Appian (2. 116 and 152) says the same, and styles Caesar a 'despiser of portents'. Cp. also 77 and 81. 4; and, further, Suet. Aug. 94. II apud Mundam locum capiens cum silvam caederet, arborem palmae repertam conservari ut omen victoriae iussit (it grew with fabulous speed till soon it was as big as its mother tree, and doves nested in it. Caesar took it as an omen that he should make his nephew his heir !).
. Caesar sailed from Lilybaeum on Dec. 25, 47 B. C. (Oct. 6 by our reckoning), very late in the year for such an enterprise (B. Afr. 2. 4).
. See 35. 2 n.

. Cp. Dio 42. 58. 3; Frontin. Strat. 1. 12. 2. For similar incidents cp. the story told by Livy (1. 56. 10-12) concerning Brutus, and the mishap of Hippias before the battle of Marathon (Herod. 6. 107.4). An identical story is told of William the Conqueror's landing in England (Roman de Rou, ii, p. 152 Seigneurs par la resplendor Dé | La terre ai as dous mainz seizie Tote est nostre quant qu'il y a). ...

. So the best MSS. Later MSS. give Salutioni. Plutarch (Caes. 52. 2) and Dio (42. 58. 1) likewise call him Salutio. Pliny, however, calls him Salvitto (7.54; 35.8), and states that he derived this cognomen from a mimus named Salvitto, presumably owing to a personal resemblance. Plutarch treats Caesar's action as a jest; no doubt it was, but it was also a concession to popular superstition. Cp. 61, where Caesar makes use of his 'freak horse' to impress popular credulity, also Dio 43. 21. 2, where he crawls up the Capitoline steps on his knees, and B. Civ. 3. 105. 6, where he announces miracles during the campaign of Pharsalus; also Val. Max. 1. 6. 12.
, 'designedly'.
. As in the battle with the Nervii (B. G. 2. 18 sqq.), the battle near Dijon before Alesia (B. G. 7. 66-7), and Thapsus (B. Afr. 82-3).
. Cp. Polyaen. 8. 23. 17. For special instances see especially B. G. 7. 27. 1 (rain); B. G. 7. 8. 2 (snow).

. Intransitive; cp. Liv. 35. 40; 5. 26 (movens = movable); Cic. Fin. 2. 10. 31, etc.; perhaps a colloquialism. Caesar's strategy owed much of its success to speed. Note also early starts in B. G. 6. 3. 1 and note on profectionem (59).

. In his last campaign before Munda. It is true that Caesar stood on the defensive during the close of 46 B. C. and that there was some delay before Munda itself. But there seems no reason to attribute this to a decline in vigour. It was winter, his troops were suffering great hardship (Dio 43. 32. 7), and the enemy were superior in numbers, while his own troops were disheartened (App. 2. 103). Pompeius is said by Appian (l. c.) to have taunted him with cowardice just before the battle of Munda and thereby to have precipitated the engagement, while earlier during the siege of Corduba operations were hampered by Caesar's illness (Dio 43.32.6). His epileptic attack at Corduba may well have slowed him down (see on 45. 1).
. These words are only found in later MSS. Whether they give the actual words of Suetonius or no, there can be no doubt that they give the sense.

. Cp. В. С. 3. 95. 1 Caesar Pompeianis ex fuga intra vallum compulsis nullum spatium perterritis dare oportere existimans milites cohortatus est ut beneficio fortunae uterentur castraque oppugnarent. Cp. also the capture of the camp at Thapsus (B. Afr. 85. 3).
. Cp. B. G. 1. 25. I (battle with Helvetii). He did the same at Munda (Flor. 2. 13. 82; Vell. Pat. 2. 55; Dio 43.37.4; Polyaen. 8. 23. 16; Frontin. 2. 8. 13).

. Cp. Dio 37.54.2; Plin. 8. 155. Both state that the peculiarity was confined to the forefeet. Dio adds that the horse was foaled when Caesar was standing for the consulship (60 B.C.), and describes the horse as having διφύας ὅπλας. ‘Polydactyly' is well known in horses and a number of cases of horses with two digits have been recorded. See Bateson, Materials for the study of Variation, pp. 360 sqq. The extreme case there recorded is of a Texan horse which had three digits on each of the hind feet and two on each of the fore feet.
. The same is recorded of Bucephalus (Pliny, 1. c.).

. Vowed at Pharsalus (App. 2. 68 and 102; Dio 43. 22. 2; Plut. Pomp. 68. 2); dedicated Sept. 26, 46 в.с. (Dio 43. 22; C. I. L. (ed. 2) i, p. 219); finished by Augustus (Mon. Anc. ch. 20). Cp. also Plin. 35. 156; Vitruv. 3. 3. 2. It stood in the centre of the Forum Iulium (see 26. 2) and was built of marble. The foundations are still traceable.

: e.g. on 'the day he overcame the Nervii' (B. G. 2. 25. 1), at Munda (Plut. Caes. 56.2; App. 2. 104; Vell. Pat. 2. 55. 3) and, unsuccessfully, at Dyrrhachium (Plut. Caes. 39. 2; App. 2. 62; B. С. 3. 69. 5).

, etc. Cp. the incident connected with a battle in Africa before Thapsus recorded by Plutarch (Caes. 52. 3), where Caesar seized an aquilifer by the throat and turned him round, saying, 'The enemy are there'; so too with slight variations, Appian (2. 95) and Valerius Maximus (3. 2. 19).

, ' and on more than one occasion when they were so panic-stricken'. The only incident recorded other than that in the preceding note occurred at Dyrrhachium; cp. B. C. 3. 69. 4 adeo ut cum Caesar signa fugientium manu prenderet et consistere iuberet, alii eundem cursum confugerent, alii ex metu etiam signa dimitterent, neque quisqam omnino consisterent (thirty-two standards were lost (B. C. 3. 71. 2). Plutarch (Caes. 39. 2) gives further detail; Caesar laid hold of the standards, but their bearers flung them away, and, in one case, when he attempted to stop a man of great strength, the fugitive raised his sword to strike him, but was cut down by Caesar's armour-bearer).
. The spike at the butt-end of the standard.

p.mentioned: non minor illa constantia eius, maiora etiam indicia fuerint
p.note: . Whether we accept this reading or minora illa constantiae eius, maiora etiam indicia fuerint (the best that can be got out of the MSS.), the connexion is so clumsy as to be almost impossible in so finished and careful a writer. The actions described in the last chapter were assuredly examples of constantia.
, 'a small merchant-vessel'.

. The same story is told by Dio (42. 6. 2) and by Appian (2.88 and 111). The latter confuses Cassius with C. Cassius 'who afterwards murdered him' and gives him seventy ships! But C. Cassius was off Sicily and South Italy in 48 B.C. (B. C. 3. 101). L. Cassius is otherwise unknown. He must not be confused with

div.p: L. Cassius Longinus who fought throughout on Caesar's side (B. C. 3. 34-6).

p.note: . The incident is not recorded in B. Alex. But Plutarch (Caes. 49. 3), Dio (42. 40. 5), Appian (2. 90), and Orosius (6. 15. 34) all relate it. The incident occurred in the attack on the south redoubt commanding the harbour (B. Alex. 17-21). See R. Holmes, R. R. iii, p. 194 (also Flor. 2. 13. 59).

. This absurdity was once and for all disposed of by Voltaire (Pirronisme de l'histoire ante vitam Caroli XII, cited by Crusius): 'Croyez plutôt César (B. Alex. 21) qui n'en dit mot dans ses commentaires, et soyez bien sûr, que, quand on se jette dans la mer, et qu'on tient des papiers à la main, on les mouille.' Appian himself says that Caesar had to duck under. Another Caesar-legend.

. The crimson cloak worn by commanders. Dio (l. c.) states that Caesar had thrown it off that it might not hamper his movements, and Appian agrees with him that it was captured by the Egyptians, who hung it on the trophy erected in honour of the victory. Cp. also Flor., 1. c.
, 'judging from their character in private life'.

. The phrase is vague; it includes (i) their rank in private lite (cp. the promotion of the mule-driver Ventidius Bassus (Gell. 15. 4. 3), the private soldier C. Fuficius Fango (Dio 48. 22. 3), and the centurion L. Decidius Saxa (Cic. Phil. 11. 12; App. 4. 87)), and (ii) their good fortune in war, for which see ch. 68 ut consolandos eos magis quam puniendos habuerit and Caesar's speech after the reverse at Dyrrhachium (B. C. 3. 73).

. Cp. 60. 1 (battles in bad weather); 69, 70 (mutinies); B. G. 7. 52 (rebuke after reverse at Gergovia); 8.4.1 (general hard ships for which donative is a consolation); Cic. Fam. 8. 17. 2 (hardships in 48 B.C.); B. Alex. 10. 5 nulla satis idonea hortatio quae neque virtutem posset notare neque inertiam.
. Cp. 26. 3 (pay); 67. I (indulgence off parade); 49. 4 and 51. 1 (indifference to ribaldries); B. G. 8. 4. I (donative).
. See examples cited in note on nuntios praevenerit (58. 1) and his escape from Dyrrhachium (B. C. 3.75 sqq.); Polyaen. 8. 23. 17.
. Cp. 60. I tempestatibus.
. No instance is recorded.
. Our only authority for this highly original exercise.
. Cp. Polyaen. 8. 23. 19; also the advice of Cyrus in Xen. Cyrop. 6. 3. 17.

. Juba had been prevented by the operations of Sittius from joining Scipio. But in Feb. 46 B. C., after Scipio had suffered a reverse, he succeeded in joining him. Juba's force is estimated by Kromayer-Veith (Antike Schlachtf. iii. 2, p. 800) at two and a half legions (say 10-12,000 men, thirty elephants, and a considerable force of cavalry (cp. B. Afr. 48). Appian (2.96) gives much larger figures (30,000 infantry, 20,000 Numidian horse, a large force of light-armed javelin men, and sixty elephants. For Caesar's contempt for the faint-hearted cp. his speech in B. G. I. 40, when his troops showed alarm at the approach of Ariovistus.

div.p: § 1. delicta...omnia. Cр. В. С. 3. 60. 1, and 73.

p.note: , 'noticed'. pro modo exsequebatur, 'punished in proportion to the magnitude of the offence'. desertorum 55.2-3.
. Cp. Polyaen. 8. 23. 21; Dio 42.

div.p: § 2. commilitones. Cp. Polyaen. 8. 23. 22; Sen. Ben. 5. 24. 1-2. This practice was forbidden by Augustus; cp. Suet. Aug. 25. I neque post bella civilia aut in contione aut per edictum ullos militum commilitones appellabat sed milites, ac ne a filiis quidem aut privignis suis imperio praeditis aliter appellari passus est, ambitiosius id existimans quam aut ratio militaris aut temporum quies aut sua domusque suae maiestas postularet. The use of the word by emperors revived in the civil wars of A. D. 69 (cp. Tac. H. 1. 35. 3 and 84. 3; Suet. Galb. 20. 1). It was probably in frequent use by officers not of the imperial house.

p.note: . Cp. Polyaen. 8. 23. 28.
. Cp. Plut. Sert. 14. 1.
. Cp. note on c. 25. 2.
. Cp. Polyaen. 8. 23. 23.
. For Caesar's revenge see B. G. 5. 58 (overthrow and death of Indutiomarus) and 6. 30-44 (annihilation of the Eburones).

div.p: § 1. viatico. Not 'journey-money', but 'money picked_up on the way', i. e. savings, acquisitions. Cp. Hor. Ep. 2. 2. 26 Luculli miles collecta viatica multis | aerumnis, lassus dum noctu stertit ad assem | perdiderat.

p.note: . The only recorded example seems to be the incident related in B. Afr. 44-6. Veteran soldiers, a few recruits and a centurion, captured at sea, were brought before Scipio, who offered them their lives if they would join him. The centurion refused on behalf of his comrades and offered to fight a whole cohort, if he might have ten of his comrades to back him. Scipio killed the centurion on the spot, ordered the veterans to be put to death with torture, and distributed the recruits among his own legions (cp. Val. Max. 3. 8. 7, where the centurion's name is given, T. Pontius). As a rule the Pompeians simply murdered the Caesarians (B. C. 3. 14. 3; 3. 28.4; 3.71.4; 2. 44. 2). On the other hand Caesar incorporated Domitius' men at Corfinium (B. C. 1. 23. 5), but only accepted volunteers in Spain (B. C. 1. 86. 3-4).

div.p: §2. famem. Cp. the famine at Avaricum (B. G. 7. 17. 4-7), at Ilerda (B. C. 1. 52), and at Munda (Dio 43. 32. 7).

p.note: . Cp. B. C. 3. 48. 1; Plut. Caes. 39. 1; Polyaen. 8. 23. 24. The herb styled chara in Caesar (Aaron's Rod = Arum Italicum) still grows near Durazzo, and is sometimes used for food by the Albanians. Veith (Feldzug von Dyrrhachium, p. 254, n. 54 a) states that troops under his command in Albania (1917-18) were forced by hunger to eat it, though forbidden; they boiled the roots, found them sharp to the taste, though not unwholesome, if thoroughly slaked. Cp. also Plin. 19. 144, where jokes made over the olus silvestre are recorded as having been made in soldiers' songs at Caesar's triumph.

div.p: §3. apud Dyrrhachium. When Pompey had broken through their lines after inflicting considerable loss. Cp. ch. 36.

p.note: . The penalty of decimation (App. 2. 63).

. B. C. 3.73; App., 1. c.; Polyaen. 8. 23. 26. The sole punishment inflicted was the degradation of the standard-bearers to the ranks, though their comrades clamoured for their death (App., 1. c.; B. C. 3. 74).
. A tenth part of a legion; 600 if at full strength. Suetonius is in error; cp. B. C. 3. 52 uno loco Volcatius Tullus impetum legionis sustinuit cohortibus tribus atque eam loco depulit.

. Caesar states the case more strongly (B. C. 3. 53. 3 sed in castello nemo fuit omnino militum quin vulneraretur, quattuorque ex una cohorte centuriones oculos amiserunt). The words ex una cohorte have perhaps given rise to the error of Suetonius mentioned in previous note.
. Another error; Caesar (1. c.) says milia sagittarum circiter XXX. Suetonius perhaps read or misread centum for circiter.

div.p: § 4. Scaevae. In the same fight at Dyrrhachium; cp. B. C. 3.53.3-4. Ср. also Plut. Caes. 16; App. 2. 60; Flor. 2. 13. 40; Luc. 6. 144-262. 3333 K

p.note: . Cp. Plut. Caes. 16.2; Val. Max. 3. 2. 22.
. At Marathon; Herod. 6. 114.

. In 49 B.C. after Ilerda. Cp. Dio 41. 26-36; App. 2.47; Luc. 5.237-73. Caesar does not mention the incident. Dio states that after addressing the mutineers Caesar distributed lots among them to decide who should be executed; he had, however, previously arranged that they should fall upon the ringleaders. Appian says that Caesar proposed to decimate the legion. They implored forgiveness; he then selected 120 to draw lots, as a result of which twelve were executed. Neither mention the threat of dismissal, which may well have been made. The legion had suffered heavily at Ilerda, and complained that they had not received the bounties promised them. Lucan does mention the dismissal (358), tradite nostra viris ignavi signa Quirites, apparently confusing this with the mutiny of the tenth legion, which he did not live to include in his poem.

. Caesar's favourite and most trusted legion (B. G. 1. 40. 15; Dio 38. 47-8; Frontin. 1. 11. 3). It was not the sole legion involved. Antony had brought back such legions as could be spared after Pharsalus. Only one remained loyal, the others mutinied in Campania. On Caesar's return from Egypt in the late summer of 47 B.C., he sent Sallust to promise a bounty of 1,000 denarii per man after the conclusion of the African campaign. The troops stoned Sallust who fled for his life (App. 2. 92; Dio 42. 52. 2). P. Sulla suffered the same reception at the hands of the twelfth legion (Cic. Att. 11. 21 and 22). Dio states that they killed two senators, whom Plutarch calls ex-praetors (Caes. 51.2). The mutineers marched on Rome. Caesar faced them in the Campus Martius, and asked what they desired. 'Dismissal' was their reply, as they hoped to force his hand (Liv. Epit. 113; Dio 55. 2; App. 2. 94). He took them at their word, promising them their bounty when he returned to Rome in triumph. He then addressed them as Quirites, and they broke out into cries of penitence. He took back all save the Tenth into service. The Tenth begged for decimation, if only they might serve him still. He forgave them and all took part in the African campaign. Appian (1. c.) gives the fullest and best account, Dio (42.52-5) differs in some details; he makes no mention of the special severity shown to the Tenth, and states that Caesar pensioned off the least dangerous mutineers, giving them lands in widely separated parts of Italy, while he took the more dangerous elements to Africa, where he set them in the

div.p: forefront of the battle and got them killed off. Shorter notices in Tac. Ann. 1. 42.5; Polyaen. 8. 23.15; Frontin. 1. 9. 4 (cp. also 4. 5. 2).

p.note: . Cp. Tac. Ann. I. 42. 5 uno verbo.
. Only recorded by Suetonius.
. The name is Numidian. Perhaps a son of King Hiarbas whom Pompey deposed in favour of Hiempsal (Plut. Pomp. 12. 4); see next note.

. The Marians under Domitius shortly after the establishment of Sulla as dictator attempted to seize Africa. They were joined by Hiarbas, king of Numidia. Pompey by Sulla's orders crossed to Africa, crushed Domitius, deposed Hiarbas, and set up Hiempsal in his place. For further details as to Hiempsal see C. I. L. ii, 3417 REGI IVBAE REgis IVBAE FILIO RÈGis IEMPSALIS N.REGIS GAVdae PRONEPOTI REGIS MASINISSae PRONEPOTIS NEPOTI. In 63 B. C. he bribed Rullus to safeguard him from annexation (Cic. L. Agr. 2. 58).
. Presumably Masintha had tried to establish himself as an independent prince, but was adjudged to be Hiempsal's tributary.

. Perhaps merely a dispute. It might, however, mean a formal altercatio in court, when Iuba, having appeared as a witness, was examined by Caesar under the form of an altercatio or debate. See Greenidge, Legal Procedure, pp. 447-9. It is not surprising to find luba as a desperate adversary of Caesar in 46 в. с.
. Sc. in custodiam.
: i. e. in 61 в. с. Cp. 14. The trial must have taken place at Rome some time before (cp. diu), perhaps in 62 or even 63 B. C.

. The praetor setting forth to his province cum imperio was attended by his lictors, and also by his personal friends and clients, who would escort him for a short distance from Rome. Masintha was concealed in a litter which was surrounded by the escort.
. See note on 52. 2. The story is recorded by Plutarch (Caes. 17. 6). It is presumably drawn from Oppius' Memoirs.
. Any kind of 'lodging'; not necessarily an 'inn', K 2

div.p: as R. Holmes (R. R. iii, 27) describes it. Plutarch (1. c.) calls it ἔπαυλιν ἀνθρώπου πένητος.

p.note: . Caesar was never nice in the choice of his supporters (cp. 27). Compare also his promotion of Rufio (76. 3), and notes on Catullus and Calvus in 73.

. In 54 B. C. He was not elected owing to a scandal in connexion with his candidature. See Cic. Att. 4. 15.7; 4. 17. 2. Caesar supported Memmius (Cic. Q. F. 3. 2. 3), and was much annoyed over his behaviour (Cic. Att. 4. 17. 3). For a detailed account see R. Holmes, R. R. ii, p. 153.

. Gaius Licinius Calvus, celebrated as orator and poet, friend of Catullus. A specimen of his epigrams is given in 49. He also attacked Tigellius, a creature of Caesar's (Porph. in Hor. Sat. 1. 3. 1). See also Sen. Contr. 7.4.6-7.

. Caesar's praefectus fabrorum (Plin. 36. 48), an eques from Formiae, who had acquired great wealth through Caesar's favour (Catull. 293 573 Cic. Att. 7. 7. 6; 13. 52. 1). Catullus accuses Caesar of an unnatural passion for him. ...
, 'accept the hospitality of'. Caesar had presumably been the guest of Catullus's father during his command in Cisalpine Gaul. Cp. also Tac. Ann. 4. 34. 8.

div.p: § 1. piratas. See 4. 1-2.

p.note: . Suetonius alone records this 'mercy'.
. See note on I. 2 commutare latebras.

. His amanuensis. Cp. the phrases servus (or libertus) a rationibus, ab epistulis, a libellis. Cp. Plut. Caes. 17. 3 (on authority of Oppius) ὠχεῖτο δὲ μεθ᾽ ἡμέραν ἐπὶ τὰ φρούρια καὶ τὰς πόλεις καὶ τοὺς χάρακας ἑνὸς αὐτῷ συγκαθημένου παιδὸς τῶν ὑπογράφειν ἅμα διώκοντος εἰθισμένων.
. A 'plain' death, as opposed to crucifixion, the ordinary penalty for slaves.

div.p: § 2. P. Clodium. See 6. 2.

p.note: . Daughter of M. Aurelius Cotta and Rutilia, and sister of the Aurelius Cotta mentioned in I. 2. She was a woman of the highest character, and did her best to keep her daughter-in-law out of mischief (Plut. Caes. 9. 1). She is described as being a most devoted mother (Tac. Dial. 28; Plut. 9. 10; cp. also Suet. 13). She died shortly before her grand-daughter Iulia in 54 B. С. (26. 1).

. Caesar had two sisters: (i) the elder Iulia wife of (a) Q. Pedius, (6) L. Pinarius (cp. 83. 2); (ii) the younger Iulia wife of M. Atius Balbus, grandmother of Augustus, through her daughter Atia. There is nothing to show which sister is meant. For her evidence cp. also Schol. Bob., p. 337 Or.

. Cp. Plut. Caes. 10. 4 μάρτυς δὲ οὐδὲν ἔφη τῶν κατὰ τοῦ Κλωδίου γιγνώσκειν (cp. negavit...comperisse above). ὡς δὲ τοῦ λόγου παραδόξου φανέντος ὁ κατήγορος ἠρώτησε 'πῶς οὖν ἀπεπέμψω τὴν γυναῖκα ;᾿ ῾ὅτι᾿ ἔφη 'τὴν ἐμὴν ἠξίουν μηδὲ ὑπονοηθῆναι. Cp. also Plut. Cic. 29. 3; Dio 37.45.2; Cic. Att. 1. 13. 3.

div.p: § 1. clementiam. Cp. (i) Caesar's own professions; Cic. Att. 9.7 (Letter of Caesar to Oppius) haec nova sit ratio vincendi ut misericordia et liberalitate nos muniamus; Plut. Caes. 48. 2 τοῖς δὲ φίλοις εἰς ῾Ρώμην ἔγραφεν ὅτι τῆς νίκης ἀπολαύοι τοῦτο μέγιστον, τὸ σώζειν ἀεὶ τῶν πεπολεμηκότων πολιτῶν ἀυτῷ ; 54. 1 εἶπε δ᾽ οὖν ῾ὦ Κάτων, φθονῶ σοι τοῦ θανάτου· καὶ γὰρ σύ μοι τῆς σωτηρίας ἐφθονήσας (also Plut. Cat. 72. 2; Dio 43. 15. 2 sqq.). (ii) Testimony of others; Cic. Att. 8. 13 (49 B. C.); Fam. 4. 4. 2. 3 nec id victoris vitio, quo nihil moderatius (46 в. с.); Pro Marcello and Pro Ligario passim; Dio 41. 62. 2 (Caesar kills only senators and knights who broke parole (48 в.С.)); 44.45 (Antony's funeral oration; Caesar burns Pompey's correspondence); Sallust, Cat. 54. 3; Flor. 2. 13.90; Sen. de Ira 2. 23.4; Vell. Pat. 2. 52. 5. (iii) Acknowledgements; Plut. Caes. 57. 2 καὶ τό γε τῆς Ἐπιεικείας ἱερὸν οὐκ ἀπὸ τρόπου δοκοῦσι χαριστήριον ἐπὶ τῇ πραότητι ψηφίσασθαι; App. 2. 106 καὶ νεὼς ἐψηφίσαντο πολλοὺς αὐτῷ γενέσθαι καθάπερ θεῷ, καὶ κοινὸν ἀυτοῦ καὶ Ἐπιεικείας ἀλλήλους δεξιουμένων; Grueber, Coins R. Rep. in B. M., i, 549 (with figure of temple, 44 B. С.).

p.note: . Cp. В. С. 1. 33. 2 Pompeius discedens ab urbe in senatu dixerat eodem se habiturum loco qui Romae remansissent et qui in Caesaris castris fuissent. Cp., too, Plut. Pomp. 61.3; App. 2. 37; Dio 41. 6. 2; Polyaen. 8. 23. 27; Cic. Att. 8. 1. 4 qui, cum omnes Caesarem metuebamus, ipse eum diligebat, postquam ipse metuere coepit, putat omnes hostes illi esse oportere; 9.7. 3 mirandum enim in modum Gnaeus noster Sullani regni similitudinem concupivit; 9. 10. 6 sullaturit animus et proscripturit iam diu; 9. 11. 3; 10.7. 1. For atrocities of the Pompeians cp. B. C. 3. 8. 3; 14.3; 71.4; B. Afr. 46. 2; Oros. 6. 15. 26.
: e.g. such as Sulpicius (cp. 29. 1), whom Caesar appointed governor of Achaia (Cic. Fam. 4. 4. 2).
, 'had promoted to be centurions'.
: i. e. Pompey.

div.p: § 2. motis, 'were under discussion'.

p.note: . Cp. В. С. 1. 74-76. In the absence of A. and P. many of their troops crossed the Segre and fraternized with the Caesarians. Informal negotiations were opened through their senior centurions. Then A. and P., learning what was taking place, returned. A. was ready to acquiesce. P. set himself to restore discipline, attacked the Caesarians who had visited his camp, and put to death all who had harboured an enemy. Caesar sent back the Pompeians in his camp with the exception of some tribunes who voluntarily joined him.
. Suetonius is inaccurate. Petreius had never thought of surrender and the words apply only to Afranius.

. Again an exaggeration. Caesar would have been perfidious if he had used force against the men who had been discussing surrender. Petreius can hardly be blamed for using armed force to restore discipline, and save a desperate situation.

. Cp. Caesar's summary of his own words to his men before the battle (B. C. 3. 90. 2) neque se unquam abuti militum sanguine neque rempublicam alterutro exercitu privare voluisse, and again his treatment of the remnant of the Pompeians (В. С. 3. 98) consolatus consurgere iussit et pauca apud eos de lenitate sua locutus, quo minore essent timore, omnes conservavit militibusque suis commendavit, ne qui eorum violaretur neu quid sui desiderarent. Cp. also App. 2.80; Flor. 2. 13. 50; Polyaen. 8. 23. 29; Dio 41. 1-4.

div.p: §3. Afranio. Cp. 34.2. Caesar had let Afranius and his troops go after Ilerda without imposing any conditions. He had rejoined Pompey (B. C. 3. 83. 2; 88. 3). Afranius and Faustus Sulla were captured by Sittius in Africa. According to B. Afr. 95 they were killed by the soldiers, according to Dio (43. 12. 2) by Caesar's orders. Florus (2. 13. 90) and Orosius (6. 16. 5) agree with Dio. With regard to the statement that they were the only Pompeians slain by Caesar's orders, there are divergent statements. Appian (2. 100) says that he put to death all of the 300 that had acted as senate whom he could find; Plutarch (Caes. 53. 3) that he killed a number of consulares and praetorii; the author of B. Afr. (85.9) that there was a general massacre after Thapsus, despite the efforts of Caesar to stop it. Florus further asserts that Pompey's daughter, the wife of Faustus Sulla, was with her two sons put to death by Caesar's orders; so, too, does Orosius. But B. Afr. (95) and Appian (2.100) explicitly state that they were saved.

p.note: . See on 27. 1. L. Caesare. Son of L. Caesar (cos. 64) and a distant cousin of the dictator. He was on Pompey's side in 49 B. C. (B. Civ. 1. 8. 2), when he approached lulius with a conciliatory, but inconclusive, message from Pompey (Cicero-Att. 7. 13a. 1-speaks with great scorn both of message and messenger, whom he styles non hominem sed scopas solutas). He was in charge of ten Pompeian warships

div.p: off the coast of Africa (B. C. 2. 23. 3) later in the same year. He is next heard of in 46 B. C. Captured after Thapsus, he was pardoned by the victor according to B. Afr. 89. 4. Dio (43. 12. 3) explicitly denies that he was pardoned. Cicero (Fam. 9. 7. 1) comments nam ut audivi de L. Caesare filio, mecum ipse quid hic mihi faciet patri?' itaque non desino apud istos qui nunc dominantur cenitare. The words are cryptic; Cicero may be optimistic or pessimistic, may refer to Caesar's mercy or his ruthlessness. (Tyrrell takes the former view (Corr. Cicero, ed. 1, iv, 295), Purser (ibid., ed. 2, p. 376) the latter.] Either is possible. But itaque non desino, etc., fits in best with the optimistic view. See R. Holmes, R. R. iii, pp. 271-2. If L. Caesar was put to death by Iulius, it may have been due to his having learned of the outrage mentioned by Suetonius (below), or L. Caesar may like other Pompeians have fallen a victim of the fury of the soldiers (see above on Afranio).

§ 4. cunctis redire. Cp. Vell. Pat. 2. 56. 1; Dio 43. 50. 1-2; Plut. Caes. 57. 2. Appian (2. 107) adds πλὴν ἐπ᾿ ἀνηκέστοις, which is true. Cp. the case of Cimber's brother (Plut. Caes. 66. 2). Dio adds the detail that he restored dowries to widows and part of estates to orphans (44 B. C.). Of individual cases the following may be noted: M. Brutus and Cassius (Cic. Fam. 6. 6. 10, etc.), M. Marcellus (Fam. 4. 4. 3-4; 6. 6. 10), Tullius Cimber (Cic. Fam. 6. 12. 2); Ligarius (Plut. Cic. 39. 3), Varro (Suet. 44. 2). See also notes on individual conspirators (80. 4, and following chapters). statuas L. Sullae atque Pompei. Overthrown on receipt of news of Pharsalus (Dio 42. 18.2). For their restoration cp. Dio 43. 49. 1 (44 В. С.); Plut. Caes. 57. 3 (where Cicero is recorded to have said that Caesar was thus providing for the safety of his own statues); Plut. Cic. 40. 2; Polyaen. 6.23. 31. Dio (42. 18.2) states that these statues stood upon the rostra. In that case the statue of Pompey at the feet of which Caesar was killed cannot be included in the number, as it stood in the Porticus Pompei (Plut. Brut. 14. 1).

div.note: Continuation of source § 4, separated at the explicit lemma coniurationes to align with Ihm 75.5.

p.note: . See 74. I (Philemon). Cp. also Cassius' design in 47 B. C. (Cic. Phil. 2. 26), Antony's alleged plots in 45 B. с. (Phil. 2.34 and 74; Plut. Ant. 13); suspicions of plots (Cic. Marc. 21); Dio 44. 15. 1.

. Cp. Cic. Fam. 6.5-7. The book is one which Cicero will not let out of his own hands (5.1); its title is Querelae (6. 8); in 7 Caecina expresses his own alarm, though he is more afraid of Caesar's verdict as a critic, than of any vindictive action (74); he concludes (7. 6), quod ad librum attinet ... peto a te ne exeat, aut ita corrigas ne mihi noceat. This Caecina was the son of Cicero's former client (pro Caecina); see Pauly-Wissowa, iii, 1, cols. 1237-8.
. Freedman of Pompey, who was his pupil in rhetoric (Suet. Gr. 27). He wrote Pompey's biography. Perhaps identical

div.p: with M. Otacilius Pitholaus ; cp. Macr. 2. 2. 13 M. Otacilius Pitholaus, cum Caninius Rebilus uno tantum die consul fuisset, dixit ' ante flamines, nunc consules Diales fiunt.

§ 1. honores nimios. 46 B. C. Supplicatio of forty days, extra lictors at triumph, praefectura morum for three years, dictatorship for ten years, curule chair in senate with consuls, princeps senatus, presidency of games in Circus, right to appoint magistrates, his chariot placed opposite the statue of Jupiter, his statue mounted on a 'likeness of the inhabited world', with inscription styling him a demigod (Dio 43. 14). 45 B. C. Triumphal garb and laurel wreath at all games (Dio 43. 43. 1), permanent title of imperator to descend to his sons and grandsons (43.44. 2), offer of magistracies even those of the plebs, consul for ten years, commander-in-chief, supreme financial control, ivory statue and chariot to appear at public games with the statues of the gods, statue erected in temple of Quirinus, inscribed INVICTO DEO (cp.
